content:
Village archive digitisation, first Saturday in the parish hall at Hollin Green. Ferdinand Quayle, who has kept the parish chest for thirty years, unlocked the oak cupboard at nine and pulled out the first of the registers. The plan is to photograph everything before the damp gets it: baptisms from 1741, burials, the vestry minute books, a run of overseers' accounts, and a tin trunk of loose papers that nobody has ever catalogued. There were five of us, and Ferdinand insisted on cotton gloves for the paper and bare hands for the parchment, which he says the grease of a clean finger does no harm to.

Our kit was modest. I brought the copy stand made from a drawing board and a length of aluminium tube, Priyanka brought her mirrorless camera and two daylight lamps on tripods, and Osgood brought a laptop with a spreadsheet already set up with columns for volume, folio, date range and condition. We agreed a naming scheme before anyone touched a page: parish code, volume number, folio, and the mark r or v for the side. Priyanka pointed out that a sloppy scheme now would cost us a week of renaming later, and she was right.

The first register is a small, fat book bound in limp vellum, with the spine split and the pages cockled like a crisp packet. The early entries are in a secretary hand that took me a full minute per line to read, and the ink has gone the colour of weak tea. Ferdinand read aloud from it while we worked. He has a story for nearly every surname: the Pargeters who ran the ferry, the widow Hesketh who was fined for keeping geese on the common, a curate who recorded the weather beside every burial for one winter and then stopped, as if the cold had beaten him too.

By eleven we had a rhythm. Osgood turned, I squared the page under the glass, Priyanka fired, and Ferdinand wrote the folio on a slip of acid-free card that sat in the corner of each frame. We managed forty-one pages in the first hour, which Priyanka worked out to be about a minute and a half each, and then a run of stained pages slowed us right down. The stains turned out to be candle grease from some long-ago clerk who read his entries at night, and Ferdinand was rather moved by it.

The vestry minute book was the surprise of the day. Halfway through the 1790s there is a heated dispute about whether to buy a second bell or mend the church roof, and the vote is recorded name by name. The roof lost by four to seven. The rector at the time, a Reverend Ambrose Tull, wrote a marginal note in a hurt little hand saying that the rain would remember who had voted. Osgood photographed that page three times because he liked it so much.

At lunch, which was sausage rolls and a flask of tea on the churchyard wall, we talked about where the files should end up. The county record office has offered to hold a copy, but their terms want the originals deposited too, and Ferdinand will not hear of it. The compromise Priyanka suggested is a public portal run by the village society, with a second copy on two external drives, one kept at her house and one with the treasurer, plus a third copy at the record office of the images only. Ferdinand agreed to think about it, which from him is nearly a yes.

The afternoon went to the tin trunk. It held bundles of receipts tied with tape, a school attendance ledger from the 1880s, several hand-drawn maps of the glebe land, and a bundle of wartime ration book counterfoils that someone had kept for no obvious reason. The maps are gorgeous, with tiny trees drawn in ink and field names such as Long Piddle and Cold Comfort. I made a note to ask the older residents whether any of the field names are still used, because if they are, we should record who says them and how they are pronounced.

We finished at four with two hundred and eighty images across the first register and part of the vestry book. Checking a random sample of twenty at the laptop, I found three slightly out of focus and one where a thumb had strayed into the corner. Priyanka wants a rule that every session ends with a proper check of a tenth of the frames before the pages go back in the cupboard. We agreed, and I volunteered to write the one-page procedure.

Ferdinand locked up and gave each of us a packet of humbugs from his coat, a habit I gather goes back to his years as a schoolmaster. Next session is in three weeks, on a Saturday when the hall is free of the toddler group, and we will start on the burial registers and the overseers' accounts. The number to remember from today is that at the current pace, roughly two hundred images an hour with five people, the whole chest is about sixty hours of work, or ten Saturdays. Ferdinand said he had waited thirty years and could manage ten more Saturdays.

Regatta committee notes, the Marlow Reach Head and Sprint weekend, entered as the studio crew. Present: Avery, Blake, Colm, Sanne, Ilse, and Gerrit from the boat club, who has coached us for six evenings and now regrets it. The purpose of the meeting was to settle who rows what, agree the transport plan for the eight, and decide whether the studio should spend the money on matching racing kit or make do with the club's spare vests. It ran ninety minutes and Gerrit had brought a tray of flapjacks, which improved the mood considerably.

The crew. Gerrit has watched us on the water and thinks the studio can field one coxed four for the novice sprint and take part in the mixed head race in a borrowed eight. For the four he recommends Colm at stroke, because he is the only one who keeps a steady rhythm without counting under his breath, Blake at three, Ilse at two, and me at bow. Sanne coxes, and at forty-eight kilograms she is under the club's minimum weight for the boat, so she has to carry a sandbag of two kilograms in the stern, which she has agreed to with dignity.

Gerrit's technical points were blunt. We rush the slide, which shortens the stroke and makes the boat check on every recovery. Blake sits late and lets the blade skim the water rather than burying it. I catch crabs when I am tired. His remedy is a routine of pause drills in the last twenty minutes of each session, with the boat held level at the finish, and he wants us to stop looking at each other's oars, which is apparently the most common reason for bad timing among amateurs.

Transport was the part that took longest. The club's trailer holds one boat and its riggers. The regatta site is a hundred and twenty kilometres away, and the only slot to launch and rig is seven on Saturday morning. Ilse offered her father's estate car for the oars and bags, and Colm said he could borrow a minibus from his cousin's roofing firm. We settled on leaving at four-thirty with the trailer behind Gerrit's pickup, which he says can pull it on the motorway without complaint provided nobody sits in the boat.

On kit, Gerrit steered us away from expensive all-in-one suits. He said a racing kit that fits badly is worse than a mismatched vest that fits well, and that the rules only require the crew to be dressed alike, which the club's spare navy vests satisfy. Sanne priced a run of eleven matching caps with the studio mark for the supporters, at four pounds each, and the committee agreed to the caps but not the suits. Blake's motion to also buy a foghorn was politely declined.

Race format was explained with a whiteboard. The sprint is over five hundred metres, two boats at a time, with the winners going into a bracket; we expect to be knocked out in the first round by a crew from the fire service who train twice weekly. The head race is a time trial over four kilometres, boats set off ten seconds apart, and it is the one Gerrit wants us to treat seriously because our time is the only thing recorded. He thinks twenty-one minutes is within reach and that anything under twenty-two would be a personal triumph.

Safety got its share of the meeting. Everyone must wear a buoyancy aid in the launch, cox included, and the club insists that each of us demonstrates the recovery drill from a capsize in the shallow end of the pool before we row on a river with any current. The pool session is booked for the Thursday before, and Ilse, who swims, says she will bring the whistle. Sanne raised the question of what to do if a boat overlapping ours forces us wide; Gerrit's answer was to hold the course, call clearly, and complain afterwards to a steward who will not care.

Spectators and supper. Twenty-six people have said they will come, and there is a pub at the bend of the river with a yard that Gerrit swears has a view of the last two hundred metres. Avery volunteered to book two long benches. Blake will be in charge of the flag and, in an unprecedented act of trust, the studio bell. Colm will take photographs, mostly of Sanne looking heroic in a lifejacket.

Decisions recorded. Entry fee paid, ninety-six pounds for the pair of races. Caps ordered, eleven. Practice sessions Tuesday and Thursday at seven, weather permitting, with the pause-drill routine. Departure at four-thirty on the day, meeting at the boat club. The one thing Gerrit asked, and it is worth writing in bold, is that no one drinks anything stronger than tea the night before, since a hangover on the slide is a very expensive lesson for everyone in the boat.

Bee log, the second half of June, the west hive at the allotment plot. I opened the colony on Sunday morning after the dew had lifted, in a light suit, with the smoker lit on a handful of dry hessian. The hive had been queenright in April when I marked the queen with a yellow dot, and I wanted to check that she was still laying and that the workers had not started to build queen cells in the corners of the frames. The morning was still and warm, about eighteen degrees, which is the ideal temperature for a first look after a rainy week.

The top super came off with a soft crack of wax. The bees were calm; I gave them two puffs and they went back to their work. The honey stores are filling well: the top box has four frames of nearly capped nectar from the lime trees along the lane and a half-frame of darker honey that I think comes from the bramble. I held up a frame and shook it lightly; nothing flew out, which means the honey is ripe enough. I left the top box on and moved on to the brood box below.

In the brood box I found the queen on the third frame, a long amber body with the yellow dot showing clear, walking calmly through the workers. The brood pattern is solid, with only a scattering of empty cells, and I estimated eight frames with brood in all stages. Eggs, one per cell and standing upright like tiny grains of rice, told me she had laid within the last three days. There were no queen cups with eggs in them. I felt relieved, since swarming season is a nervous business for a second-year beekeeper.

The one worry was the varroa count. I slid the board under the mesh floor that had been in place for a week and counted the fallen mites in a square of ten centimetres by ten. There were nine, which extrapolated across the board gives a natural drop of roughly two a day, still under the threshold of three a day where the textbooks say to take action. I will check again in ten days, and if the number climbs I have thymol strips ordered for the end of the season, after the honey is off.

I fed nothing. In May I gave the colony two litres of light syrup because the cold snap had kept them in for a fortnight, but now the forage is plentiful and syrup would only crowd the brood nest. What I did do was add a second brood-box excluder to the store cupboard and set out a shallow dish of water with pebbles in it at the corner of the plot, since the bees had been visiting the neighbour's dripping tap and I did not want a complaint. By noon there were a dozen drinking at the dish.

Friday I had a short talk with Mr Adeyemi at the next plot, who keeps two hives of his own and has been at it for twenty years. He told me his rule of thumb: never work the bees in a thunder mood, never wear a scent, and never argue with a colony about where it wants to build. He also said the lime flow is early this year, by a week, and that I should be ready for the supers to fill faster than I expect. I promised him a jar in return for the tip, which he waved away and then reminded me of twice.

Reading list for the next fortnight. I have borrowed a book on drone-comb management from the library and marked the pages on queen replacement. I have also promised the association secretary a short talk at the September meeting on a first-timer's mistakes, and I have a draft list of eleven: forgetting to check the water, using the smoker too hot, splitting a colony too late, leaving the entrance reducer on through a flow, dropping a frame, wearing shorts, and more that are best left for the evening in question.

The number I want to remember from this visit is thirty-two, which is the count of frames I now own including spares, of which twelve are drawn comb and the rest still foundation. That gives me scope to expand into a second brood box next spring if the colony overwinters well. For now, I closed up, wiped the hive tool, and put the smoker out in a bucket of sand. The whole inspection took thirty-five minutes and I did not get stung once, which I will not write down in the group chat for fear of tempting fate.

Museum volunteer rota meeting, the industrial heritage museum in the old mill at Denby Weir. Four of the studio team have signed up for the second Saturday of each month as stewards, and this was the first planning session with Rosalind Achterberg, the volunteer coordinator. We met in the mill office above the weaving shed, a long low space with a view of the wheel pit, and she opened by telling us that the museum has three paid staff and sixty volunteers, of whom a quarter are over seventy and a fifth are students.

The job of a steward is mostly to stand in one gallery and answer questions. Rosalind assigned each of us a home gallery: Avery gets the water-power gallery with the working model of the overshot wheel, Blake gets the spinning gallery, Sanne and Colm share the print and pattern gallery by the entrance. She stressed that we are not expected to know everything, and that the best answer to a hard question is to say we will find out and then write it on the card by the door. The cards are read on Monday by the curator, who answers them and sometimes puts the question on the museum's blog.

Rota rules. Shifts run in two blocks, ten till one and one till four, with a half-hour handover in which the outgoing steward briefs the next. Nobody works more than one block at a time on their own. Every steward wears a green apron and a name badge, and must sign the visitors' book in the morning and out at the end of the day. Rosalind said lateness is the commonest failing, and she asked us to text her by half past nine if anything goes wrong so that she can call one of the reserves, of whom there are nine.

Safety and access. The mill has a lift to the first floor but not to the wheel pit, so a steward at the pit end must be ready to direct wheelchair users to the video display at the top of the ramp. The looms are demonstrated only by trained operators, on Sundays, and stewards must never switch anything on. There is a first-aid box in the office and a defibrillator by the shop, and Rosalind will run a fifteen-minute walk-through of it at the start of our first shift. She has also asked us not to lean on the handrail by the pit because the bolts loosened last winter and the repair is scheduled for March.

Training. New stewards shadow an old hand for two shifts before they are on their own, and the pairing is chosen by Rosalind. Ours are: Avery with Mr Lomax, a retired millwright who knows every belt in the building; Blake with Beatrix, a student who gives tours in French; Sanne with Dorothea, the museum's longest-serving volunteer, who has been coming since 1994. Colm asked to shadow anyone who has a good biscuit supply. Rosalind said she would see what could be done.

The visitor numbers were surprisingly specific. In the last year the museum had eleven thousand four hundred visitors, of which about three thousand were school groups, and the busiest day was the Easter Monday with six hundred and twelve people. The quiet months are January and February, when a steward may see only thirty people in a whole block. Rosalind said the quiet days are her favourite for training because the newcomers can practise their patter on staff.

We talked about what the studio could offer beyond stewarding. Blake suggested a small kiosk of interactive displays for the spinning gallery, which the studio could build in its own time; Rosalind was cautiously keen but said any equipment must pass the museum's electrical check, which takes a fortnight. Avery offered to help the curator move the guest cards and questions from paper to a shared spreadsheet, since the current system is a shoebox. She accepted that on the spot and mentioned that the shoebox is nearly forty years old.

Rosalind closed with the dates. First shifts are the second Saturdays of April, May and June. Induction and the defibrillator walk-through happen on the Tuesday evening before the first, at six, and tea is provided. Aprons will be in the office in a labelled bag for each of us, and we are to bring sturdy shoes because the stone floors are cold and uneven. She made us promise not to touch the guest cards until the curator has read them, and we promised.

Science fair jury notes: the Ashdown District Junior Science Fair, where Avery and Blake sat on the panel as sponsor judges. The fair filled the sports hall at Ashdown Middle School with about eighty projects from pupils aged eleven to fourteen, and each of the six judges was given a clipboard, a scoring sheet with four headings, and a badge that said Judge in a font that made it look like a warning. The head of science, Mrs Vandermeer, gave us a briefing on the stage at ten: judging is from ten-thirty to twelve-thirty, scores must be in by one, and no judge may tell a child their score.

The rubric had four headings scored out of five: the question, the method, the evidence and the presentation. Mrs Vandermeer explained that the question is the most important, and that a modest question honestly answered beats an ambitious one that cannot be tested. She had a small speech about the difference between a fair test and a demonstration, which I wish I had heard at school. She also told us that a project with a working volcano would be marked exactly like any other and that we should not be bribed by fizzing.

My first stand belonged to Tobias, twelve, who had asked whether paper aeroplanes fly further after being folded with a crease pressed by a thumbnail or by a ruler. He had folded a hundred and twenty planes, thrown them along a school corridor with a tape measure on the floor, and recorded the result in a notebook with a mean and a range for each method. The ruler-creased planes flew a mean of nine point four metres against seven point one for the thumbnail. He told me he was a little embarrassed that the difference was so obvious. I asked him how he would check that it was not the thrower, and he said he had asked his sister to throw half of them, which is the sort of answer that earns full marks on method.

Next was a girl called Imogen, thirteen, who had grown cress under four coloured filters and measured the height after a week. She had good photographs and a neat graph, but she had put all four trays on the same shelf and I asked whether the shelf had equal light. She went pink and admitted that the tray under the red film had been near a radiator. I marked her method down and wrote a friendly note suggesting a repeat with the trays rotated daily. She looked genuinely delighted to have something to fix.

The judges met over sandwiches at twelve-thirty to compare scores. There was good agreement about the top three, an unusually calm discussion for a panel, and one argument about a project on whether music affects the speed at which people solve a jigsaw puzzle. Blake was for it on the grounds of enthusiasm, while the retired chemist among us, Dr Brannigan, was against on the grounds of eight participants and no control. We eventually settled on a commendation instead of a place, and Dr Brannigan wrote a paragraph on how to recruit thirty participants.

The winners were announced at two by the head teacher. First place went to a pair of twins, Hanne and Jonas, aged eleven, for a project measuring how the salt content of a sandbag affected how quickly it dried after rain; second to Tobias; third to a boy named Achille, who had built a device to count how many times the school gate was opened at lunchtime. The sponsor prize of a hundred pounds in book tokens, offered by the studio, went to Imogen for the best failure, which we felt was a true compliment.

Afterwards Mrs Vandermeer took us aside. She said that most of the projects are copied from the internet, and that the ones that stand out are those where the child has changed something on purpose to see what happens. She would like judges to stay for a full morning next year, and to come to the school in the spring to give a talk to the whole year group. Blake said he would do it if he could bring a demonstration involving a large amount of custard. She agreed with a fixed expression.

The takeaway I wrote on the drive back is that the number of samples matters more than the cleverness of the idea, and that children ask better questions than their answers suggest. I also noted that Imogen's cress had grown a mean of eleven millimetres taller under the blue film, which is exactly the sort of detail I have promised to look up. The school will send us the final scores by post at the end of the month, and the twins' project may go forward to the regional final in May.

Tram museum restoration day, notes from the shed at Cranford Depot. Twelve of us from the studio spent a Saturday helping the volunteer restoration team with car number sixty-three, a four-wheel tram built in 1911 that ran on the Cranford lines until the last service in 1952 and then spent thirty years as a summerhouse. It arrived at the depot in pieces, and the crew has been working on it for six years. Our job was to strip and paint the lower saloon panels, but first, of course, we needed the safety talk.

The talk was given by Delphine Marchetti, the shed foreman, a woman in a blue boiler suit with a voice built for cavernous spaces. She told us that the shed has an inspection pit that is not to be approached without a hat, that the overhead wire is dead but should still be treated as live, and that a heavy tool dropped on the floor of a tram makes a sound that upsets her more than it upsets the tram. Hi-vis and steel toecaps were issued; Colm got a size ten and complained about the size until she gave him an eleven.

The tram itself is astonishing. It has a varnished timber body with teak pillars, a curved stair to the upper deck, and a driver's platform open to the weather, with a brass controller handle the size of a rolling pin. The lower saloon has a cracked ceiling and eleven of the original twenty-two seats. The mahogany panels are covered in nine layers of paint, most of them a colour that Delphine called municipal cream. Under it is the original livery of chocolate and cream, which we were going to reveal, in patches, by scraping.

We were split into teams. Sanne, Blake and I worked on the lower panels with chemical stripper and plastic scrapers, while Colm and the others sanded the rails and cleaned the brass fittings with a soft cloth and a rather dangerous-smelling polish. The stripper had to sit for twenty minutes before scraping and we were told to keep the fumes away from our faces. The first swatch that we revealed was a warm brown with a delicate gold line, and Blake, who had been cynical, said quite quietly that it looked like a proper thing.

Lunch was in the depot canteen, a converted wagon with a kettle and a plate of cold sausages. A volunteer named Hubert, who is eighty-one and has been coming since the museum opened, told us how the tram was found: a farmer had used the body as a summerhouse for his grandchildren and refused all offers until he died. The family then gave it to the museum for one pound. Hubert showed us a photograph of it on a lawn, full of hollyhocks, with the trucks nowhere to be seen. He said the trucks had been found in a scrapyard two counties away, under a heap of railings.

In the afternoon Delphine introduced us to the electrics. The wiring had been rewired in 1932 and again in the seventies, and the team is planning a third and final rewire in the winter, using cloth-covered cable to match the original look. She let each of us close a small knife switch on a test bench and watch a lamp glow, which sounds trivial and was one of the most satisfying moments of the day. Sanne asked whether the tram would ever run on the public road; Delphine said only on the museum's own track, which is eight hundred metres long, and only on the open days.

By four we had stripped the offside lower panels and started on the nearside. The paint we removed filled a bucket and a half, and Delphine weighed it on a set of luggage scales for the record: eleven kilograms of nine-layer paint, which she wrote on the wall of the shed in chalk, where a dozen previous measurements sit. We swept up and returned the tools to their outlines on the pegboard, an exercise Delphine takes very seriously, since a missing spanner can hold up an entire week.

The decision at the end was to come back. The restoration team has asked the studio to adopt the car's next task, which is refitting the upper deck seats, and Avery, Colm and Sanne signed up for the next two Saturdays in March. The studio will also sponsor a small plate on the tram's dash, to be engraved with the names of the twelve of us. Delphine says the tram will run for the first time in a hundred and eleven years, on the eleventh of October next year if the boiler inspector is kind, and that we are all invited.

Chess club tournament, the Thornbury Winter Open, notes written the evening after round five. The club rents the upstairs space over the old post office on Tuesdays, and once a year it runs a seven-round rapid tournament with twenty-four entrants, a sixty-minute clock and no increment. I entered in the under-1600 section as one of the lower seeds, which is a polite way of saying I was ranked eleventh of fourteen. My aim was to win two games and lose none to a blunder. The tournament director, Bartholomew Nkemelu, ran the draw at half past six with the air of a magician revealing a card.

Round one was against a young man named Ollie, probably fifteen, who played the Scandinavian and lost a knight to a fork on move fourteen. I was ashamed of how much I enjoyed it. My advantage did not last; I dithered for twenty minutes over a trade that was clearly fine, and in the last ten minutes I had to play on with less than a minute to spare. He resigned with three seconds left on my clock, which I count as a win of a rather nervous kind.

Round two brought me an older opponent, Mrs Ferreira, who has been playing correspondence chess for forty years and treats a rapid game as a kind of insult. She played the Caro-Kann with total composure and slowly squeezed me. On move thirty-one I had to choose between grabbing a pawn and defending a back rank, and I grabbed the pawn, and lost. She was very kind about it afterwards and showed me the winning idea on the board with her long fingers, which was to attack the king before taking anything at all.

Between rounds I ate a plain sandwich in the stairwell, which is the only spot where nobody can see your face. The stairwell is where the real tournament takes place: people whisper opening variations, argue about whether the clock was pressed, and swap stories about a legendary player who once lost on time with a mating attack on the board. Bartholomew wandered through periodically to tell us that we were late, which we were.

Round three was a draw against a quiet man named Alasdair, after a long, careful game in which neither of us dared to take a risk. The endgame was a rook and four pawns each, all on one side, and the position was so balanced that I offered a draw on move fifty-two with about six minutes left on each side. He accepted with a slight bow. It was a good game and I felt proud of the accuracy, though a stronger player would have found a plan to press.

Round four was where I found out what happens when you play a much lower-rated child. The opponent was Priti, twelve, rated about one thousand and two hundred, who moved instantly and beat me in thirty moves with a clean kingside attack. I looked at the game afterwards with her and she said, quite matter-of-factly, that she had studied the opening at home for three weeks. I realised I had not studied anything for three weeks, unless you count reading about the opening in the bath.

Round five, tonight, I got white against a man in a brown pullover named Cornelius who had been on a winning streak. We reached a queenless middlegame and I found a nice knight manoeuvre to d5 that won a pawn. He fought hard and made a real mess of the last fifteen moves. The clock showed four minutes for me and ninety seconds for him at the end. He shook my hand with a look I recognised, the look of somebody who wants to be alone with his thoughts.

My tally after five rounds is two wins, one draw and two losses, so two and a half points, which places me around eighth in the section. Two more rounds on Tuesday and Thursday. Bartholomew, closing the evening, told everyone that the prizes are a small trophy for the winner in each section and a bottle of sherry for the best game, decided by a panel of three. I doubt it will be me. The number to remember is that the tournament fee was eleven pounds, and that I have spent nearly that much on sandwiches over the week.

Lighthouse open day, organising notes from the meeting with the trust at the old station on Skerry Point. Blake and Avery represented the studio, which has volunteered to help run the annual open weekend and to build a simple visitor counter for the entrance. The trust's chair is Ingeborg Tallis, a retired ferry captain with a handshake like a bosun's knot, and she took us up the tower before we sat down, because she says nobody can plan an open day without climbing the stairs at least once.

There are a hundred and twenty-eight steps to the lantern gallery, in a cast-iron spiral with a rope handrail. Ingeborg counted aloud in a gravelly voice for the first thirty and then went silent, which I took as mercy. At the top the lens is a huge many-faceted glass beehive taller than a person, which she says has not been lit since 1976 but which the trust hopes to turn on for a single night in the autumn. The view was a slate sea with a line of white where the tide meets the rocks, and a small boat working a lobster pot near the reef.

Visitor flow was the main topic. The stairs hold twelve people at a time, and the gallery only eight, so the trust runs a system of ticketed slots of twenty minutes with a steward at the bottom and another at the top. Last year, on the busiest day, the queue reached the car park, and a family from Aberdeen waited ninety minutes only to be told the gallery was full. Ingeborg wants this year to run smoothly and hopes that an honest counter at the door will let stewards release visitors in batches rather than trickling them in.

The counter. Blake proposed a simple design: a small box at the door with a pressure mat under a rubber runner and a display that shows how many people are inside. Ingeborg listened to the plan with her eyes half shut, and then asked whether it would work in salt spray and a gale. Blake said the enclosure would be sealed, and that a hand-cranked backup with a paper tally sheet would sit beside it. She nodded and said that the paper sheet was the wisest thing she had heard all morning.

Other jobs. The trust needs a volunteer to run the tea urn in the old oil store, a team to manage the car park on the grass field, and someone to lead a children's trail around the compound, with clues hidden behind the fog signal and inside the winch house. Avery offered to draw the trail map, since the clue cards need a friendly, hand-drawn look. The trust also asked whether the studio could manage a short recording of the keeper's diary entries from the 1920s, read aloud, to play on a loop in the lower lobby.

The diaries themselves are a fine thing. Ingeborg brought out a green cloth-bound book from the trust's cupboard and read us a page from a storm in January 1927, in which the keeper, a man named Alfred Rudge, noted that the sea had thrown a boulder the size of a dinghy over the wall and that his wife had baked through the night to keep the family calm. The tone is drily practical; he wrote, at the bottom of the page, that the light had not failed and that he had a cold. Avery took photographs for the reading project.

Money. The trust's budget for the weekend is nine hundred pounds, mostly for insurance and the toilet hire, and it collects about two thousand three hundred from admission and the shop. Ingeborg was clear that she does not want the studio's help to become an expense and that she would rather have three afternoons of honest labour than a cheque. We agreed on three volunteer afternoons in the run-up, one for the counter, one for painting the railings, and one for the map.

At the door she gave us each a small enamel badge of the lighthouse and told us that the weekend of the open days is the last in September, subject to weather and to the ferry. She pointed out that the whole enterprise depends on somebody remembering to bring the key to the lantern, which was left in a pocket in 2019, and that we were now formally responsible for reminding her. We said we would put it in the calendar with an alarm.

Glacier hike write-up, the Fjaerland ice tongue, a guided day with three strangers and one very patient guide. I had wanted to walk on a glacier for years without ever finding the nerve, and when the guiding company had a cancellation for the Thursday I said yes before I could think about it. The office was a wooden hut beside the car park at the foot of the valley, with a rack of crampons, a shelf of helmets and a hand-painted sign saying that the ice has no opinion about your plans. Our guide was called Solveig, forties, weathered, with a laugh that carried across the moraine.

The kit check took twenty minutes and Solveig did it as if she were packing for a long expedition rather than a six-hour outing. Each of us got a harness, a helmet, an ice axe with a leash, and a pair of mountaineering boots that were a half-size too large, which she fixed with an extra pair of socks. She showed us how to fit the crampons: heel bail first, then the toe strap, then a hard tug to check that nothing moved. The other three walkers were a retired couple from Leeds, Malcolm and Jean, and a young Dutch engineer named Rutger, who asked more questions about the physics of ice than anyone had planned for.

The approach was a forty-minute march along a gravel path beside a milky river the colour of skimmed dairy produce. The valley floor is littered with boulders the glacier dropped when it was larger, and Solveig pointed out a line on the far slope where the ice stood in her grandfather's time. She said it has retreated about a kilometre in her own lifetime. The moraine crunched under the boots like a wet beach. At the edge of the ice we stopped, put on the crampons, and stood in a circle while she gave the rules: walk with feet apart, keep the ice axe in the uphill hand, never step in the blue water, and never, ever stand below a wall of ice.

Walking on the glacier is stranger than I had expected. The surface is not smooth but corrugated with rills and small hummocks, dusted with black grit that heats in the sun and melts tiny pits. The crampons bite with a squeaky crunch and you feel unnaturally safe, as if wearing something that was made for the job, which of course you are. The ice itself, where it has been cut by meltwater, glows a startling turquoise, and in the deeper crevasses the colour goes to an electric blue that I have only ever seen in photographs. Solveig let us lie on our stomachs and look down into a narrow one, sixteen metres deep by her rope, where a thread of water ran with a faint tinkling like a glass being filled.

Our route wove between the crevasses in a long slow curve. Twice she had us cross a snow bridge, one at a time, on a taut rope, and she explained that in the morning the bridge is hard from the night's frost but that by the afternoon the sun makes it mush. Jean, who is seventy-one and had said she had a fear of heights, was the first across the second one, and she stepped over with such lightness that Malcolm burst into applause. Rutger measured the slope of everything with an app on his phone and announced that the steepest section we crossed was twenty-eight degrees.

Lunch was a flask of soup and a packet of oat cakes, eaten sitting on our packs on a dry patch of ice above a small meltwater lake. Solveig told us a story about a winter she spent working at a hut, when a fox came each evening and sat at a respectful distance until somebody threw it a crust. She also explained the ice's movement: the tongue we were on advances about forty centimetres a day in summer, which is slow enough to be invisible and fast enough to open a new crack in the time it takes to eat a sandwich. I looked at the ground with fresh respect. Solveig added that the local rescue team practises a crevasse extraction twice a year on this very tongue, and that the drill involves a pulley, three people and a stopwatch. Her own record for hauling a dummy out of a slot fifteen metres deep is nine minutes and forty seconds, which she said with the quiet pride of an athlete, and which Rutger promptly worked out was about a metre and a half per minute of vertical lift.

The one adventure of the day was the ice wall. Solveig had a short section of vertical ice about six metres high, rigged with a top rope, and offered anyone who wanted a go at climbing it with two axes and front-pointing crampons. I went second, after Rutger. Kicking the front points into the ice makes a satisfying thunk, and you learn quickly to trust your feet. About four metres up my arms began to burn, and I forgot everything except the next swing. When I reached the anchor I could see for miles down the valley, the fjord silver at the bottom, and I realised I had been holding my breath.

The descent was quiet. We walked back along our own tracks, the light shifting from white to gold, and as we came off the ice we sat on the moraine to remove the crampons. Solveig collected our gear into a sack and wrote each of our names in the ledger with the total time on the ice, which came to four hours and ten minutes. She asked us to put a stone on the cairn at the bottom of the trail, a custom that has been going for years and now stands the height of a small person.

Practical notes for a future trip, since I will forget. Warm layers matter less than dry ones; I sweated through my first base layer on the way in and was cold on the way out. Sunglasses are essential and I had brought a poor pair. Two litres of water was right. The company charges the equivalent of ninety-five pounds for the day, with boots and crampons included, and a tip of ten per cent is customary. Solveig said the busiest week is mid-July, when up to forty people cross the ice in a day, and that she prefers the last week of August when it is nearly empty.

I finished the day with a bowl of fish soup at the hotel by the ferry, staring at the same glacier from a distance, seeing the patch we had walked on as a tiny grey scratch in a great white slope. Malcolm and Jean sat with me and told me about their walks in the Lake District. Rutger left early to catch a bus. In the evening I rang my sister and heard myself talk without stopping for eleven minutes. I did not mention it, but the thing I most wanted to say was that the ice makes a sound, a faint creaking like a ship at anchor, and that I will hear it for a long time.

Pottery kiln firing, a diary of the day at the Longmeadow community studio. I had made eleven pieces over the winter term, mostly mugs and a couple of bowls, and the studio holds a communal glaze firing at the end of each term, in a big electric kiln that the members call the Beast. My pieces had already been bisque fired, which means baked once at a low temperature so that they are hard and porous and ready to take glaze. The glazing happened the previous Thursday, and today was the loading and firing. The studio manager, a soft-spoken woman named Odalys, had asked for help from eight members to load, and I was number six on the list.

Loading a kiln is a puzzle in three dimensions. The Beast has a chamber the size of a small wardrobe with four shelves that sit on posts, and Odalys had a rule: nothing may touch anything else, and nothing may touch the wall. Glaze that melts will glue a piece to whatever it meets, so a mug that sits a finger's width too close to a plate is a disaster. We began with the largest pieces at the bottom, a big platter and a set of storage jars belonging to a retired teacher called Cuthbert, and worked upwards, wiping the foot of each piece with a damp sponge to remove any glaze that would stick to the shelf.

My own pieces were the hardest to place because I had over-glazed. A teal bowl had run in the bisque and left a bead of glaze along the foot ring, which Odalys scraped off with a small blade while giving me a look. She said the number-one mistake of a beginner is to think a thick glaze is a strong glaze. The mugs, thankfully, were fine, and I put three in a row on the third shelf with a fingertip of space between. Cuthbert produced a small tray of cones, little pyramids of ceramic that bend at a known temperature, and set one in a spot where we could see it through the spyhole.

The firing programme is a slow climb. Odalys set it at a hundred and fifty degrees an hour up to six hundred, then two hundred an hour to a thousand and eighty, followed by a fifteen-minute soak and a natural cool. The whole cycle takes about eighteen hours including the cooling, so nobody sees the result until the next day. She warned us that opening a kiln too early can crack the pieces with a sound like small gunshots. Cuthbert, who has done it, said that the sound is worse than the loss.

While the kiln heated, the studio ran its usual Saturday, which meant the throwing benches were full and a dozen people were making things. I watched a girl of about nine learn to centre clay under the guidance of a patient older man, and I listened to a conversation between two members about whether a certain ash glaze is safe for food. The consensus, delivered with the certainty of people who have argued about it before, is that it is fine for a mug and dodgy for anything acidic. I made a note to ask Odalys for the test results on the studio's own glazes.

At three o'clock the first cone began to bend, the smallest one, and Cuthbert whispered like a man at a football match. We all peered through the spyhole at the orange glow inside, a fierce, silent light that looked like the heart of a small sun. The second cone went at about four, and the third, the one that matters, at ten to five. Odalys turned off the power with a click and there was a small cheer. I felt a ridiculous tightness in my chest for something I had spent an entire winter making.

I could not come back the next morning, but Odalys sent a message at noon with a photograph of the shelf, saying that the teal bowl had come out a deep sea green and that one of the mugs had a pinhole in the glaze, which she said she would tell me how to fix. I went in that evening and unloaded the pieces in the empty studio, the shelves still warm to the touch. The green bowl is the best thing I have made. It rings like a bell when I flick it with a nail, a sign that the firing was clean.

Money and admin. Each glaze firing costs the studio about sixty pounds in electricity, split across the pieces by weight; mine came to seven pounds forty. Members pay a term fee of a hundred and thirty-five pounds, which includes clay and glaze, and a second-year member gets a discount. I have promised Odalys that I will help clean the shelves next time, which involves a grinder and a mask, and that I will stop putting my name on the base in permanent marker, since it burns to a smudge.

The thing I will remember is Cuthbert, watching the cone. He said, when the power went off, that in forty years he had never got used to the wait, and that he thinks of it as the most honest part of the craft, because nothing you say or do in the next eighteen hours will change what comes out. I said that sounded like a good way to live. He said it was also a good way to stay calm about a kiln.

Stargazing weekend at the dark-sky campsite near Kielder, notes from the second night. The forecast had been terrible all week and then cleared on Friday afternoon, so we drove up in two cars with a folding telescope, a red torch, and a flask of hot chocolate that would not survive the night. There were nine of us from the astronomy society, camped in a field at the edge of the forest, with a sign that asks visitors to keep white light off after dusk. The camp warden, Fergus, gave us a talk at the gate about the sky being the darkest in England, with a number on the map of a Bortle class of two, which he said in the tone of a man reading a football score.

The set-up on Saturday evening took an hour. Bertrand, who owns the big Dobsonian, a thirty-centimetre mirror on a rocking base, lifted the tube out of the back of his car with the caution of a man carrying a sleeping child. I put up my small refractor on its tripod and aligned the finder by daylight on a distant electricity pylon, which is the trick everyone tells you and nobody does. Nadia laid out a groundsheet, a sleeping bag and a star chart under a dim red light, and lay flat on her back with binoculars, declaring that this is the only way to see the sky properly.

By nine the sky was fully dark, and it was as if somebody had thrown a bag of glitter across the ceiling of the world. The Milky Way stood overhead in a pale mist, with dark lanes running through it, and I could see the Andromeda galaxy with the naked eye as a smudge no bigger than my thumbnail. Someone pointed out the Pleiades, tight as a tiny dipper, and we passed round the binoculars to see how many stars we could count. Nadia got fourteen; Bertrand, who claims to have exceptional eyes, said he counted nineteen and would not be argued with.

The first target in the big telescope was Jupiter, low in the east, and it showed four moons in a line and two dark cloud bands. Everyone gasped, though we have all seen the same picture a hundred times. There is a difference between a picture and light that has been travelling for forty minutes to land in your eye, and Bertrand said as much in a hushed voice. A small girl, the warden's daughter, wandered over in her pyjamas and looked, and was silent for a full minute, and then asked whether the moons had names.

Later we looked at deep-sky objects: the Ring Nebula in Lyra, a small smoke ring of a thing; the double cluster in Perseus, two glittering handfuls of sugar; and the great globular cluster in Hercules, which through Bertrand's mirror resolved into thousands of individual stars. He kept a logbook where he wrote the object, the time, the seeing on a scale of one to five, and a comment. For the globular he wrote five and the comment: oh. I copied the entry into my own notes because it seemed to me the best possible summary.

Around midnight a bank of cloud came in from the west and swallowed the stars one by one. We sat in the dark, drank the last of the chocolate, which by then was cold, and told stories about the strangest thing each of us had ever seen in the sky. Nadia described a fireball that lit up her whole street on a winter night in 2009. Fergus, joining us with his own flask, said that the campsite once had a visitor who saw a satellite flare and rang the police, which led to a long conversation about what the police could do about it.

Sunday morning was wet and grey. We packed away the gear, wiped the dew from every lens with a soft cloth, and ate a proper breakfast in the campsite's wooden hut, which sells a full fry-up for eight pounds fifty. Bertrand, who had not slept, made a tally: we had logged forty-three objects in a total of six hours of viewing, and he had counted sixty-one meteors, of which we had all seen fewer than a dozen. Next year the society plans to hold the weekend around the August meteor shower and to book the field two months earlier.

What I take away is a small change in habit. On Sunday night I turned off the outside light on my own flat and stood on the balcony, and for the first time in years I noticed a dozen stars over the rooftops. I am going to buy a red bulb for the hallway, and a proper planisphere, and keep a logbook. The first entry, when the clouds allow, will be Jupiter, in five words: four moons, two bands, still amazed.

Dairy cellar visit, an afternoon at the Ashcombe goat farm and its maturing cave. My cousin Delia booked us a tour after a friend told her about a farmer who makes twelve kinds of fresh and aged goat produce in a stone outbuilding and lets visitors taste as many as they can manage. We drove out on a bright day in late October along lanes so narrow that the hedgerows brushed both mirrors, and found the farm at the end of a track with a hand-painted sign that said Goats, Dairy, Please Close The Gate. The farmer, Wilhelmina Oduya, came out in green wellingtons and an apron, followed by an elderly Labrador that she said was in charge.

The tour began with the goats. There are a hundred and forty of them, mostly Saanens and a few brown Toggenburgs, milked twice a day in a shed with a raised platform and a row of steel stanchions. Wilhelmina says the goats are creatures of habit and will queue in the same order every morning, and that a new goat will be pushed to the back for a week. One of them, named Bathsheba, chewed a corner of Delia's coat with what looked like real interest. We were handed a bucket of feed and told that a goat prefers oats to almost anything, except something that belongs to somebody else.

In the dairy the milk goes into open vats and is warmed to thirty-two degrees before the rennet is added. Wilhelmina let each of us stir the curd with a long steel harp, and it felt like moving a warm cloud through a bathtub. She explained that a fresh curd is ladled into moulds by hand and left overnight to drain, after which it is salted and turned. The whole process, she said, is about rhythm rather than recipe: the temperature of the day and the health of the goats change the milk, and a good maker adjusts by touch.

Then came the cave, which is really a converted cellar dug into the hillside, forty steps down a dank stone stair with a low ceiling and a slick floor. The temperature is a steady eleven degrees and the humidity ninety-two per cent, which Wilhelmina monitors with two dials she checks every morning. Along the walls stand rows of spruce planks, each holding a dozen small rounds, white and wrinkled and grey-blue, in various stages of ripening. She said the cave has its own flora of moulds and that the smell is a sign of health; she took a deep breath and beamed, and we followed suit, less convincingly.

The tasting was a serious matter. We were given a wooden board with eight small pieces in a clockwise sequence, from the freshest to the oldest, together with a bowl of oat biscuits and a jug of water. The first, a fresh curd with lemon and thyme, was tangy and creamy. The fifth was a small ash-coated round aged for three weeks, with a thin, lemony rind and a chalky heart. The last, aged for eleven months, was hard, nutty and sharp, and Delia declared it the best thing she had put in her mouth in years. Wilhelmina told us that it is a house rule never to talk while tasting, though everybody did.

She answered questions with such candour that I wrote much of it down. A round costs about four pounds to make and sells for eight, she said, after the vet bills and the electricity; the margins are thin, and the cave is the only part of the business that makes money on its own. She employs two staff and her son, and the biggest challenge is finding people who will get up at half past five. A young man asked what she does with the whey, and she said that it goes to the neighbour's pigs, who have grown fat and opinionated.

The farm shop is a lean-to next to the dairy with a honesty box, a fridge of cold produce and a shelf of pots of quince jelly. We bought six pieces, a jar of jelly and a bag of oat biscuits, and Delia insisted on a small ash-coated round for her mother's birthday. Wilhelmina wrapped each piece in waxed paper and told us how to store them: in the bottom of the refrigerator, in a box lined with damp paper, and out for an hour before serving. I asked her how long they would keep, and she said, with a straight face, that in her house they have never been kept.

On the drive back Delia and I talked about how the day had shifted our sense of the food. There is a lot in the shop that comes from a factory and has the same name and taste every time. This was the opposite: each round is a small event, the sum of one particular weather, one flock and one pair of hands. I was struck by the idea that nothing on the plank was quite the same as its neighbour. I bought a small notebook for tasting notes the next day and wrote the date, the farm and eleven months on the first page.

Allotment dispute, minutes of the meeting I did not want to attend, called by the site secretary for a Wednesday evening in the hut. Our site at Millbrook Lane has forty-two plots, about half of them held by people who turn up every week and half by people who turn up when they are reminded. The trouble started in August with a complaint from Mrs Halvorsen on plot nineteen about a compost heap belonging to plot twenty, which she said was infested with rats. The owner of plot twenty, a large man named Desmond who grows dahlias and grudges, said it was a healthy heap and a matter of principle. By September there were emails.

The chair was Perpetua Osei, a woman who has held the post for nine years and has the manner of a magistrate who would rather be at home. She had prepared an agenda with five items and a note in bold that speakers should keep to three minutes. Twenty-nine people were present, more than at any meeting since the water tank burst in 2021. I sat at the back with my seed catalogue and pretended not to have opinions, although I have plot twenty-one, on the other side of the heap, and a well-formed view of the rat.

The first item was the compost heap itself. Desmond spoke first and produced photographs of a tidy pile, a cover of carpet and a thermometer, and he said that it was hot in the middle, at sixty-one degrees, which kills weed seeds and does not welcome rats. Mrs Halvorsen replied that she had seen a rat on the path, and she had a witness, the man on plot seventeen, who said it might have been a vole. A long argument followed over the difference between a rat and a vole, in which several people demonstrated with their hands.

The second item, which was really the first, was the site rules. Rule six says that compost heaps must be enclosed on all four sides and kept at least a metre from any boundary, and Desmond's heap is seventy centimetres from Mrs Halvorsen's fence. He said that the rule had never been enforced. Perpetua agreed that it had not, and that enforcement was now the difficulty. There was a proposal from the floor to measure every heap on the site, which was met with a groan so heartfelt that it went into the minutes.

The third item concerned the shared water tank. The new tank, installed last spring, has a lock, and only sixteen keys were cut, which has caused resentment among plot holders who did not receive one. The treasurer, a thin, careful man called Gideon, explained that the cost of each key was four pounds fifty and that sixteen was what the budget allowed. It emerged that eleven of the sixteen keys are held by people who have not visited in the last year. A vote was taken to reissue keys by seniority of attendance, which passed by nineteen to six with four abstentions.

The fourth item was waiting lists. There are thirty-eight names, and the average wait is three years and four months. Perpetua reported that the council will grant no more land, and she proposed to split a few of the larger plots into halves, which would give ten more people a place. This was resisted by the older members, who like their full plots, and supported by the younger ones, who cannot manage a full plot around a job. I said, and I do not know why I spoke, that a half plot done well is better than a whole plot done badly. There was silence, and then one or two people clapped.

By half past nine everyone was tired, and Perpetua moved to compromise. On the compost, Desmond will move his heap to a spot a metre from the fence, using a set of new wooden bays that the association will buy for a hundred and twenty pounds. Mrs Halvorsen will agree not to bring the matter up again unless she can produce a photograph of the animal. A working party will meet on the second Sunday of October to build the bays, and Desmond and Mrs Halvorsen will have to share a wheelbarrow, a clause that Perpetua wrote into the minutes with obvious pleasure.

Afterwards, outside the hut, Desmond found me by the gate and said, gruffly, that I had a point about the halves, and that he had once nearly given up his own plot when his knee went. He then offered me a tray of dahlia tubers, which I accepted, since refusing seemed dangerous. Mrs Halvorsen passed by and sniffed, but she nodded to me, so I count the evening as a diplomatic success. I walked home in the dark with a lump of tubers under one arm and the feeling that I am now, somehow, on the committee.

The number to remember is six: the new bays cost a hundred and twenty pounds, the heap has to be a metre from the fence, and we have six weeks until the first frost to get it done. I am supposed to bring a spirit level. There is also a note in the margin, in Perpetua's handwriting, to remind me that I have volunteered to draft the new rules on compost, which I do not remember doing, although the minutes are clear.

Cider pressing weekend at Hartswell Orchard, a diary of two days with the cousins and a borrowed press. My uncle Ranulf has forty old apple trees on a slope behind his cottage in Herefordshire, and every autumn he holds a pressing weekend for anyone who will come and carry crates. The trees are a mixed lot: Kingston Black, Dabinett, Yarlington Mill, a couple of Foxwhelp that he inherited with the land, and a single enormous tree of unknown variety that he calls the Duchess, which bears the wrong fruit every second year and is loved anyway. We arrived on Friday evening with sleeping bags and a crate of ginger biscuits, and were assigned a bunk in the hay loft before we had our coats off.

Saturday began with a walk to check the fruit. Ranulf's method is to shake a branch and see what falls, and he tastes a windfall from each tree with a squint that tells you what he thinks. The Dabinett were ready, dark red and bittersweet, and the Kingston Black too, small and mottled and fiercely sharp. The Foxwhelp, he said, needed another week. We took four wheelbarrows and a dozen plastic crates and began to gather what had fallen, with the rule that anything bruised is fine and anything rotten goes to the pigs, and anything with a wasp in it is a matter for the individual conscience.

By eleven we had ninety crates, roughly a tonne and a half, stacked under a tarpaulin beside the barn. Ranulf's daughter Philippa, who does this for a living at a commercial cidery in Somerset, arrived with a box of hydrometers and pH strips and took charge of the science. She explained that a good cider blends the varieties in about the ratio of two bittersweet, one bittersharp and one sharp, so that the finished drink has enough tannin for body and enough acid for life. Her spreadsheet said that from our crates we should expect about nine hundred litres, though she added, with a sigh, that in her experience the answer is always less.

The press is a beautiful, heavy, wooden thing, a rack-and-cloth model from the 1920s that Ranulf bought at an auction and restored over a winter. It works by layering ground apple pulp, called pomace, between cloths of coarse hessian, stacking the layers to a height of about a metre, and then screwing a slab down onto the stack. First the apples have to be milled. A small petrol-driven scratter, which rips the fruit into a coarse mash, sat in the corner of the yard making a noise like an angry lawnmower, and we took turns feeding it crate after crate while wearing ear defenders and looking faintly heroic.

Layering the stack, which pressers call the pile, is a skill. You lay a cloth in a wooden frame, spread a scoop of pomace to about the depth of a hand, fold the cloth over it like an envelope, and repeat. My cousin Isaura was in charge of folding, and she had a neat, quick style. My own envelopes leaked at the corners, and Philippa took one look and said that they resembled parcels wrapped by a toddler. By the time we had built the first stack, twelve layers high, the whole yard smelled of apple, with a faint background of wet dog.

Pressing itself is astonishing. As the screw goes down, juice begins to run, first in drops and then in a stream the colour of dark honey, down a channel in the base and into a bucket. The sound is a low, continuous trickle. Philippa held a hydrometer in a jug and announced that the first bucket had a specific gravity of one point zero six two, which in her language is a good, sweet must. Ranulf dipped a finger, tasted it and said, in a voice full of reverence, that it was the best juice since 2014. It was, to be fair, the best juice I have ever had, thick and sweet with a bitter edge that lingered.

We pressed until dark, working in relays. Somebody fetched a pot of stew that Ranulf's wife had left on the stove, and we ate it out of enamel mugs sitting on straw bales with the press dripping behind us. Philippa explained fermentation in a short talk: the wild yeasts on the fruit will do the job if you let them, but she prefers to add a cultured yeast to avoid off-flavours, and to keep the barrels cool, at around twelve degrees, so that the fermentation is slow and the aromatics stay. She said that the biggest mistake for a beginner is to be impatient, and that a proper cider is not ready until Easter.

Sunday was for cleaning and filling. We washed the cloths in a stream of cold water, hung them to dry on the fence, and sluiced the press with a hose. The juice was pumped into four old oak barrels that Ranulf had rinsed with sulphite the week before, and the bungs were fitted with airlocks that bubble gently as the yeast wakes up. By the time we stood back the day had turned overcast and a light drizzle had begun, and a jackdaw watched us from the barn roof with an air of professional interest. Before we left the yard Philippa took a sample of each barrel in a small glass tube, labelled it in pencil, and promised to test the sugar again after ten days. She says a healthy ferment loses about two points of gravity a day at first and then slows to a crawl, and that if it stops too early the cider will stay sweet and sticky and be fit only for pouring on porridge. Ranulf grunted that his cider has never yet been fit for porridge and has never yet been badly behaved either.

The final tally, which Philippa wrote in chalk on the barn door, was seven hundred and eighty litres of juice from a tonne and a half of fruit, or a little over half a litre per kilo. Ranulf said the Duchess had contributed exactly a crate and a half of the wrong fruit, and that he would blend it in and hope. My share for carrying and folding was thirty bottles of last year's cider, which I loaded into the boot of the car in a folding crate, and a promise of a return visit in April to help with the racking.

Driving back in the dusk I thought about how this weekend seemed to run on slow time. Nothing about it could be hurried: the apples ripened when they were ripe, the juice ran at its own pace, and the cider would be done when it was done. My phone had no signal in the valley and I did not miss it. In the back seat, the crates clinked softly every time we turned a corner. When I got home I opened one bottle straight away and it was dry, cloudy and faintly funky, with a taste of orchard floor, and it was exactly what I wanted.

Dry-stone walling course, two Saturdays on a hillside above Ambleside with the Fell Farmers' training group. I signed up on a whim after seeing a wall that had collapsed in the winter storms along the lane near my sister's house, and the course was advertised as open to beginners and the moderately fit. The instructor was a wiry man of about sixty named Thaddeus Rook, who has been building walls since he was fourteen and says he still sees new ways to spoil one. He met us at nine at a gate, in a battered waxed jacket, and handed each of us a pair of leather gloves and a small hammer.

The first job was to look at the wall. Thaddeus led us along a fallen stretch, a gap of about eight metres where the stones had slumped into the field, and explained the anatomy. A dry-stone wall is not a heap of stones but a structure, he said: two faces of large, carefully laid stones that lean slightly together, a hearting of small rubble between them, and through-stones that span the whole width and tie the faces together. On top sit the copes, upright stones that lock everything down. The batter, meaning the inward slope of each face, is about one in six, and he showed how to check it with a wooden frame shaped like a tall triangle.

Then we took the old wall apart, or rather what was left of it. Thaddeus insisted we sort the stones as they came off: big foundation stones in one row, through-stones in another, hearting into a wheelbarrow, copes on a tarpaulin. It took two hours, and there was a fair amount of grumbling about backs. I found a stone shaped exactly like a loaf and became attached to it, and Thaddeus said it would make a good cope if I stopped stroking it. By eleven the gap was down to its base course, a line of huge boulders half-sunk in the soil, and he pronounced that the previous builder had done the foundations properly.

Rebuilding is the interesting part. The rule is one over two and two over one, meaning that each stone should sit across the joint between the two below it, so that no vertical crack runs through the face. Thaddeus told us never to pick up a stone twice. We had to look at the gap, decide which stone fitted, and lay it, since dithering wastes a great deal of energy. I lifted stones that felt as heavy as a small child, tried them in a place, rejected them, tried again and eventually developed a sort of intuition for the fit. It was the first time in months that I forgot to look at my phone.

Lunch was on the hillside in a thin, bright sun, with a view down to the lake and a wind that made the flask tea a necessity. Thaddeus told us stories about walls. In the Dales there are five thousand miles of them, many built during the enclosure acts of the eighteenth century by gangs of men paid by the yard, and an old rule of thumb holds that a good waller can build a metre of wall in a day. He said that a wall built well will last two hundred years without any mortar, and that the plastic and steel of a modern fence will not last thirty.

In the afternoon I began to see what he meant about the through-stones. Each one has to span the entire width of the wall, about seventy centimetres, and be laid a little proud of the face so that a sheep can see it. There should be one about every metre along the wall, at a height of half a metre. I found a long thin slab at the bottom of the pile and lugged it into place with a crowbar, and Thaddeus, who had been watching in silence, walked past and said, without looking, that it was a decent bit of work. Coming from him it was like receiving a medal.

The second Saturday was colder and wetter. We finished the wall to a height of about a metre and ten and started on the copes. These are set on edge, all leaning the same way like a row of books, and packed tight with wedges of small stone so that they cannot be dislodged. My sister came up to see how we were doing and stood at the gate with a flask, taking photographs and pretending to be a supervisor. The rain began at two and ran down the backs of our necks. Thaddeus said that walling in the rain is the only honest test of a wall.

By four we had closed the gap: eight metres of rebuilt wall, complete, with fifteen through-stones, forty-two copes and a wheelbarrow of surplus hearting. The farmer whose field it was, a taciturn man named Mr Braithwaite, came down and inspected it from end to end, running his hand along the top. He said nothing at all for about a minute, which Thaddeus told us afterwards is the highest praise a farmer can pay. He then offered us a glass of something from a bottle in his coat, and we drank it in a row, as the light went, looking at our wall.

I came home with blistered palms and a heavy sense of achievement, and a certificate that says I have completed the course in the presence of a competent waller. My sister has asked whether I will do the wall along her lane, and I have said that I will consider it once my hands have recovered. There is a course fee of a hundred and forty pounds, which includes lunch on both days, and Thaddeus runs six weekends each year. The number I remember best is eight, the length of the gap, and the thing I remember second-best is the stone the shape of a loaf, which went into the wall at knee height and is, I hope, staying there.

Church organ pipe repair, notes from four Thursdays in the loft of St Winifred's, where I help the parish organ committee. The instrument is a two-manual pipe organ built in 1893 by a firm in Bristol that no longer exists, with eleven speaking stops and a wooden pedal board worn into two shallow dips by a century of shoes. The congregation has been complaining for years that it sounds tired, and last spring the organist, a silver-haired woman named Winifred, though she says the coincidence is a curse, arranged a survey. The surveyor's report ran to nineteen pages, and the committee has turned it into a plan for a staged repair, of which the first stage is what I have been helping with.

The organ builder we hired is a small firm from Wells with two staff, a master named Lucian Mabey and his apprentice, Yasmin. Lucian is a lean man in his fifties with hands like carved wood and a habit of tapping each pipe with a knuckle as if he were taking its pulse. He arrived on the first Thursday with a van full of felt, leather, glue pots and a set of tuning cones. He explained that the greatest damage to an organ is dust and damp, and that in this case the leather of the bellows had perished and caused a slow leak, so that the wind pressure had dropped by about a third.

The first job was to open the swell box, a wooden cupboard with louvred shutters that houses one of the manuals' pipes. Inside, in the dim light, were rows of metal pipes, their surfaces white with a chalky bloom of lead oxide and a coat of grey dust as soft as a moth's wing. Some of the smaller pipes had been crushed by a careless hand and one, a flute, had a crack from top to bottom. Lucian took photographs of every rank and drew a plan of the layout on graph paper with a pencil the length of a finger. I helped by holding the torch and handing him tools.

The bellows were the heart of the matter. The organ uses a large single-fold reservoir, a wooden box with a leather-hinged lid weighted with lead sheets, fed by an electric blower installed in 1962. When the leather cracks, the wind escapes and the organ sounds breathless, especially in the loud stops. Lucian and Yasmin spent two full Thursdays stripping the old leather, scraping the hide glue from the wood with a warm blade, and recovering the bellows with new sheepskin, which arrived in a roll like a carpet. The glue smell filled the whole church, a sweet, sharp smell of an old farm scullery, and the vicar wandered in to ask whether we were baking.

On the third Thursday the pipes went back. Each of the four hundred and seventy-six pipes had to be cleaned, checked for cracks, and refitted in its own hole, in the correct order. Yasmin, who has a spectacular memory for the layout, called out numbers while Lucian slotted the pipes into their places with a sound like a dozen glasses being put down. The largest metal pipes, in the open diapason, are as tall as a person and as thick as a drainpipe, and they had to be carried up the ladder one at a time. I took the heavy end of one, with real terror, and was told that dropping a pipe is a mistake you make only once.

Tuning is the delicate part. The organ is tuned by adjusting the length of each pipe, using a slide or a tuning cone that is tapped gently to flare the top. Lucian tuned the entire instrument from a single reference note, using his ear, an electronic tuner and a certain amount of muttering. He starts with the middle octave of the principal and then works out to the extremes, listening for beats between adjacent notes. He said that the difficulty is that temperature changes the pitch: a cold church is flat and a warm one sharp, so he heated the nave for three hours beforehand with a set of electric radiators he brought in the van.

On the final Thursday Winifred sat at the console and played the first piece, a simple chorale prelude. The sound was warm, full and clean, with a bass that shook the pew under my knees. She played it through twice and then stopped, put her hands in her lap, and said quietly that she had not heard the instrument like this in fifteen years. Lucian looked at his boots. A few members of the congregation who had arrived early to set out chairs stood at the back and listened without a word, and one of them, an old man with a stick, wiped his eyes.

The money side, which I helped with, was more nerve-racking than the tuning. The total cost of stage one was eleven thousand four hundred pounds, of which the parish fund had six thousand and a heritage grant covered four thousand. That left fourteen hundred pounds to raise, and the committee decided on a sponsored organ crawl, in which supporters visit five local churches and play or listen to the instruments. Winifred has offered to play at every stop, and I have offered to drive. The vicar suggested that the sponsorship money be advertised in the parish magazine under the headline Help Us Breathe.

Stage two is scheduled for next autumn and will involve the pedal board and the mechanical action, which is the linkage between key and pipe, and which Lucian says is worn in places to the thickness of a cigarette paper. Between now and then, the committee has to raise a further nine thousand pounds. I have been put in charge of the fundraising spreadsheet, an honour I accepted with a sinking heart, and I have promised to learn the basics of registration so that I can turn the pages for Winifred at the concert in the spring. She says that the turner has one job, which is to be invisible, and one more job, which is not to sneeze. I have since practised turning with a stack of paper on my own shelf, and it is harder than it looks: you must wait until the last bar of the page, reach across without touching the keys, and lay the sheet flat so that it makes no rustle at all. Winifred watched my first try and pronounced it adequate, which I gather is the highest grade she awards before the third year.

The most beautiful thing I learned from Lucian is that an organ is never finished. Each stop has its own character, and each pipe is voiced by hand, and the whole instrument responds to the building it lives in. He said, tapping a pipe, that a good organ is like a good marriage and requires regular attention, small repairs, and a decent amount of heating. I wrote it down word for word in my notebook, next to a small sketch of a bellows, and the date, which was the twenty-third, the day we heard it breathe.

Canal lock restoration week, a volunteer log from the Wendover Arm, written for the studio's team page. Eight of us gave up a week of leave to work with the Canal Restoration Trust on Lock Nine, one of a flight of fourteen that was abandoned in 1962 and has been slowly reclaimed since 1997. The lock is a brick chamber about seven metres long and three wide with wooden gates at either end, and when we first saw it the chamber was full of brambles, silt and one abandoned shopping trolley that the site leader called a vintage. The site leader, a jolly, bearded man named Cormac Ekwueme, met us at the gate in a yellow hard hat and gave us the week's plan on a sheet of paper.

Monday was clearance. We waded, in waders, into the chamber to strip out saplings and drag out a silt that had the consistency of old porridge and the smell of a pond in August. Sanne discovered a bicycle frame, Colm a bottle from a defunct local brewery, and Blake a small dead fish, which he handled with great tenderness. By four o'clock we had filled the skip and moved forty tonnes of silt by wheelbarrow to a bank on the far side, and the chamber was down to its brick floor. Cormac took photographs from a ladder and told us this was one of the fastest days he had seen.

Tuesday brought the brickwork. Some of the courses on the chamber walls had been eaten away by frost and roots, and the job was to rake out the failed mortar and repoint with a lime mix, which sets more slowly than cement and lets the wall breathe. A mason named Perrin, a quiet woman in her sixties with forearms like a boxer, taught us the technique: a hawk of mortar in one hand, a pointing iron in the other, and a wet brush to finish. My first attempt looked like a snail had crossed the wall, and she scraped it out without comment. By lunch, mine looked passable, and Perrin's face relaxed by a millimetre.

The gates on Wednesday. The lock's old gates had rotted away, and the trust had built a new pair from oak in a workshop a few miles off, each gate weighing about a tonne and a half. Lifting them into place required a crane, a gang of eight and a great deal of shouting. The crane was hired for the morning at a cost of four hundred and eighty pounds, and the operator, a stoic man with a crossword in his pocket, swung the gate above the chamber while we guided it with ropes. It settled on the heel post with a deep thud that I felt in my ribs, and there was applause from three passers-by on the towpath.

Thursday was the paddle gear. Each gate has a pair of paddles, wooden sluices that let water in and out, operated with a windlass, a cranked steel handle. We assembled the paddle frames, greased the racks and pinions with a thick black grease that ended up on everything, and fitted the ratchets. Ilse turned out to have a knack for machinery and took charge of aligning the spindles.
