When we cranked the first paddle up and heard the gate creak, everyone stopped what they were doing and looked over. Cormac said it was the sound of the canal coming back to life.

The lunches on site were a highlight. A retired couple, Hilda and Bertram, run the trust's canteen from a trailer and produce, every day, a vat of soup, a mountain of sandwiches and a tray of traybake known as the lock-keeper's revenge. Bertram, who is eighty-three, told us that he had worked on the canal as a boy, loading coal, and that the water was a foot higher then. On Wednesday he brought an old photograph of the lock with a horse-drawn boat and two children sitting on the beam, and we passed it round with reverence.

Friday was the test. Cormac had arranged for the water to be let in from the pound above, by opening a valve on the feeder, and the whole team stood on the lock side with a flask of tea. The water came slowly, first a trickle, then a rush, filling the chamber inch by inch, and Colm was put in charge of watching the new brickwork for leaks. There was one, a single damp patch on the north wall, which Perrin marked with a piece of chalk. At eleven-forty the water level with the upper pound, and Cormac lifted his arm and asked us to open the top gate.

There was nothing to see, really: a stretch of green water in a brick box with a clean, gently rippling surface. But everyone stood in silence for a moment, and then Cormac asked whether anyone had a boat. It turned out that a member of the trust owned a small narrowboat named Tansy, which was fetched from the next pound, and she was drifted into the lock at a snail's pace, to a small cheer. The gates were closed behind her, the water was let down, and she dropped a metre and a half. It took nine minutes. It was, we agreed, the best nine minutes of the year.

The tally for the week, on Cormac's whiteboard, was two hundred and forty hours of labour, fifty-one tonnes of silt, four hundred bricks repointed, and one bicycle. The trust will need another three years to finish the flight, and it estimates that it needs to raise two hundred and ten thousand pounds. The studio has decided to pledge one week of volunteer time each summer, and to sponsor a set of gate furniture, each piece stamped with the studio's name. Sanne is designing the plate, which is to read, in small print, that Lock Nine was reopened by people who were meant to be on holiday.

Staff play production diary, the studio's Christmas performance of a Victorian farce, from the first read-through to the closing night. Every December the office puts on a play for the families of the team, staged in the parish hall next to the old chapel, with a cast of amateurs and a director who takes it far too seriously. This year the director was Colm's sister-in-law, Perpetua Lindqvist, a drama teacher of great charm and no mercy, and the play was a farce in three acts about a country solicitor, a stolen pig and a case of mistaken identity. Blake was asked to play the solicitor, Avery the pig's owner, and Sanne the pig, a role she accepted after some negotiation about whether she had to make noises.

The read-through in late October was held on a wet Tuesday with fourteen of us on folding chairs in a circle. Perpetua handed out scripts bound with treasury tags and asked us to read our lines flatly, without acting, so that we could hear the rhythm of the words. Blake read the solicitor as if he were reading a mortgage agreement, which Perpetua said was a great start. She explained that farce works like a machine: every door has to open at exactly the right moment, every entrance has to interrupt an exit, and the audience must never suspect that anyone is trying to be funny.

Rehearsals were twice a week, Tuesday and Saturday. In the first three weeks the cast learned the moves, and it became clear that nobody could remember the second act. Perpetua drew a plan of the stage on the floor with masking tape, with a door at each side and a sofa in the middle, and she had us walk through the scene without speaking, following a chalked track as if we were pieces in a board game. Blake got stuck between the sofa and the door twelve times in one evening and eventually asked for a stool on which to sit and rethink his life.

The costume budget was seventy pounds, which Perpetua regarded as generous. Ilse, who sews, took charge and rummaged through the charity shops of three neighbouring towns. She came back with a black frock coat with a torn lining for the solicitor, a fake fur collar, two bowler hats and a pair of spectacles with no lenses. The pig's costume was the greatest challenge. Sanne wanted to be tasteful, Perpetua wanted to be honest, and in the end Ilse stitched a pink sweatshirt to a hood with two felt ears and a curly tail made from a pipe cleaner. Sanne wore it for the first time at a dress rehearsal and burst into helpless laughter that lasted four minutes.

Props were a kind of comedy of their own. The play calls for a dead pig, a live pig, a stack of legal papers, a bottle of port and a pair of trousers that fall down at the crucial moment. The dead pig was a stuffed toy the size of a dachshund, the live pig was Sanne, the legal papers were photocopies of the studio's lease, and the trousers were fitted with a strip of velcro. The port was blackcurrant squash. Colm, in charge of props, insisted on testing the trousers over and over in the corridor until he was satisfied that they would come down on cue and not a second earlier.

The technical rehearsal, three days before opening, ran for five hours and ended at midnight in a state of near collapse. The lighting was a pair of borrowed spotlights and a dimmer that failed at the end of every second scene, plunging the stage into darkness at the exact moment of a kiss. Perpetua, sitting at the back, wrote notes in a small black book and read them out after each act in a tone of gentle despair. Her main note for Blake was that the audience must be able to hear him in the last row, and that a whisper is not a projection.

The first night, a Thursday, drew a hundred and four people, which is more than the hall holds by regulation, and the fire marshal, a retired postman named Norbert, counted heads by the door with a clicker and a stern expression. Backstage, in the chapel vestry, the cast crammed into a space the size of a bus shelter and applied make-up in the light of a single bulb. A child of three, somebody's nephew, wandered in and asked Sanne whether she was really a pig. She said yes. He asked whether she was going to be eaten. She said not tonight, and the whole vestry fell about.

The performance itself went by in a blur. The first act moved well, with a good laugh at the appearance of the dead pig, and there was a lovely moment when Avery, trying to hide the bottle of port, sat on the sofa and discovered that Colm had left the stuffed pig on the cushion. In the second act the velcro failed, and the solicitor's trousers came down half a minute early, in the middle of a sombre speech about the law, to an explosion of laughter that made it impossible to continue for a full minute. Blake, showing unexpected presence of mind, looked out at the audience, sighed, and said, in character, that the law is a harsh mistress.

The second night was a little flatter, as second nights are. The third, on Saturday, was the best. The hall was full again, and this time the audience contained a few strangers from the village who had heard about the play through the pub and turned up with cushions. The pig received a huge round of applause and a bunch of carrots at the curtain call, thrown by a man in the front row. Perpetua came out from the wings for a bow, wearing a sequinned cardigan, and thanked everyone in a short speech that she managed without notes.

Money went to charity. The tickets were six pounds each, with a free mince pie, and after expenses the play raised four hundred and thirty-six pounds, which the team gave to the hall's roof fund. The vicar, who had come on the second night, said the hall had not had such laughter since the fete of 1998. Norbert, the fire marshal, said that the hall had not had such a crowd since the same fete, and that the next time he would want the numbers agreed in advance.

We struck the set on Sunday morning with tea and leftover mince pies. The sofa went back to Colm's sister-in-law, the frock coat to Ilse's wardrobe, the trousers to a bin with honour, and the pig costume to a peg in the studio's cupboard, where it has become a kind of mascot. Perpetua wrote us each a short note on a card. Mine said that I had a lovely, dry way with a line, and that I should never, ever attempt to learn the second act from the script in the bath. She has asked whether the studio would like to do a spring play, and the vote at the next team meeting was seven in favour and three abstentions.

For the record, a few numbers. There were fourteen in the cast, eleven rehearsals, one hundred and four people on the first night, four minutes of laughter at the dress rehearsal and one minute in the second act. There were also two pounds forty of velcro. The thing that will stay with me, though, is the vestry on opening night: fourteen people in half a cupboard of borrowed costumes, no one speaking, everyone listening to the murmur of the audience through the door, and Perpetua, whispering, that this was the best part and we should remember it.

Model railway exhibition, the studio's stand at the Eastfield Model Engineers' annual show. The society holds its show in the leisure centre in the first weekend of March, and this year it invited the studio to take a stand for the demonstration of a small layout that Blake and Colm have been building in their spare hours. The layout is a fictional branch line in the north of England, set in 1958, forty inches long by twenty wide, with a single station, a coaling stage, a level crossing and a small village with a pub called the Fox and Compass. It runs in four-millimetre scale, which is the ordinary British size, and it took fourteen months to build.

We arrived on Friday afternoon to set up, having borrowed a van from Ilse's uncle. The exhibition hall, a big echoing space with a sprung floor, was already full of trestles and the smell of solder. There were sixty layouts in all, from a huge American-style mountain railway that filled a whole corner to a tiny scene in a suitcase, and the society's secretary, a brisk man in a tweed waistcoat named Cuthbert Ainsley, walked us to our patch and pointed at a socket and a length of blue tape on the floor. Our space was two metres by one and a half, which is generous, and had a curtain to hide the tools.

Setting up took three hours. The layout travels in two boards, hinged together, and had to be bolted on to a pair of legs. Blake fixed the electrical connections while I held the torch and Colm arranged the scenery: a hedge, a tiny farmer with two cows, a bus shelter. The most delicate job was to hang the backscene, a painted sky on hardboard, which Sanne had done in soft grey-blue with a hint of rain. When the lights went on, the whole tiny world sprang into life and a passing exhibitor said that it looked like a railway poster from an era that never quite happened.

The controller is the heart of the layout. Blake built a handheld unit with a knob for speed and a switch for direction, and a small panel at the front with push buttons for points and signals. There is a running-order card by the station, and the trains are meant to run to it, so that the station clock, a tiny brass movement, tells the visitor which train is due. Blake was, I think, more worried about the clock than the trains. On Friday night, before we went home, it was four minutes fast, and he set it back by hand, with a screwdriver the size of a matchstick.

Saturday opened at ten. By eleven there were about four hundred visitors in the hall, of all ages, and a queue at the pie stall. Our layout ran a passenger train, a goods train and a shunting engine in turn. The passenger train was a small green tank engine with two carriages in cream and crimson, and it ran round the line at a walking pace with a faint hum. Children crowded to the front and pressed their noses to the barrier rope, and one boy asked, with total seriousness, whether the people inside the train could see him. Colm said yes and waved to them.

By lunch Colm had explained the layout to about two hundred people, and his voice was a whisper. He learned that visitors ask four kinds of question: how long did it take, how does it work, where can I buy one and what is that building for. The last was the most difficult, because the building in question was a signal box, and there was a man who wanted to know the exact date of the signalling regulations that applied to it. Cuthbert appeared with a walking stick, a tie with tiny locomotives on it, and an answer that took nine minutes.

Sunday brought a dramatic incident. At half past twelve the shunting engine came off the rails at the level crossing and dragged two wagons on to the road, where it sat, wheels in the air like a dead beetle. A boy of about six shouted that it was a crash, and a small crowd gathered. Blake, imperturbable, lifted the engine with a pair of tweezers, cleaned the wheels with a cotton bud and returned it to the track, telling the crowd that this was a normal part of railway operation and that the fireman was uninjured. There was applause.

The judging happened at three. The society gives prizes in six classes, and our layout was entered for best new builder, which is decided by a panel of three retired engineers who walk round the hall with clipboards. They spent eleven minutes at our stand, and one of them, a man with an enormous white moustache, asked Blake to run the train slowly through the points and then in reverse. He then crouched at eye level and stared at the level crossing for a long time. He finally said, in a gravelly voice, that the fence posts were of the correct height and that this was the first time he had seen it done properly.

We did not win. The prize went to a beautiful reproduction of a Welsh slate quarry with two hundred and forty figures, and a certificate of commendation went to us for scenery, which Sanne pinned to the backscene with a drawing pin. The panel's written comments said that the layout showed real promise, that the track work was excellent, and that the goods yard would benefit from more clutter. Blake read this out loud several times over supper. He said that more clutter is exactly what he intends to add.

Financially the weekend cost the studio about a hundred and sixty pounds, most of it for the stand fee and the van. In return, we gained three commissions from visitors who wanted small scenic models built for them, a list of forty names of people who would like to help, and an invitation from the society to join as a group member, at a fee of twelve pounds a year. We also gained a firm view about the future of the layout: it will be extended by a further board, to include a small engine shed and a canal wharf, in time for the autumn show at Peterborough.

On Sunday evening we packed everything into the van, boards first, then legs, then the tools, then a very well-behaved farmer and two cows in a shoebox. Blake sat in the back with the controller on his lap and would not let go of it. As we drove out of the car park he said, to no one in particular, that he had never before spent two days having other people look at something he had made. He said it was more nerve-racking than a presentation to a client, and much more fun. Colm said that he had run out of things to say by ten on Saturday, and I think that is the highest compliment the layout could receive.

Footbridge consultation, notes from the public meeting about the new crossing over the river at Tanner's Reach, attended by Avery and Blake as neighbours of the site. The council's planning officers have proposed a pedestrian and cycle bridge to link the office quarter on the east bank to the station on the west, replacing a stretch of towpath that floods four times a year. The meeting was held in the library annexe on a Tuesday evening, with sixty-five chairs set out and about ninety people crammed in, and a panel of four officials sat at a long desk under a projector screen that would not stay on.

The chair was Marguerite Oyelaran, the council's head of transport, a composed woman with an iPad she seldom looked at. She began by explaining the scheme in a calm voice. A bridge of forty-two metres, a steel deck three metres wide, with a gentle ramp on each side to allow wheelchairs and pushchairs. The estimated cost was two million eight hundred thousand pounds, of which nine hundred thousand would come from a regional transport fund and the rest from the council's capital budget. Construction, if approved, would start in the spring of the year after next and take fourteen months.

The design was shown on a set of boards around the walls. The winning concept, chosen from a shortlist of three, is a slender arched bridge in weathering steel with a timber handrail and lights set into the deck. It has a tall single arch in the centre to allow river boats to pass beneath, and a pair of seats halfway across for people to stop and look at the water. An architect from the consultancy, a young man named Leopold, described it as a piece of urban sculpture, and a woman at the back audibly said that she preferred something that was not sculpture and did not cost that much.

The questions began at once. The first was from an elderly man who owns a boat moored under the site, and he wanted to know how much clearance would remain at high water. Leopold said three point two metres, and the man said that his cruiser needed three point four. There was some awkward shuffling of papers. Marguerite said the figure would be checked against the river authority's survey, and promised a written reply within fourteen days. The man said he had been promised written replies before, and this was the fourth.

The second theme was cyclists and walkers. A representative from the local cycling group, a stout woman in a fluorescent jacket named Bronwen, said that she supported the bridge but not the ramp gradients, which at one in twelve are too steep for a loaded bicycle. A member of the pedestrians' association, a slight man with a folder, said that any shared path with cyclists is a menace, and that in his experience of a similar bridge in another city, three pedestrians had been knocked down in a year. The two of them then argued for six minutes, until Marguerite said that a separate cycle lane would add four hundred thousand pounds and that no one had budgeted for it.

Neighbours' concerns were next. A resident of the flats on the west bank, a woman named Isadora, said that the bridge would overlook her balcony and that she had lived there for twenty years in the belief that nobody could see in. Leopold explained that the deck would be screened by a slatted panel on that side, and that the height of the panel was a matter for the detailed design. She said she would like it in writing, and he said he would try. There was a short silence in which I could hear the projector, which had turned itself off, ticking as it cooled.

The safety issue was flood risk. A retired engineer named Barnaby, who had prepared a printed statement, said that the western ramp was below the level reached by the flood of 1987 and that any bridge which is closed when it is needed most is a poor bridge. Marguerite said that the ramp was designed to the level of a one-in-a-hundred-year flood plus an allowance for climate change, and that she would ask the engineers to provide the figures. Barnaby replied that the figures were on page nine of the appendix and that he had seen them and did not believe them. The audience, which had been listless, suddenly woke up.

Blake asked the question that the studio cares about, which is what will happen to the towpath during construction. The current route is used by about three hundred people a day, including many staff on their way to the station. Marguerite said that a temporary diversion would be put in place, adding about seven minutes to the walk, and that the towpath would be closed for the six weeks of the piling. She apologised for the inconvenience in a way that was so polite it was almost a threat. Blake asked about the lighting on the diversion, and she made a note.

Avery raised a question about how the consultation would be counted. It had been advertised as a chance to shape the design, but nothing in the pack explained how the views would be weighed or what would change as a result. Marguerite said, after a pause, that the officers would produce a report to the planning committee summarising the responses, and that the numbers for and against would be recorded. A voice from the back asked whether that meant a vote. She said it did not, and the voice said, in that case, what was the point of coming.

By nine the chairs were emptying and the tea urn had run dry. At the end Marguerite invited written comments until the twenty-first of the month, either on a form or online, and said that a revised design would be shown at a second meeting in the new year. As we left, the man with the boat was pressing his card into the hands of the architect, and I heard him say the number three point four several times, slowly, as if to a child. On the pavement, Blake said that he had come to oppose the bridge and now was not sure what he thought, which he described as a great success for the democratic process.

Our written response, drafted the next morning, made three points. We support the bridge in principle; we ask that the western ramp be raised above the historic flood mark; and we ask for a lit, level and signposted diversion for the whole period of the works, with the towpath reopened in stages. We signed it with the studio's name and the two of us, and posted it on the twentieth. The number from the evening that I am most likely to remember is three point four, the height of a cruiser, and the fact that a bridge worth two million eight hundred thousand pounds might be decided by a difference of twenty centimetres.

Mountain rescue fundraiser, planning notes and a full account of the sponsored hill walk that the studio ran for the Dunnock Fell Rescue Team. The team is a volunteer group of thirty-four people who respond to about eighty call-outs a year on the fells above our valley, and it has to raise almost all its own money, because a rescue team in this country is a charity and gets no state funding. Colm's brother-in-law, Emrys, is a member, and it was through him that the studio was asked to organise a sponsored walk of the ridge, with a target of five thousand pounds. There were twenty-three of us in the end.

Planning began in April with a visit to the team's base, a converted garage at the end of the valley road, where two members, the team leader, Hepzibah Ndlovu, and the treasurer, Godfrey, gave us a talk. Hepzibah, in a red jacket with a reflective stripe, described the year's call-outs: forty-one for walkers who were lost or benighted, sixteen for injuries, seven for climbers, and six for missing persons, of which two ended sadly. She spoke calmly and briefly, and the whole hall, a group of people who work at screens, went very quiet. She said that the most common cause of a call-out is a phone battery dying at four in the afternoon.

The route was a circular walk of nineteen kilometres, starting at the car park at the head of the valley, climbing to the ridge by a steep path called the Stair, following the ridge for eight kilometres over three summits, and returning by a stony bridleway. The total ascent was nine hundred and forty metres. Emrys walked it with Blake and Avery a fortnight before to check the ground, and reported that there was a boggy section near the second summit that would need a diversion and a stile that had fallen apart. He also said the weather on the ridge changes three times an hour.

Safety was the team's first condition. Hepzibah insisted that every participant carry a map, a compass, a whistle, a head torch, a spare layer, food and water, and that the walkers travel in groups of four with a designated leader. She also insisted that the studio provide four marshals with radios at key points on the route, each of them a member of the rescue team in a red jacket. We were required to register every walker by name at the start and count them at the finish, and Godfrey produced a sheet of paper with a column for the time out and a column for the time in.

Fundraising went better than we had feared. Sanne set up a page on a giving platform and posted the link on the studio's social channels, and in the first week it collected eight hundred pounds, mostly from clients and friends. The studio itself pledged to match the total up to a thousand pounds. Ilse ran a cake sale at the office, with a trestle and an honesty tin, and raised a hundred and sixty-two pounds, of which forty were from a man who paid for a single flapjack with a twenty and refused change. By the eve of the walk the total stood at three thousand nine hundred and eighty pounds.

The day itself, a Saturday in the middle of June, dawned bright and windy. We gathered in the car park at eight, in a thin light with the summits clear against a pale sky, and Hepzibah addressed us from the tailgate of a Land Rover. She read out the forecast, a light north-westerly with gusts of thirty miles an hour on the tops, cloud base at eight hundred metres, and a fifteen per cent chance of showers. She told us that the ridge is exposed and that anyone who felt unwell should say so at once. We formed six groups, and each group leader was handed a laminated card with the emergency number.

The climb up the Stair was hard. It is a steep, eroded path of loose stones that gains four hundred metres in under two kilometres, and by the halfway mark the groups had strung out in a long line, panting and joking. Colm, who does not run, was laughing at a joke of his own, and Sanne, who does, went up like a mountain goat and had to be asked to slow down. I followed with Blake, who took photographs at every turn on the pretext of the fundraising page. At the top of the Stair the wind hit us like a wall, and we crouched behind a cairn to eat flapjack.

The ridge was glorious. A narrow crest of grass and rock, with a sheer drop on the north side and a long green slope on the south, running between summits with names like the Anvil and the Old Man. From the Anvil we could see the whole valley laid out like a map, with the reservoir a silver coin at the bottom, and beyond it a line of blue hills as far as the sea. A marshal, a young woman in a red jacket named Tegan, was sitting on a rock at the third summit with a flask and a radio, and she waved and ticked us off her list with a professional smile.

At the second summit we met the boggy section, and the diversion Emrys had marked with stakes and red tape. Most of us followed it, but one group, led by Ilse, decided to take a short cut and sank to the knees. She emerged twenty minutes later with one boot in her hand and a look of great dignity. The rest of the day she walked in a sock and a plastic bag, and Tegan radioed ahead to ask for the team's spare pair, which arrived in the boot of a Land Rover at the bridleway, to a hearty cheer from everyone but Ilse.

We finished at about half past three, the last group arriving with a sunburnt nose and a torn jacket. Godfrey counted twenty-three names at the finish line and ticked them off, one by one, with a small smile. In the car park the team had set up a tea stall and a hand-painted board with the running total. The final figure, after the studio's match and the gift aid claim, was five thousand and thirty-eight pounds, which Hepzibah announced through a loudhailer to a small cheer and a large sigh of relief.

At the end, Hepzibah asked us to stay for a demonstration. Two members of the team, in helmets and harnesses, showed us a stretcher, a vacuum splint and a radio repeater, and explained how a call-out works, from the first ring of the phone to the last person off the hill. She said, in a tone we all remembered, that the best thing anybody can do for the rescue team is to be careful, and the second best is to fund it. Then she handed each of us a badge and said, with a straight face, that we were now officially the studio's rescue team, and that she would call us when needed. I am not entirely sure that she was joking.

Bell ringing practice night, my first six weeks in the tower at St Aldhelm's, written up for myself because the method names are already sliding out of my head. A colleague of my mother's, a retired surveyor named Humphrey Onwuka, heard me say that I wanted a hobby that involved no screen and no talking, and he invited me to visit his tower on a Wednesday. I went in a fleece and trainers, expecting to stand at the back and watch. Ninety seconds after I arrived, a bell rope was in my hand, and Humphrey was telling me not to let go of it under any circumstances.

The tower is Norman at the base and Perpendicular at the top, with a spiral stair of seventy-one steps, and it holds six bells hung for full-circle ringing. The ringing chamber is a small square space halfway up, with a wooden floor worn into hollows by generations of feet, a noticeboard covered in certificates, and a row of ropes that end in fluffy red-white-and-blue woollen grips called sallies. On the wall there is a peal board recording a performance in 1911 that lasted three hours and ten minutes. The bells are above our heads in a frame, and you never see them; you learn to feel them through the rope.

Handling a bell is nothing like I had imagined. A bell rung full circle rests mouth-up when it is at rest, balanced on a wheel with a rope round the rim, and when you pull it swings a full turn, mouth-down and back up. The sallies go up and down like a slow piston. Each stroke, you pull the sally on the handstroke, then catch the rope by the tail end on the backstroke, and the trick is to control the bell by how you release rather than by force. Humphrey, standing behind me, said that ringing is ninety per cent timing and ten per cent courage, and that the courage is only needed at the start.

For the first three Wednesdays I learned only to handle the bell. This meant ringing the smallest, called the treble, up and down again and again, while an instructor held the rope. My hands blistered. I let the sally go once, and it rose through the ceiling like a startled snake, and three people yelled. Humphrey retrieved it with a hooked pole and said that everyone does it once, and that his own moment came in 1978 and cost the church a pane of glass. He seems to derive real comfort from other people's disasters.

Then came the rounds. Ringing rounds means that all six bells ring in order from the highest to the lowest, one after another, at a steady interval, so that they make a descending scale. The skill is to place your bell in the right position in the row by adjusting the timing of each stroke. I had to listen, with an intensity I have rarely tried, to the sound of the bell before mine, and let go at exactly the right instant. On the fourth try I got it right and heard my own bell drop into the pattern like a stitch into a fabric. The captain, Ottoline, a formidable woman in a tweed skirt, said nothing and nodded once.

The tower's community is a delight. There are eleven regular ringers, ranging in age from fifteen to eighty-nine. The oldest, Percival, is the tenor ringer, and has rung the heaviest bell, a thirteen-hundredweight beast, for sixty-one years. He is deaf in one ear and refuses to acknowledge it. There is a family of three, mother, father and teenage daughter, who came together and are now inseparable. There is a doctor, a plumber, two teachers and a man who works at the sewage plant. Everyone brings a mug and a biscuit and the conversation between exercises ranges from the price of copper to the perils of hip surgery.

The next stage is called call changes, where the conductor calls out orders such as three to five and the ringers swap places in the row by ringing a little slower or faster. Ottoline conducts with a loud, bright voice and a remarkable ear. The first time she called a change and I got it right, I felt an absurd flush of joy. On the second, I panicked, pulled a stroke too soon and knocked the whole row off by a beat. The bells in a tower do not forgive; you hear your mistake in front of the whole street. Ottoline gave me a long look and said, kindly, that the mistake is not the sin, and stopping is.

After that come the methods. A method is a pattern of changes rung from memory, a bit like a dance, and each has a name: Plain Bob, Grandsire, Stedman, Cambridge Surprise. In Plain Bob Doubles, for five bells, each ringer follows a path called a blue line, and the trick is to know where you are by ear and by counting. I have been given a diagram of the Plain Bob line, a set of zigzags, and I have taped it to the fridge, where it is the only thing on the fridge apart from a takeaway menu. I get lost after about eleven blows. Humphrey says that everyone does and that the answer is to ring a little every day in your head, on the bus.

The practice night itself follows an order. At half past seven the ringers gather in the chamber and the captain announces the plan. Ottoline calls for a quarter of an hour of rounds to warm up, then twenty minutes of a method, then a break, then call changes. At eight-thirty the bells are lowered and the ringers go to the pub. On Sundays there is a service ringing at a quarter to ten, which lasts twenty minutes. I have not yet been allowed to ring for a service, since the congregation has ears, and Ottoline says that I will be ready in the spring.

Some numbers. The heaviest bell in the tower is the tenor, at thirteen hundredweight and two quarters, or about six hundred and eighty kilograms. The bells were cast in 1902 by a foundry in Loughborough and were rehung in 1996 with new fittings. The ropes have to be replaced every twelve years and cost around sixty pounds each. The tower's annual budget is about four thousand pounds, mostly for insurance and maintenance, and it is raised by a raffle, a summer fair and the generosity of the rector. A new ringer, Humphrey tells me, costs the tower nothing and repays it a hundredfold in noise.

The most peculiar thing about bell ringing is how it changes the way you hear. On my walk to the station I now stop when a church peals, and I count the bells, and listen for the rhythm. I can hear when a band is ringing in a rope-sight style and when a bell is being struck late. Last Sunday I stood on a bridge and heard a tower two miles away ring a beautiful touch of Grandsire, and I felt, for a moment, a kind of grief that I could not be one of the ringers. Then I remembered that on Wednesday, in a few days, I would be.

Last week Ottoline gave me a small green booklet, the ringers' handbook, with the rules of the tower and the words of the Ringers' Prayer. She also gave me a date, the second Saturday in March, for a striking competition at a neighbouring tower, and asked whether I would be prepared to sit in the band as a spare. I said I would be honoured. Humphrey said, gruffly, that I would probably be sent to hold the coats. I did not mind. I have written the date on the calendar in pencil, next to a diagram of a blue line, and I am practising in my head on the bus.

Fossil hunting on the Jurassic coast, a long weekend at Charmouth with the geology evening class. The class had been meeting for a term on Thursdays in a school science lab, and its tutor, an unflappable woman named Dr Adaeze Fairbrother, had promised a field trip if we all finished our homework. Fourteen of us signed up for the weekend, and we stayed in a hostel above the beach with bunk beds and a drying cupboard that smelled of warm socks. Dr Fairbrother, who has worked on this coast for twenty years, gave a talk on the Friday evening with slides of ammonites and a warning about the tide.

Her briefing was the most important part of the weekend. The cliffs between Charmouth and Lyme Regis are made of soft blue-grey mudstone and shale, deposited about a hundred and ninety-five million years ago in a warm shallow sea, and they slump constantly into the beach. The lower Lias, she said, is the richest fossil ground in Britain, and the fossils are washed out by the sea and left on the shingle. Do not go near the cliff face, she said, because the slumps are heavy and fast, and the fossils are best found on the loose stones on the beach. No hammers on the cliff, and no digging at the base.

The tide times set the plan for the day. Low tide on Saturday was at ten to eleven, with a height of point six metres, so we had a spell of about three hours on either side to search. Dr Fairbrother gave each of us a little card with the tide times printed on it and a stern instruction to be off the beach before the water turned. She also told us that after the storms of the previous winter there had been a huge fall of mud near the Spittles, and that the best hunting was on the stretch from the river mouth eastward.

I walked with a young man from the class named Tancred, who is a nurse and wanted to find an ammonite for his mother's birthday. We set out at nine, on a bright, cold morning with a low sun, following the line of the shingle at the foot of the cliff. It is a curious sort of walking, head down, scanning the pebbles, looking for anything that is not a pebble. After twenty minutes I found my first fossil, a little pale grey curl in a stone, which turned out to be the arm of a brittle star. Tancred said it was more than he had found, and stared at his own feet with renewed determination.

The first real find was Tancred's. He lifted a flat grey stone the size of a dinner plate and turned it over and there, in section, was an ammonite about the size of a hand, with the ribs of its shell visible as a spiral of tiny ridges. He held it up like a trophy. Dr Fairbrother, who had come up behind him, took a hand lens from her neck and looked at it in silence for half a minute. She said it was a Promicroceras, a small and common species, but a very good specimen, and that it was about a hundred and ninety-four million years old. Tancred blushed.

Over the next two hours we found more. Someone found a piece of belemnite, a bullet-shaped fossil that is the internal skeleton of a squid-like animal. Someone else found a fragment of fossil wood, black and shiny, a chunk of a conifer that grew on a shore long ago. I found several small ammonites in nodules, and a curious flat object that Dr Fairbrother identified with delight as the plate of a sea lily, a stalked relative of the starfish. She said that an amateur who finds a sea lily has already earned the weekend, and that I should keep it flat and dry. I wrapped it in a paper hanky and put it in my breast pocket.

The tide turned earlier than the card suggested. At about half past twelve we noticed the waves reaching the edge of the shingle, and Dr Fairbrother blew a whistle and called us to the path. There was a moment of confusion when Bertha, a woman who is seventy and completely fearless, refused to leave a stone she had been working at with a small chisel. She was eventually persuaded by two of the group taking an arm each. She had found a stone with a fossil fish scale, and she would not be parted from it.

The afternoon was for identifying and recording. We laid our finds on the hostel's dining benches in rows on sheets of newspaper, and Dr Fairbrother, in a cardigan, went along with a notebook and a hand lens naming each. The nurse's ammonite was declared the find of the day. There were twenty-six ammonites in the group's collection, seven belemnites, three pieces of fossil wood, one sea lily, one fish scale and a large number of stones that were just stones. She reminded us that a fossil is not worth anything unless you record where you found it, and that a label with the date, the place and the layer is what turns a curiosity into a specimen.

On Sunday we visited the museum in Lyme Regis, a small stone building on the main street with a huge collection and a cafe smelling of scones. The star of the museum is the display about a girl who found a complete ichthyosaur skeleton on these cliffs in the early nineteenth century, when she was twelve. Her name was Hester Pryor, and the museum has her tools, her notebooks and a cast of the skeleton, and there is a portrait of her with her dog. Dr Fairbrother told us that Hester was ignored by the scientific establishment for most of her life, and that she sold her fossils from a small shop to pay the rent.

We went home on Sunday evening with our finds wrapped in newspaper in shoeboxes. The final cost was a hundred and ten pounds for the weekend, including two nights in the hostel, breakfasts and a supper of fish and chips on the harbour wall. Dr Fairbrother told us that next spring's course would be on the Cretaceous chalk, and she handed out a reading list and a small chart of the geological time scale. I stared at it on the train, with a sea lily in my pocket, and thought about a hundred and ninety-five million years of silence and the twelve-year-old girl on the beach.

When I unwrapped the sea lily at home it fell into two pieces, and I stuck them together with a drop of glue and set them on my desk next to the lamp. It is about the size of a two-pence piece, with a flower pattern of tiny ridges around a hole. I have a label for it, in pencil on a scrap of card: crinoid stem plate, Charmouth, foot of the cliff east of the river, the twenty-first, found by me. I do not know why it moves me so much. Perhaps because it was alive, in a warm sea, when nothing else on the planet was thinking.

Wind orchestra concert tour, the four days in the Ardennes with the Harmonie Concordia. Through a colleague's cousin I found myself, at the age of thirty-four, sitting third clarinet in a community wind orchestra of forty-eight members whose average age is somewhere near sixty. The orchestra rehearses on Monday evenings in a school gymnasium in south London, and for the past year I had been learning to hold my own in the Lincolnshire suite. In April the orchestra's conductor, a mild, bespectacled Belgian named Florimond Van den Broeck, announced a tour to his home town of Bastogne to play at a spring festival, and asked who wanted to come. Thirty-one of us said yes.

We travelled by coach and ferry. The coach, a white forty-nine-seater with a toilet that nobody would use, left the school at six on a Thursday morning with the instruments in the hold and the tuba in a row of its own. The oboist, a woman with a cheerful face named Beatrix, had brought a bag of boiled sweets and a rota for who sits where, and she carried it with military efficiency. Florimond, in a corduroy jacket, sat at the front and studied the programme with a pencil, humming. By the time we were on the ferry at Dover half the orchestra was asleep, and the other half was arguing about a passage in the suite.

Bastogne was cold and clean and full of tanks. The town is known for a battle in the winter of 1944, and there are Sherman tanks and memorials on every corner, and the festival was being held in the square in front of the church, under a canopy of bunting. The visiting orchestras were put up in a former army barracks with rows of iron beds and a canteen serving soup and beer. My bunk was over the trombonist's, and he announced on the first night that he was a sleep-talker and would not be held responsible. I lay awake listening to him give a long speech in what I think was Flemish.

Our first rehearsal on the Friday morning was in a school hall. Florimond drew up the seating plan on a sheet of paper, and the whole orchestra, in coats and scarves, played through the festival programme: a brisk march, a suite of Flemish folk songs, the suite and an arrangement of a film theme that we had rehearsed for ten weeks and still did not quite trust. The hall's acoustic was dead, and Florimond, tapping his stand, said that the whole thing sounded as if it had been played in a cupboard. He asked us to play louder, and then, in a fit of despair, to stop watching him.

The festival began at two. There were seven visiting orchestras, from the Netherlands, France, Germany and Luxembourg, and each was given a half-hour slot on a temporary stage. The Dutch orchestra played first, a large and gleaming ensemble in blazers, with a virtuoso bass clarinet and a repertoire of Broadway numbers. The German one, in green waistcoats, played a march so tightly synchronised that I could not tell where one player ended and the next began. Beatrix leaned over and whispered that we were going to be a disgrace, and then, that we would be a disgrace with heart.

Our slot was at twenty past four, when the light was going and the cold was setting in. We filed on stage with our instruments and our numb fingers and sat under the canopy while a stagehand adjusted the microphones. I looked out at the square and saw perhaps two hundred people, mostly in coats, sitting on folding chairs, with a few children on their parents' shoulders. Florimond raised his baton, glanced at us with an expression I shall never forget, a sort of tender terror, and gave the downbeat. We began the march. The sound rolled out across the square and bounced back from the church, and I felt my fingers loosen.

We played the suite third, and it was the best we have ever played it. In the middle section, where the clarinets have a long melody in thirds, I found myself listening to Beatrix on the oboe and following her breath. A boy of about ten in the front row was conducting with a pencil, and there was a moment near the end, in a hushed passage, where every person in the square was silent and I could hear a flag flapping. When the last chord died away, there was a pause of about two seconds and then the whole square erupted. Florimond turned, his glasses fogged, and mouthed a word I took to be thank you.

That evening, the orchestras were guests of the town at a banquet in the market hall. A long line of trestles was laden with sausage, potatoes and a stew of beef cooked in dark beer, and the mayor, a large man in a chain, made a speech in three languages. Somebody had brought an accordion and the Dutch orchestra, the Germans and the French were soon singing in a mixed chorus that grew louder with each toast. I sat with the trombonist, who turned out to be a retired schoolteacher named Cornelius, and who told me at length about his allotment and his late wife, and gave me his recipe for pear jam.

On the Saturday we performed a second concert, a short one, in the church. The sound in the church was magnificent, warm and generous, and we could hear each other properly for the first time. Florimond added a piece that was not on the programme, a slow chorale, and asked us to play it very quietly, with the sound just at the edge of silence. It lasted three minutes, and as the last note faded, someone at the back of the church coughed, and then someone began to clap, slowly, and then the whole church joined. I did not dare look at the others.

The journey home on Sunday was quieter. We stopped at a service station near Ghent for lunch, where Beatrix produced a bag of small Belgian chocolates from her coat and handed them round the coach. Someone had brought a bottle of jenever, and the trombonist made a toast in his sleep. Florimond stood in the aisle and delivered a short speech, thanking us for our patience and our courage, and telling us that the concert in the church was the finest music he had heard in ten years. Then he sat down, put his head on the seat, and slept until Dover.

The costs, as the treasurer reported, came to two hundred and sixty pounds a head, including the coach, the ferry, the barracks and the banquet, and the orchestra's sponsor covered the rest. Next year's tour is planned for a town in Saxony. I have already told the section leader that I will come, and I have promised Beatrix that I will practise my scales. Cornelius has sent me, by post, a card with the pear jam recipe: two kilos of fruit, one of sugar, a stick of cinnamon, and, in his cramped handwriting, the words play louder.

Knitting fair stall, a full day behind the counter for the Marsden Wool Circle at the autumn craft fair. My aunt Rosamund has run the circle's stall for eleven years and broke her wrist in September, so I was drafted to stand in for her with a folding chair, a cash tin and a laminated price list. The fair takes place in the covered market hall on the first Saturday of October, with eighty stalls under a glass roof, and the wool circle's pitch is beside a man who sells hand-turned wooden spoons and a woman who sells jars of quince paste. I arrived at seven to set up in the dark, carrying four boxes of finished goods up a flight of stairs.

The stock was a delight and a burden. There were forty-two hats, thirty scarves in a range of thick, soft colours, a dozen pairs of fingerless mitts, eighteen baby cardigans, and a heap of small felted animals made by a member named Gwendolen, who is ninety and does a fox that is famous throughout the county. Rosamund had left a note pinned to the lid of the top box: hats at twelve pounds, scarves at eighteen, mitts at nine, cardigans at twenty-two, animals at four, and do not, under any circumstances, discount the fox.

The morning was slow. The doors opened at ten, and for the first hour the only visitors were stallholders swapping their wares. A man in a flat cap bought a scarf for his wife and then returned ten minutes later to ask whether the scarf was itchy. I said that it was merino, which is soft, and he said that his wife's neck was a law unto itself. By eleven the aisles were filling up with families and older couples, and there was a queue for the tea urn at the far end of the hall.

Selling turned out to be an odd mixture of shyness and performance. People would stop and stroke a scarf and look at the price and then move away without a word, and I learned that the best thing to do is to say nothing for a full ten seconds and then mention that each piece is made by one of eleven women in the village, and that the pattern is on the label. This worked so well that I sold twelve hats before noon. A girl of about seven insisted on trying on every hat in turn and ended by buying a pink one with an enormous pompom, paid for with a fistful of coins from her mother's purse.

At lunch I ate a pie from the stall opposite and looked at the stalls near us. The wooden spoon man, a burly person named Torquil, told me that he makes about six hundred spoons a year on a foot-powered lathe in a shed and sells them at four fairs. The quince paste woman, whose name was Delphine, said that she cooks quince in a cauldron in her yard for eight hours and sells out by the second Saturday. We agreed that fairs are like a small society in which everybody depends on a cold day and a good tea urn.

The afternoon brought the serious buyers. A woman in a beautiful green coat spent twenty minutes selecting a set of five baby cardigans for a charity shop that she runs, and asked whether she could have a discount for quantity. I said that I would ask, and rang Rosamund, who sounded groggy and said yes, ten per cent, but not the fox. A retired teacher bought all thirty of the scarves' matching mitts, and a group of students from the local art college bought four hats between them and asked to photograph the stall for a project.

The fox drew a crowd. Gwendolen had made a little group of them sitting in a row on a piece of moss-green felt, each with tiny embroidered eyes and a tail tipped in white, and children kept coming to hold them. A man in a suit asked how much for the fox, and I said four pounds, and he said that was a ridiculous price for a work of art. He paid ten and told me to keep the change for the Wool Circle. I put it in the tin with a slight pang, thinking that Gwendolen would never accept it.

By four, the hall was quiet again. I counted the tin, which took a while because half of it was in coins, and found that I had taken three hundred and eighty-seven pounds and fifty pence, of which twenty-one pounds were from the fox and its neighbours. There were eleven hats and nine scarves left, and I packed them into the boxes, folding each with the tissue paper Rosamund had insisted on. The wooden spoon man came round to help me carry the boxes to the car, and left me with a spoon in a paper bag, which he said was for my aunt's wrist.

I took the money and the leftover stock to Rosamund's house that evening. She was on the sofa with her arm in plaster, and she made me sit down and give her a full account, item by item, as if I were reporting on a battle. When I told her about the man in the suit and the ten pounds for the fox, she put a hand over her mouth and said that it was the best price a fox had ever fetched. She wrote the total in a ruled exercise book, in a slanting hand, next to the figure from the year before. It was up by forty-one pounds.

The lesson from the day is that a stall is a small business run on trust. The takings, after the pitch fee of forty pounds, went to the circle's fund, which pays for a hall for its Thursday meetings and for wool for the members who cannot afford it. Rosamund has asked me to stand in for her at the Christmas fair as well, and I have said yes, and asked for her to teach me to knit. She said that I would be no good at it and that she would begin on Sunday.

Bat survey at Saint Cuthbert's, a summer evening walk-and-count organised by the county bat group. The parish church has a colony of common pipistrelles roosting in the gap between the roof timbers and the stone parapet, and the group counts them every July as they leave at dusk. I was one of six volunteers, each given a folding stool, a clicker counter and a small hand-held detector that turns the bats' ultrasonic calls into a rhythmic clicking. The lead surveyor, a quiet man in his fifties named Ezekiel Hartigan, met us at the lychgate at half past eight and issued a torch with a red filter, since white light disturbs the bats.

Ezekiel began with a short briefing. The church is a known maternity roost, he said, where females gather in early summer to give birth and rear their young, and in the last three years the count has been between four hundred and six hundred. The emergence begins about twenty minutes after sunset, and it can be over in twenty minutes or last an hour, depending on the weather. Our job was to stand at six points around the building, each watching one exit, and to click the counter once for every bat that flew out. We were to say nothing and touch nothing, and not to worry if we saw none for a long time.

I was assigned the north-east corner, by an old yew tree, where a gap under the parapet lets the bats slip out into the churchyard. The evening was warm, with a low orange sun turning the tombstones rose-coloured, and a blackbird was singing on the roof. I sat on my stool with the counter in one hand and the detector in the other and waited. The detector was set to a frequency of forty-five kilohertz, where the pipistrelle calls, and produced a soft crackle of static. Somewhere a wood pigeon cooed, and a car passed on the lane.

At nine-oh-eight the sun dropped behind the hill and the light went a deep grey-blue. At nine-twenty-two the detector gave a sudden burst of clicks, like a Geiger counter, and a tiny dark shape flickered out of the gap and spiralled up into the sky. I clicked once. Then another followed, and another, and within a minute there were a dozen, then thirty, then a steady stream, pouring out of the parapet like smoke from a chimney. I lost count of what I was counting and simply clicked, my thumb moving on its own, while the detector rattled in my hand.

It was one of the most thrilling things I have ever seen. The bats were so small, each about the size of a thumb, and so quick that I could only see them as a flicker against the last of the light. They circled above the yew tree, swooping between the branches, and then streamed away over the field towards the river, where the insects are. The detector gave a strange, wet chatter as each one passed, and I heard, in the pauses between them, the faint rustle of a pipistrelle's wings as it flew close to my head. I could have sat there all night.

The flow ended at ten-fifteen, abruptly, and I clicked the counter one final time and looked at the total. It read two hundred and nine for my exit. Ezekiel came round with a notepad and took each of our numbers, adding them in his head and writing the sum at the bottom. The six of us had counted a total of five hundred and twelve, which was higher than last year's four hundred and eighty-three and a sign that the colony was thriving. He wrote it down carefully, with the date, the temperature, the time of the first emergence and the last.

Afterwards we gathered on the church path and Ezekiel made hot chocolate from a flask. He told us about the bats' diet: a single pipistrelle can eat three thousand midges in a night, and a colony this size clears a small cloud of insects from the river. He also explained the legal side. All bats and their roosts are protected by law, and it is an offence to disturb them, even in a church, so the parish must ask permission before repairing the roof. The churchwarden, a nervous woman named Prudence, had brought a folder of forms and did not look reassured.

Ezekiel spent the last ten minutes describing what the group does through the rest of the year: winter hibernation counts in caves and cellars, a helpline for people who find a bat in the house, and training for volunteers. He asked whether any of us would like to attend a workshop on handling injured bats, held in a village hall in September and costing fifteen pounds. I put my name on the list, and I have since bought a pair of thin leather gloves.

I walked home under a sky just beginning to show stars. In my ears I could still hear the crackle of the detector, and every time I passed a lamp post I looked for a tiny flickering shape in the light. Halfway home I saw one, small and dark, wheeling round a street lamp, and I stopped and watched for a full minute. I have never noticed before how many of them there are. The figure I keep repeating to myself is five hundred and twelve, the number that came out of the roof of a small church in the fading light.

Community radio transmitter upgrade, notes from the technical day at Riverside FM, where the studio is a sponsor and Blake and Colm volunteered to help. The station broadcasts from a converted signal box beside the canal, to about forty thousand listeners in the valley, and its old transmitter, a valve-era beast installed in 1996, has been failing for a year. The station manager, Ludovica Ashworth, secured a grant to buy a new one, and a retired broadcast engineer named Ambrose Pettifer offered to supervise the installation. He asked for two strong volunteers and a person who could read a wiring diagram, and we came as three.

The signal box is a two-storey brick building with a flat roof and a small yard, and the studio is on the upper floor, up an iron stair, with a mixing desk, two microphones and a shelf of records. The transmitter lives in a locked cabinet downstairs, beside a rack of amplifiers and a heater that makes the whole ground floor smell of hot dust. Ambrose, in a boiler suit, walked us round on the Saturday morning and showed us the aerial feed, a thick coaxial cable running up the wall through a hole in the brick, and the mast, forty metres of galvanised steel in the yard.

The new transmitter arrived on a pallet at nine, a sleek grey box the size of a large suitcase, and it took four of us to carry it into the building. Ambrose explained that the old one had a power output of fifty watts and the new would have a hundred, but that the licence would allow only eighty, so the extra would be held in reserve. He said that ninety per cent of the job was wiring and ten per cent was persuading the regulator's engineer that the wiring was right. I held the diagram, Colm held the torch, and Blake held a screwdriver in his teeth.

Removing the old transmitter was the messy part. The cabinet was full of dust, cobwebs and, to our surprise, a mouse's nest made of shredded foam, complete with a small store of sunflower seeds. Ambrose lifted it out in a dustpan and carried it to the yard with a serious expression, saying that in thirty years he had never found a mouse that did not have opinions about cabling. We disconnected each lead in turn, labelled it with masking tape, and lifted the old unit onto a sack truck. It weighed forty kilograms and had a brass plate inscribed with a serial number and a date.

Fitting the new one took the rest of the morning. The connections are simple in principle: the audio feed comes in from the studio, the radio signal goes out to the aerial, and power comes from the mains through a filter. In practice the audio feed had to be re-terminated with new connectors, and the aerial cable needed a new plug soldered on. Ambrose taught Colm to strip and solder with the patience of a man shaving a peach, and the connector came out perfect on the third attempt. Ludovica appeared with a tray of sandwiches and stood at the door, watching, with her hands clasped.

The critical stage was the power-up. Ambrose connected a dummy load, a big finned resistor that soaks up the transmitter's output without radiating it, and switched on the new unit for the first time. The display lit up in a cheerful green and a fan started, and he adjusted the drive until the power meter read exactly eighty watts. He then checked the frequency with a small counter, and the reading was steady to the fifth decimal place. He said that the previous transmitter had drifted by about a kilohertz per week and had to be nudged with a screwdriver, and that this one would not.

At two in the afternoon he connected the real aerial and asked Ludovica to go upstairs and put on a record. The station was off the air for exactly four minutes, and when it came back the sound in the speakers was startlingly clean, with none of the hiss that had been a feature of the old transmitter. Ludovica had chosen a jazz record and we listened to the first three minutes standing in the yard, our faces turned to the mast. A man walking his dog on the towpath stopped and said that the signal was better than he had ever heard it.

The regulator's engineer arrived at four with a laptop and a spectrum analyser and inspected the installation with the manner of a doctor. He measured the output, the harmonics and the modulation, and found that the second harmonic was slightly high, which he asked Ambrose to reduce with a filter. Ambrose retrieved one from a cardboard box in the corner and fitted it in ten minutes. The engineer measured again, wrote a number in his notebook and signed a form, and there was a moment of silence before Ludovica clapped.

The costs came to eleven thousand two hundred pounds, of which the grant covered nine thousand, and the studio's sponsorship of fifteen hundred pounds covered most of the remainder. Ludovica offered the studio a free on-air announcement, a fifteen-second message played twice a day for a year, and Blake wrote the script over a sandwich. It says, in a very plain voice, that the station is supported by a local studio that has, for the first time in its life, been thanked by a mouse.

We left at six, coated in dust, with a small sack of sunflower seeds as a memento. On the walk to the car I realised that the old transmitter, on its sack truck, was still in the yard with a tarpaulin on it. Ambrose said he intended to fix it up and give it to the local museum as a piece of broadcasting history, and Ludovica said that it would be a fitting end. I looked at the old brass plate with its faded date, and I thought about twenty-nine years of programmes going out through a metal box in a cupboard.

Falconry experience day, the studio outing to the Highcliffe Hawk Sanctuary, written up as a team record. Twelve of us went on a Friday in May, in two cars, for a day of handling birds of prey in a walled meadow at the edge of a country estate. The sanctuary is run by a husband and wife, Anselm and Marguerite Tredwell, who keep forty-three birds and offer a programme of courses for beginners. We were greeted in the yard by a small dog, a large goose and Anselm, in a leather glove, who held out a hand and said that the first rule of falconry is that the bird is in charge.

We began with a talk in the sanctuary's barn, over tea in mugs the size of buckets. Anselm explained that falconry is a partnership between a person and a wild animal that could leave whenever it chose. The birds are trained with food, patience and trust, and they are flown at a weight that keeps them keen but healthy, weighed every day on a set of scales like those used for parcels. He introduced the equipment: the glove, which is thick leather with a long cuff; the jesses, which are leather straps on the legs; and the leash and swivel. Everything was laid out on a bench with its name on a card.

Then came the birds. We were taken to the mews, a long low shed with a row of perches, and there they sat, each hooded or watching with a steady golden eye. There was a Harris hawk called Bramble, a barn owl called Ghost, a kestrel, a pair of buzzards, a peregrine as sleek as a knife, and an eagle owl the size of a toddler, whose name was Herbert. The eagle owl fixed his orange eyes on Sanne and did not blink. Marguerite, a tall woman with iron-grey hair and a low voice, said that the birds could tell who was frightened, and that it was best not to think about it.

The first flight was with Bramble. Each of us in turn put on the glove and stood in the middle of the meadow, with a piece of raw chick between finger and thumb. Marguerite released the hawk from a post twenty metres off, and she came in low and fast across the grass with her wings barely moving, and landed on the glove with a light thump and a scrabble of claws. The weight of her was startling, a pound and a half, and the grip of her feet was strong but not painful. She ate the chick in three gulps, looked at me with a wild sideways glance, and flew away.

Ilse was next, and she was superb. She held the glove out at exactly the right angle, kept her nerve, and when Bramble landed she murmured something and the hawk stayed for a full minute, preening, before she flew back to the post. Colm was less lucky. The hawk landed on his head, and, in the confusion, on his shoulder, and finally on the top of his hat, where she stayed, eyeing the crowd. Marguerite told him not to move. He stood as still as a statue for four minutes, until the hawk decided, with disdain, to leave.

The owl was the most enchanting. Ghost, the barn owl, flew silently down the meadow from a fence post, her white face floating like a moon in the shade of the trees, and settled on Blake's glove without a sound at all. Anselm said that the owl's feathers have a soft fringe that muffles the noise of the air, and that a mouse hears nothing until the moment it is caught. Blake said that he had never felt so peaceful. The owl turned her head, in a movement that seemed to go all the way round, and looked at him with dark, calm eyes.

After lunch, which was a sandwich in the sun on a rug, Anselm gave a demonstration of the peregrine, called Flint. She was flown to a lure, a leather pad on a long cord swung in a circle, and the display was breathtaking. She rose to about two hundred metres, circled, and stooped, folding her wings and falling in a fast, straight line at more than a hundred miles an hour, and swept up at the last second to strike the lure. There was a gasp from all of us. Anselm said that a peregrine in a stoop is the fastest animal in the world, and that Flint's record was a hundred and thirty.

We asked a lot of questions. Sanne wanted to know what happened if a bird did not return, and Anselm said that it happens perhaps once in a career, that the birds carry a small radio tag, and that most come back on their own after a night in a tree. Avery asked how long the birds live, and he said that a hawk can reach twenty in captivity, and that Herbert, the eagle owl, was thirty-one. Colm asked whether the birds had ever bitten anyone, and Marguerite said that they had, and that it had been Anselm, more than once.

The price for the day was ninety pounds a head, and we were given a certificate and a photograph of ourselves with a bird. The sanctuary is a charity, and a fair proportion of the money goes towards the treatment of injured wild birds brought in by members of the public. In the yard, on the way out, we passed a pen with a crippled buzzard that was being nursed back to health, and Marguerite told us that she would be released in the autumn. We each dropped a few coins into a tin and left with sandwich crumbs on our shirts, a rare quiet in the car, and one very long feather Ilse had been allowed to keep.

Sailing club winter maintenance weekend, the working party at Tarn Reach, where the studio's four dinghy owners had to put in their sixteen hours. The club has forty boats, a slipway and a clubhouse with a bar that opens on Sundays, and every February the members are asked to turn out for two Saturdays of scrubbing, painting and repairing before the season begins. Blake and I brought a pair of overalls each, a thermos, and a sandwich in a plastic bag. The organiser, a cheerful man named Godwin Tarrant with a face like a walnut, met us at the gate at half past eight with a clipboard and a list of forty-three jobs.

The jobs were divided by ability. Godwin looked at me, asked whether I had used a sander, and gave me a sheet of rough paper and a pot of filler. Blake was put in charge of the rescue boat, a rigid-hulled boat with a forty-horsepower outboard, which had to be checked for leaks, its fuel lines replaced and its safety kit counted. There were two dozen other members, most of them retired and wearing thick jumpers, standing about in twos and threes in the cold yard, discussing the weather, the state of the slip and the vices of the committee.

I was assigned to a battered wooden dinghy called Puffin, which belongs to a widow named Winifred Osei and has been in the club for fifty-two years. The hull was cracked along one seam and the varnish was peeling, and my job was to sand it back to bare wood, apply a coat of primer and fill the cracks. It took the whole morning, and my arms ached, and the dust got into my hair and my sandwich. Winifred herself came down at eleven with a folding chair and sat next to me, supervising, with a tartan blanket over her knees and a flask of soup in her lap.

She told me the history of the boat while I worked. Puffin was built in 1971 in a yard in Cornwall, in marine plywood, by a man who later became a bishop, and Winifred's late husband bought her second-hand for two hundred pounds. They sailed her together every summer for thirty years, and she has won the club's slowest boat trophy eleven times. Winifred said, with dignity, that the trophy is a great honour, and that any fool can sail fast. She then handed me a piece of sandpaper of a finer grade and told me to go with the grain.

Blake meanwhile was having an adventure with the outboard. The engine had not started for a year, and the club's mechanic, a taciturn man named Osgood, took it apart on a bench in the boatshed and found that the carburettor was blocked with gum. He cleaned it with a spray and a piece of wire, put it all back and pulled the cord thirty times without result. On the thirty-first the engine coughed, spat, and roared into life, and a cloud of blue smoke filled the shed, and Godwin appeared at the door and said that this was the best sound he had heard all year.

At lunchtime the members gathered in the clubhouse, where the bar had been opened early for soup, and two big pots of stew and a heap of buttered rolls sat on trestles. The talk was of the coming season: the race calendar, the new starting line, the price of insurance and the question of whether the club should buy a second rescue boat. A young member named Fenella, a nurse, made a case for it with a set of figures on the back of an envelope. Godwin listened, nodded and said that this would be a matter for the annual meeting, and that everyone should keep it in their prayers.

The afternoon was for painting. Osgood, who is the club's unofficial boatwright, showed me how to brush on the primer and how to feather the edges, and told me that the best paint job is one where you do not see the brush. I did three coats on the port side and one on the starboard, and Winifred, from her chair, made a running commentary. By four the light was going and the wind had turned bitter, and Godwin called the day to a close with a whistle. The results were displayed on the whiteboard in the clubhouse: eleven boats sanded, six painted, one engine running.

At the end of the day Godwin handed out cards to be stamped, one for every four hours of work, and the members lined up like children at a school fete. I had earned two stamps, and Blake three. The club rule is that each member must complete four stamps by the end of March or pay a fee of sixty pounds to be excused, and I said, in a moment of foolishness, that we would come back the following Saturday. Winifred said that Puffin would need a second coat, and would I like to come to her house afterwards for cake.

The next Saturday I did, and Puffin looked magnificent, all deep blue with a white stripe, and Winifred insisted on a photograph. We drank tea in her parlour, at a small round desk covered with a lace cloth, while she told me about the year the club held a regatta in a gale. At the end of the afternoon she gave me a small brass cleat from her husband's toolbox and asked me to keep it in my pocket for luck. It is on my desk now, next to the pen tray, and every time I see it I think of a long-haired man with a plywood boat and a slow, contented smile.

Lichen survey on the heath, a morning with the Field Studies Society at Wenlock Common. The society organises an annual recording day for the county's lichen list, and I joined for the first time on a cold, bright Saturday in November, when the trees are bare and the crusts on the branches are easiest to see. There were nine of us, led by a small, intense woman named Dr Cordelia Vance who carries a hand lens on a cord round her neck and a spare in her pocket. She told us at the start that lichens are not plants but a partnership between a fungus and an alga, and that we would not be able to tell one from another until we had looked at a hundred.

Our task was to record every species on a set of thirty old oaks along a lane at the edge of the common. Each tree was tagged with a number on a yellow plastic disc, and the method was to walk once round, look at the trunk from ground level to head height, and write in a notebook the name of every lichen growing there. Dr Vance handed each of us a hand lens with a magnification of ten, a field guide with a crumpled spine, and a small bottle of chemical reagent, which she warned us not to drink.

At the first tree I found nothing that I could name. The trunk was covered in a mosaic of grey, green and yellow patches, some crusty and flat, some leafy and curling at the edges, some with tiny black or orange discs on the surface. Dr Vance appeared at my elbow and pointed to a bright orange patch, and said that it was Xanthoria parietina, the common sunburst lichen, which is a sign of nutrient-rich air. She moved her finger to a pale grey rosette with a wrinkled surface and said that it was Parmelia sulcata, which has a network of fine ridges like a map of rivers.

By ten I had begun to see it. The bark was not a background but a landscape, with territories, borders and neighbourhoods. On the north side of each trunk a cool green crust of Lecanora grew in a broad band, while on the south, where the sun beat, the orange patches took over. Dr Vance said that the presence of a species called Usnea, a pale green tuft that hangs like a beard, is a sign of clean air, and she led us to an old oak at the end of the lane where a long, wispy, silvery tuft hung from a branch. We stood in silence, in a small circle, looking up.

The count of the day, which we tallied over a flask at noon, came to sixty-three species across the thirty trees. The richest tree, number nineteen, carried twenty-seven on its own, and Dr Vance was clearly delighted. She said that the previous survey, eleven years ago, had found forty-eight, and that the increase reflected a general improvement in air quality following the closure of a brickworks. She logged the results in a spreadsheet on her phone, with her thumbs, and told us that the county records centre would receive them by Monday.

The chemical test was a small drama. To identify some species, you put a drop of reagent on the inner layer of the lichen and see what colour it turns. Dr Vance let me apply a drop of a solution to a grey crust, and the patch turned instantly a deep blood red, which she said meant that it was Ochrolechia. I felt a childish pleasure, as if I had made a spell work. I asked whether the test harmed the lichen, and she said that it did, slightly, and that this was why we only test a single patch and always leave the rest.

I went home with cold hands and a list of nineteen new names in my notebook, and I have since borrowed a book on the lichens of Britain from the library, a heavy volume with hundreds of colour photographs. I now find myself looking at the walls, the pavement and the gravestones on my street, and seeing patches of grey, green and gold that I had never noticed. The society meets on the first Sunday of each month, and the subscription is fifteen pounds a year. I have paid it.

Printing workshop, a Saturday course in hand-set wood type at the Bickerdike Press, taken by four of the studio's designers as a treat. The press occupies a former dairy behind a bookshop and has thirty drawers of type, three cast-iron presses and a proofing bench stained with a century of ink. The instructor, a stooped, kindly man named Lachlan Ferreira, welcomed us in an apron the colour of a bruise. He told us that everything we would learn that day was invented five hundred years ago and has not really been improved since, and that we should keep our sleeves away from the rollers.

We began by learning to set type. The wooden characters are stored in a wide shallow case with a compartment for each character, arranged in a pattern that Lachlan said had been developed for speed rather than logic, so that the most common characters are nearest the hand. Each of us had a composing stick, a small metal tray held in the left hand, and the job was to pick the characters one at a time, upside down and back to front, and place them in a row. My first line took eleven minutes and read, on inspection, as a mirror image of a nonsense word.

Spacing is an art of its own.
