Between the words and lines you must insert pieces of blank metal and wood, called furniture, to fill the gap, and the whole block must be locked into a frame, called a chase, tightly enough that you can lift it without a single piece falling out. Lachlan showed us how to tap the block level with a mallet and a flat piece of wood, and how to tighten the quoins, small wedges, with a key. He said that the difference between a good printer and a bad one is that the bad one has lifted a form and heard a sound like a handful of rain.

The poster we set was a four-line text on the theme of a village fete, in three sizes of type, with a decorative border cut from wood. Blake, who is a typographer by training, was in heaven, and immediately began to argue with Lachlan about the kerning of a capital character. Lachlan said that the wooden type has no kerning, and that the eye must do the work. They settled on a compromise involving a sliver of card. Sanne, meanwhile, had made an accidental masterpiece by dropping a whole line and setting the pieces in the order they fell.

Printing was the thrilling part. We locked the chase onto the bed of the press, rolled a thin film of black ink over the type with a hand roller, laid a sheet of thick cream paper on top and pulled a big lever. The impression was deep and crisp, with a slight ridge that could be felt with a fingertip. Lachlan lifted the sheet with a flourish and held it up to the light. A hush fell on the group. We made twelve prints each, and by the end of the afternoon the bench was a mass of drying posters and our hands were black to the wrist.

At the end of the day we were given our prints in a cardboard tube and a certificate. The course cost seventy-five pounds each, including materials, and the press offers a more advanced course in the spring on printing in two colours. Blake has hung his poster over his desk and says that it is the only thing in his life that he has made by hand that has no undo button. Sanne has framed hers and given it to her mother. I have a copy, folded, in a book, and it smells faintly of linseed oil, ink and the old dairy.

Cricket club roller, the sad and instructive story of how the village club spent one winter buying a groundsman's machine. I have played for the Netherby Second XI for three seasons, mostly as a lower-order batter with a reputation for running people out, and in October the treasurer, a large, gentle man named Eldred Mowbray, called a meeting in the pavilion to discuss the state of the square. The old roller, a pre-war iron cylinder pulled by hand, had finally cracked, and the pitch had developed a hump at one end that made the ball behave like a rabbit. Twenty-two members sat on plastic chairs in their coats and voted on what to do.

The debate was long. The president, a retired colonel with a moustache, argued for a new motorised roller at a cost of three thousand eight hundred pounds. The captain of the First XI said that the money should go to new nets. An elderly member named Cecil, who has been the club's scorer for fifty years, said that everything was much better in his day, when the roller was pulled by a pony called Duchess. Eldred, from the chair, said that he had no pony in the budget. The vote to buy a roller passed at last by fourteen to seven with one abstention, and Eldred was authorised to find one.

The search took the whole of November. Eldred brought back a folder of brochures and a list of secondhand offers, and the committee visited three machines in three counties on a series of wet Saturdays. The first, a small green roller from a golf club, was too light, and the second, from a school, had a broken engine. The third was offered by a farmer in the next valley, a two-tonne diesel machine of great age and charm, painted a faded red and called, on a brass plate, the Mowbray Special, although no relation to Eldred. The price was one thousand four hundred pounds, or nine hundred and fifty with a promise of tickets to the dinner.

We went to inspect it on a bitter Sunday in early December, a delegation of five, with Cecil in the back seat giving advice. The farmer, who wore a cloth cap and spoke in monosyllables, wheeled the roller from a barn and started it on the second pull. It shook, coughed, filled the yard with smoke and settled into a deep, steady chug that seemed to me, as a person who knows nothing about engines, wonderful. Cecil walked round it twice, poked a finger into the oil and pronounced it sound. Eldred wrote a cheque on the bonnet.

Getting it home was an adventure. The club does not own a trailer, so we borrowed one from a member who runs a plant hire firm, and towed the roller across two miles of country lanes at eleven miles an hour, with Eldred at the wheel of the club's van and the rest of us walking behind like mourners. A tractor got stuck behind us for the last mile and the driver waved cheerfully. When we finally reached the ground, the light was fading and the pavilion clock struck four. The roller was unloaded down a plank with a great deal of shouting.

The first roll of the season was on a March morning, when the frost had just gone. Eldred, in a waxed jacket, climbed on the seat, started the engine and rolled the square up and down in long parallel strokes while the rest of us watched from the boundary with flasks of tea. Cecil counted the passes aloud, and at eleven he raised a hand and said that it was flat. I took a ball from my bag and bowled it onto the strip, and it bounced true and even, and everyone applauded, which is not something that normally happens to my bowling.

The season has been a good one. The Second XI won eight games and lost seven, and the First XI finished third in the league. The roller has been used every week and has developed a personality; it has a habit of stalling in the second half of the outfield, and Eldred has a special name for that patch. The total bill, with a service, a new set of tyres and a garage of its own built from pallets, came to two thousand one hundred and forty pounds, which Eldred read out at the annual meeting to a satisfied hum. The colonel, apparently moved, has proposed a plaque.

Digitisation weekend at the Hallby village archive, notes for myself and for the parish history group. The archive lives in the old schoolmaster's cottage behind the church, two cramped chambers of grey steel shelving, and for years its only visitors were the three of us who volunteer on Tuesdays. This spring the county heritage office lent us a flatbed scanner and a small grant for storage, so Saturday and Sunday were set aside to make a first real dent in the collection.

Saturday began with Gunnar Ekdahl, the group's chairman, unlocking the cottage at eight and grumbling that the scanner box was larger than the desk it was meant to sit on. We cleared the map drawers to make space. Gunnar has kept the archive since he retired from the sawmill, and he knows where everything is without reading a label, which is exactly the problem: none of it is written down. Our first decision was therefore to make a simple list before scanning anything, one line per box, with a shelf number in pencil on the lid.

The list took the whole morning. Box one held minute books of the fishing cooperative from 1921 onward, box two the school registers, box three a jumble of photographs with no names on the back. Astrid Lund, who is eighty-seven and was born in the parish, sat with a magnifying glass and put names to about a third of the faces. She identified the man with the enormous moustache as the ferryman, and said his boat was called the Perseverance and that it leaked. Gunnar wrote all of this on slips of acid-free paper and tucked them into the sleeves.

We agreed some rules to keep the work honest. Every item is scanned at four hundred dots per inch, saved as an uncompressed image, and given a file name made of the box number, the item number and a short word. Nothing is cropped. Fragile pages are handled with clean cotton gloves, and anything that cracks when opened is photographed with the lid of the box as a stand instead of being forced flat. Elin, the youngest of us at fifty-two, was made keeper of the log, in which she notes the start and end time of every session and who scanned what.

By lunch, which was a flask of soup on the church steps, we had scanned forty-one school register pages and I had learned how much a flatbed scanner dislikes a curled page. The trick, discovered by Elin, is to lay a sheet of clear acrylic over the paper. It flattens the curl and does no harm, though it doubles the reflections until you tilt the glass a fraction. After that the pages came out clean and the pace roughly doubled.

The afternoon belonged to the maps. The parish holds an enclosure map on linen, about a metre and a half wide, showing every strip of the common land before it was divided. It cannot go on the scanner, so we photographed it in eight overlapping tiles on the floor of the old school hall with a borrowed camera on a tripod, then Elin stitched the tiles at home that night. Reading the result on her laptop on Sunday, we found a field name none of us had ever heard, Sorrow Acre, on the low ground by the stream. Astrid laughed and said her grandmother had used it for a plot where nothing ever ripened.

Sunday was quieter and better organised. We had a rhythm: Gunnar fetched a box, I scanned, Elin logged, Astrid read out anything she could add. We reached the cooperative minute books before noon. They are written in a careful sloping hand, and the entry that stopped us all was for a winter meeting when the members voted to buy one shared motor for the boats rather than five separate ones, at a cost of four hundred and ten crowns. Gunnar said the fishermen argued for two evenings about who would be allowed to borrow it first.

A practical problem appeared at three. The external drive we bought filled faster than we predicted, because uncompressed images are enormous, and by the end of the day we had used nearly a third of it on only six boxes. Gunnar wanted to switch to compressed files. Elin and I argued for keeping the large ones and buying a second drive, on the grounds that the whole point is to do the job once. We compromised: keep the large masters on two drives, one kept at Elin's home and one in the cottage, and make small copies for the website.

I should record the smaller lessons so they are not lost. Pencil, never pen, near the documents. Label the scanner glass with masking tape so the tool cannot wander off with a volunteer. Bring a proper lamp, since the cottage has one bulb and it flickers. Keep the door open when the sun is on the slate roof, because the old school hall gets hot enough to make the gloves sticky by two. And do not let Gunnar tell the stories while scanning is happening, because everyone stops and listens, which is delightful but slow.

At closing time we counted. In two days we scanned two hundred and sixty-three items from eleven boxes, of which the school registers and the cooperative minutes were the bulk, plus the eight map tiles and a folder of forty photographs that now carry at least a provisional name. Elin entered the numbers in the log. It is not much against the roughly ninety boxes still on the shelves, but Gunnar reckoned that at this pace, with volunteers on Tuesdays and one weekend each season, the whole archive could be finished in about three years.

Before leaving, the group agreed the next steps. Elin will draft a short note for the parish website inviting anyone who recognises faces to write in. Astrid has promised to bring her own shoebox of family pictures on Tuesday to see whether any of the unnamed ferry photographs match. I offered to build a simple spreadsheet with the box list, and Gunnar, to general surprise, asked me to make it readable on paper as well, since half the committee does not use screens.

One more detail from Sunday deserves a line. Near closing, Gunnar found a slim ledger tucked behind the school registers, bound in green cloth and unlabelled. It turned out to be the daily record of the ferry across the narrows, kept by the ferryman himself between the wars, with the weather, the number of passengers and a note of every cow carried. Astrid read out the first page and said the handwriting was his. On a day in late October the entry says only: fog, nobody crossed, played cards. We agreed that it goes to the top of the queue for the next weekend.

Walking home along the stream I passed the low ground that turned out to be Sorrow Acre. It is a wet, rushy strip now, with a heron on one bank and a rusting harrow half swallowed by nettles. I stood there a while imagining the enclosure surveyors with their chains, and the grandmother who gave up on the plot, and felt the odd satisfaction of a name returning to a place after a hundred and some years of silence on a linen map in a drawer.

Beekeeping season log, kept from the first spring inspection to the honey harvest. I took over two hives from my uncle Torvald when his knees finally refused the ladder to the orchard, and this is my first full year with them. He left me a battered inspection kit, a smoker with a scorched bellows, and a single instruction: never hurry near the frames. I have tried to obey it, mostly successfully, with a few lapses noted below.

Early April. The first warm day above twelve degrees, and I lifted the roof of the left hive for a peek. Bees were flying in and out with orange pollen on their legs, which Torvald says means the queen is laying and the colony is raising brood. I did not open the frames, since the rule is to wait for fifteen degrees. Instead I set a sheet of sugar fondant on the top bars in case stores were low. The right hive was quieter. I crouched with an ear against the wall and heard a faint hum, so I trusted it was alive and left it alone.

Mid April. Proper first inspection on a sunny Saturday with Torvald standing at the gate in his cap, forbidden from touching anything. Left hive: a healthy laying queen, solid brood, plenty of stores. I had marked her with a white dot last year on his advice, and found her after a slow scan of the fourth frame, sitting calm as a queen in a gathering. Right hive: less impressive, a small cluster, patchy brood and a scattering of drone cells in the middle of worker comb. Torvald pronounced it a failing queen and said I would need to requeen or combine.

Early May. I ordered a mated queen from a breeder near Vaxholm, who posted her in a little wooden cage with three attendants and a candy plug. She arrived on a Tuesday, warm from the van. The old queen in the right hive had to be found and removed first, which took forty minutes and a lot of squinting, and then I hung the new one in her cage between two frames. The bees need a few days to accept her scent, so the candy plug lets them eat their way to her slowly. Five days later I found her walking the comb, and I let out a whoop that startled the neighbour's dog.

Late May. Swarm season. The left hive grew crowded, and on the twenty-third I found three queen cells hanging from the bottom of a frame like peanut shells. Torvald phoned that evening and told me to split the colony before the bees did it for me. I carried out the split on Sunday: moved the old queen with half the brood and stores into a new box on a fresh stand, left the queen cells in the original hive, and hoped for the best. Two days later a small cloud of bees hung in the plum tree anyway, and I had to coax them into a cardboard box with a brush and a good deal of nerve.

June. The main flow began with the lime trees on the avenue and the last of the clover in the ditch by the road. I added a super, a shallow box for honey, to each hive and watched them fill it. A nectar flow has a smell you can identify after a while, sweet and faintly green, like cut hay and warm wax together. On one afternoon I stood ten metres from the hives and could smell it without opening anything. Torvald visited, sniffed the air at the gate, and said I was going to have a good year.

Early July. A sting on the wrist, the first proper one, because I broke my own rule and hurried. I was lifting a frame with one hand and the smoker had gone cold. The bee stung through the cuff of my glove. I scraped it out with a fingernail, remembered that the sting keeps pumping venom for a while, and my wrist swelled to the size of a small apple by evening. No lasting harm, only a lesson: keep the smoker lit, keep the cuffs tight, and if a hive sounds cross, close it up and return in the evening.

Late July. Weighing the situation. The right hive with its new queen had built up nicely, though it will not give me a surplus this year. The left hive and its split had produced more than I expected. Torvald recommended waiting until the cells in the supers were capped with white wax, because uncapped honey is too wet and will ferment in the jar. I checked every frame against the light. About four in five were capped by the last day of July, and I took the rest of the decision to wait one more week.

Harvest day, the ninth of August. Torvald arrived at seven with his old extractor, a stainless drum with a crank that he refuses to replace. We cleared the supers with a bee brush and a fume board, carried them into the shed, and sliced the wax cappings with a heated knife. Then we spun the frames, six at a time, cranking until our forearms burned. The honey ran golden and thick into a bucket through a double sieve, and the whole shed smelled like a warm cake. We got forty-four kilograms from the left hive and its split combined, and I nearly cried over the first spoonful.

Jars were the next puzzle. I had bought a hundred and twenty, which turned out to be far too many, so I gave forty back to the shop and kept eighty. Each jar took a hand-written label reading the year, the site, and the words lime and clover. I filled them from a tap on the bucket and learned that a tilted jar avoids bubbles. Friends came round for jars in exchange for a promise not to ask for a discount. My sister Liv took six and swore she would eat one a week.

A word about equipment and money, since Torvald asked for a proper account. The hives, two brood boxes and four supers between them, were his and cost me nothing. I spent about eleven hundred crowns on the new queen, the fondant, a second smoker so that one can always be relit while the other cools, a pair of goatskin gloves with long cuffs, and the glass jars. Selling twenty of the eighty jars at the church sale in September brought back almost exactly the cost of the queen and the gloves, which Torvald said was the correct outcome for a first year: nobody should expect to profit until the second.

He also insisted I keep a notebook by the hives, and I now write a line after every visit: the date, the temperature, whether the bees were calm, how many frames were covered, what I saw. Reading back through it in the evening, I noticed that the calmest days were the warm still afternoons after a shower, and the crossest were thundery mornings, exactly as the books say. It is satisfying when a diary confirms an old wives' tale.

Autumn reflections. Feeding for winter comes next, with a thick sugar syrup in early September and a treatment for the mites after that. Torvald is drawing up a small calendar for me in his careful capitals and has promised to inspect the entrances once the first frost arrives. I sat on the upturned crate by the hives this evening as the light went, watching the last foragers come home heavy and slow. I have done this for one season and I understand only a tenth of it. Still, the hives are alive, the shed smells of wax, and I am already planning where a third hive might stand.

Regatta diary, the river club's summer races. I am not a rower by talent, more a rower by stubbornness, and this year the Norrfors club asked the veteran crews to fill the coxed four for the Saturday sprint. I have been going down to the boathouse on Wednesday evenings since April, and the regatta was the first time I raced in front of an actual crowd. I write this the day after, sunburnt across the nose, while the details are still fresh.

Friday evening was the boat check. The four is called Marta, after the club's first secretary, and she is a wooden hull that has been repainted so many times that the deck feels lumpy. Our coach, Henrik, spent an hour going over every oarlock and gate, tightening the little nuts with a spanner he keeps on a string round his neck. He also weighed us, not for vanity but because the class has a minimum weight for the crew, and we squeaked over by a whisker. Sofia, our cox, was well under the limit and had to carry a small sandbag in the stern, which she treated as a great indignity.

Saturday started at six. The mist lay on the water in strips and a couple of swans drifted through the course like inspectors. We rigged the boat in the half dark, carried her down to the pontoon, and watched the marshals set out the buoys. Our heat was at ten past nine, against crews from Ljusdal and a university club whose oarsmen looked twenty years younger than us. Henrik gave the briefing on the pontoon: a smooth start, a steady rhythm through the middle, and a push in the last two hundred metres. He said nothing about winning, which was wise.

The start was clumsy. Someone, and I think it was me, caught a crab on the second stroke and the blade slapped the water sideways. We lost a length before the boat settled. Sofia, in that calm bossy voice she uses only in races, called for a reset and counted us back into rhythm. By the five hundred mark we were level with the university crew, and by the one thousand mark we had drawn ahead, though the Ljusdal boat stayed a canvas behind the whole way. We won the heat by about two seconds, and I could barely hold the oar afterwards.

Between races the club served soup and sausages under a gazebo, and the whole bank filled with picnic rugs and children with tiny flags. I sat with my feet in the shallows and let a cousin of Sofia's, who had turned up to watch, explain the rules of the handicap system to me, which I still do not fully understand. The one thing I retained is that older crews get a time allowance, so our slower pace would be measured against our ages instead of the clock alone.

The final took place at half past three. This time the wind had picked up and the course was choppy. We had the outside lane, which was exposed, and three other boats. Henrik hugged each of us on the pontoon, which he never does, and said the boat was ready if we were. The start was much cleaner this time. We rowed the first five hundred at a rating of thirty-two, which is fast for us, and I felt the boat lift and run between strokes in a way it never does in practice. Then the wind hit, and the rhythm broke for two or three strokes.

Sofia saved us. She said our names one at a time, quietly and firmly, and then a phrase she had been saving all summer: long and easy, you have plenty. We caught the rhythm again with about three hundred left. Then the final push, with everyone shouting from the bank, and I stopped hearing anything except the hiss of the water and my own breath. We crossed the line second, half a length behind a crew from Sundsvall. With the age allowance, the judges announced a few minutes later, we were first in the handicap class.

The medal ceremony was a bit ridiculous and I loved it. A club official read the results in a slow voice, every name spelled out, and the medals were hung by a very small child dressed as an admiral. We each got a wooden disc on a blue ribbon. Sofia held hers up to the sun and said it smelled like a pencil. Henrik stood at the back, not applauding, just nodding slowly, which from him is the highest praise available.

Afterwards we carried the Marta back up the slipway and hosed her down. The old rule of the club is that the crew washes the boat before anyone eats, and nobody has ever broken it. My hands had blisters in three places, one of which burst in the shower and made me swear loudly enough that the man in the next cubicle asked if I was all right. I bandaged up and went to the clubhouse for the evening meal, a long trestle affair with a very good fish stew.

A few things to remember for next year. Bring a hat, a proper one, since the tip of my nose is still the colour of a boiled prawn. Practise starts more often than the middle of the race, because that is where crews win or lose. Ask Henrik about the new oar handles before the club buys them. And write down which seat I was in for the heat, since I have already forgotten whether it was two or three, and the photographs disagree with each other.

The piano tuning saga, in instalments. My mother's upright has stood in the hall of the family flat since before I was born, a dark Swedish instrument with two candle brackets and a lid that sticks. When she moved into sheltered housing she gave it to me on the understanding that I would restore it to something playable. It arrived by van on a wet Tuesday and I have been trying to make it sing ever since.

The first sound it produced in my flat was a groan. Middle C responded with a dull clunk, the third octave seemed to have no strings at all, and one note near the top rang for a full ten seconds like a bell in a tunnel. I assumed the worst and rang a tuner recommended by a neighbour, a soft-spoken man called Bertil Stenmark, who came on Thursday with a black case of tools that looked like a surgeon's kit.

Bertil spent the first half hour just listening. He played scales and chords, hummed along, sometimes lifted the lid and stared into the workings with his head tilted like a blackbird. Then he said what I had hoped he would not: the instrument had not been tuned in about fifteen years, and it had sunk far below standard pitch. Raising it in a single go risks snapping strings, so he proposed a pitch raise first, then a tuning a fortnight later, and a third visit after the wood settled.

I learned a lot about pianos in that hour. There are over two hundred strings, and most notes have three of them, tuned to the same pitch, so a single key hits a little choir. When the choir is out of step you get that wobbling, wailing sound. Bertil demonstrated by muting two strings with a strip of felt and plucking the third, then unmuting them one at a time so I could hear the beats slow and vanish as he turned the pin. It was magical, like seeing a fog clear from a photograph.

The first visit lasted two and a half hours. He raised the pitch bit by bit, working from the middle outward, and warned me that the piano would drift flat again over the next days. When he left the hall smelled faintly of felt and machine oil, and the instrument sounded almost like an instrument, although still slightly sour in the treble. I played the only piece I know by heart, a simple waltz, and I could hear the difference in the third bar.

The sticking lid, on the other hand, turned out to be a hinge problem. Bertil mentioned in passing that a bent pin and some old wax had jammed it. I fixed it with a screwdriver and a candle stub in ten minutes, which felt disproportionately triumphant. I have since learned that a lot of piano repair is exactly like that: unglamorous, physical, and very much about small friction.

Two weeks later he came back for the proper tuning. This time he spent more than three hours, checking each string against a fork and then against the octave above. He also found a cracked hammer felt in the fourth octave and a dead damper, which he adjusted with a thin steel rod. While he worked, my daughter Maja, who is nine, sat on the floor beside the stool and watched him with great seriousness. At the end he handed her a small tuning hammer and let her turn one pin a quarter turn, under supervision. She has not stopped talking about it.

The third visit was for the voicing, which I had never heard of. It means adjusting the hardness of the felt on the hammers so the tone is even. He pricked the felt with a needle in a few places, listening after each. The sound became softer and rounder, less like a hammer on wire and more like a voice. It cost extra, but I found I did not care, because I could finally play a chord in the hall and feel it in the floor.

Now the accounting. Three visits, a set of new felts, one replaced damper spring and a bottle of polish for the case came to a bill that I will not repeat here except to say it exceeded what I paid for the sofa. Bertil is a fair man and wrote the whole thing out by hand. He also gave me a small hygrometer to keep beside the piano, and told me to keep the flat between forty and fifty percent humidity, especially in winter, since a dry radiator will wreck the tuning faster than any child.

I have taken up lessons again after twenty years. My teacher is a retired schoolteacher on the second floor, Mrs Karlberg, who insists on scales and doesn't put up with sloppy thumbs. On the first evening she played the opening of a Chopin nocturne on the restored piano and said, without looking at me, that it had a nice old tone. I felt a huge, silly pride, as if I had built the thing myself. My mother will visit on Sunday and I want her to hear the candle brackets shake a little on the low notes, the way they did in her day.

Glacier hike write-up, three days above the valley of Sarek's southern neighbour. I went with Mira's brother Tomas and his friend Katarina, both of whom have done a lot more of this than I have, so I mostly followed and tried not to slow anyone down. The plan was a guided crossing of a small glacier with a licensed guide, an overnight in a mountain hut, and a return over a high pass. Everything about it was new to me, including the crampons.

We met the guide, a wiry woman in her forties named Ylva Berglund, at a car park at the end of a gravel road. She examined our boots one by one and made us take everything out of our packs so she could check it. She rejected my cotton socks, my jeans, and a heavy bottle of water I had brought on the theory that thirst was a serious risk. From a battered duffel she produced wool socks, a spare fleece, and a pair of gaiters. I was slightly embarrassed and very grateful.

The approach was four hours of steady climbing through birch scrub and then bare rock, alongside a torrent the colour of dirty milk. Ylva walked at a pace so slow that I doubted her at first, then realised that she was saving our legs for later. She stopped every hour for a sip and a bite of chocolate, made us drink whether we were thirsty or not, and pointed out things I would have missed: a ptarmigan sitting motionless on a boulder, a line of fresh reindeer tracks, the faint scars where the glacier used to reach fifty years ago.

We reached the edge of the ice in the early afternoon. It was not the clean white sheet I had imagined but a grey, dirty tongue strewn with stones, pitted with holes and streaked with meltwater channels. Ylva sat us down on a flat rock and taught us to put on the crampons: boots on, straps tight, check both sides. Then she walked us through the walking technique, which is essentially to stamp flat-footed like an irritated giant, keeping the feet a little wider than normal so the spikes do not catch the trousers.

Roping up was next. We tied ourselves to a rope at intervals of about eight metres, with Ylva at the front and Katarina at the back. Ylva explained the plan for a fall into a crevasse, which is that the person who falls shouts, the others drop flat and dig in their axes, and nobody tries to be a hero. She made each of us practise the drop on a gentle slope. I did it badly the first time and rather better the second. It is odd how much comfort there is in being told exactly what to do when everything goes wrong.

The crossing itself took about two hours. We climbed a shallow slope of granular ice that crunched under the spikes like a bag of sugar, stepped around holes that looked bottomless, and jumped a narrow crack that Ylva called a baby. Around us, the air had a faint blue cast and a sound I can only describe as ticking, the ice adjusting itself in the warmth. Midway Ylva stopped us at the edge of a moulin, a shaft where meltwater plunges into the glacier, and let us listen. The roar came up from far below, muffled and enormous, and nobody said anything for a minute.

The hut was on a rocky shoulder on the far side, a small red building with a wood stove and eight bunks, run by a volunteer association. Someone had left a stack of dry birch by the door and a note asking the next party to replace it. Ylva cooked a huge pot of pasta with reindeer sausage, and we ate it from tin bowls while the sun turned the ice orange and then pink. Tomas produced a small bar of chocolate he had been hiding all day. Katarina wrote in the logbook that we had crossed in good conditions and seen a mountain hare.

I slept badly, as always in new places, and got up at five to walk outside. The valley was full of cloud, and above it the peaks stood clear and cold against a pale green sky. There was a silence so complete that I could hear my own blood. I stood there in my socks on a slab of rock, which was a mistake, and came back inside with numb toes and the feeling that I had seen something I would keep for years.

The return over the pass was the hardest part of the trip. It was a steep scree slope followed by a snowfield, with a wind that stung the face and made speech impossible. Ylva led us in a zigzag, telling us to place each foot deliberately and not to look down. My legs shook on the descent, and at one point I slid twenty metres on my back before stopping against a boulder, unhurt but humbled. Ylva simply held out a hand and pulled me up, and said that everybody does that once.

We arrived at the car park at four in the afternoon on the third day, filthy and euphoric. Ylva shook hands with each of us, checked our packs one last time, and gave me the sock advice again for the future. I drove home with the glass wound down, smelling of woodsmoke and old sweat, and slept eleven hours. My knees are still complaining a week later, but I have already asked Tomas whether we can do the same crossing in September, when the meltwater channels have frozen and the light is lower and sharper.

Judging at the county school science fair, notes on a long Friday. The organisers asked local employers for volunteer judges this year, and I was drafted along with a retired pharmacist, a woman from the water authority and a very quiet man who turned out to be a beekeeping instructor. We met at eight in the sports hall of the Lindgren school, where eighty-odd exhibits stood in rows on trestles under a banner that had been painted by the youngest pupils and included the word science spelled two different ways.

The head of the jury, a chemistry teacher named Barbro Sund, gave us a scoring sheet with four criteria: the clarity of the question, the quality of the method, the honesty of the conclusions and the presentation. She stressed the third one most. In previous years, she said, some judges had been dazzled by colourful boards and awarded prizes to projects that proved nothing. She wanted us to look for children who could say what they did not know.

My first stand belonged to a ten-year-old boy, Elias, who had tested whether different brands of paper towel absorb the same amount of water. He had cut squares, dripped water from a syringe, and counted the drops until the paper was soaked. His board was a mess of tape and pencil, but when I asked why he used a syringe instead of a spoon, he answered without hesitation that a spoon would be different every time. He also admitted that his results were unclear, because two brands scored the same. I gave him nearly full marks for the third criterion.

Next, a pair of twelve-year-old girls had built a small model wind turbine from a fan motor and measured how many little bulbs it could light with different numbers of blades. Their graph showed three blades lit two bulbs, five lit three, and eight lit none, because the blades were too heavy. They had no explanation for the last result and said so plainly, which delighted me more than any tidy answer. The pharmacist beside me leaned over and whispered that they would go far.

Not every project was so honest. One older boy had a large, glossy poster about an invented miracle fertiliser and a long list of impressive results, but when I asked how many plants he had used, he answered that he had planted several. Pressed for a number, he said perhaps six. Six plants, in a single pot, over a week. I asked if he thought this was enough to be confident. He looked wounded and said his teacher had told him it was fine. I did not want to crush him, so I suggested he try again with thirty plants and a control group, and wrote a polite comment on the sheet.

The lunch break was a paper bag and a lukewarm cup of tea in the staff area, where the judges compared notes. The woman from the water authority, whose name was Ingegerd, had been particularly impressed by a project on cleaning muddy water with layers of sand and charcoal. She had asked the child what would happen with oil in the water, and the child replied that it would probably fail and offered to test it on Monday. Ingegerd said that was the answer of a scientist, and wrote her top score in ink.

The afternoon was mostly for the older pupils, whose projects were more ambitious. A boy from the ninth year had modelled how a rumour spreads through a class using dice, a clever simulation with a little grid of probabilities that took him a week to work out. A girl had recorded the birdsong outside her flat every morning for a month and matched each species to the weather. Her notebook was beautiful, full of tiny sketches and columns of numbers, and the correlations she found were modest but carefully stated. I gave her the highest mark I awarded all day.

Deliberation began at three in a corner of the sports hall. Barbro laid the sheets out on the floor and we sorted them into piles, arguing politely. The jury ended up agreeing on the top three quite quickly, but the fourth place produced a heated dispute about whether the paper towel project deserved recognition for honesty over accuracy. The beekeeping instructor, who had said almost nothing all day, cleared his throat and said that a child who could describe an unclear result was worth ten who could not. We gave the boy a special mention.

The prize-giving was at four. Each winner received a certificate and a small trophy shaped like a beaker, and the whole school clapped, some more enthusiastically than others. The girl with the birdsong notebook was announced as first prize in the older category, and her mother, in the third row, burst into tears. Elias came up for his special mention and took it with great gravity, shook my hand, and asked whether I was the man who had asked about the syringe. I said I was. He said it was a good question.

I drove home with the strange lightness that comes after an afternoon among children who are still willing to say they do not know. In the car I thought about how rarely adults do that, and how much better our meetings would be if they did. I wrote to Barbro that evening to say I would gladly judge again, and she replied within the hour with a list of dates for next year, including the words, in capitals, please bring the same clipboard.

Chess club tournament, the Saturday rapid event at the Sjoberg community hall. I have played at the Tuesday club for six years without ever entering a proper tournament, on the excuse that my rating would embarrass me. This time our secretary, Olof Wikstrom, put my name on the list without asking, saying that the field was small and friendly and that the entry fee included lunch. That was the argument that worked.

We gathered at nine and the arbiter, a tall retired policeman called Leif, explained the format: five rounds, fifteen minutes each on the clock with a ten-second bonus for every move, and pairings drawn by the Swiss method, meaning that winners meet winners as the day goes on. There were twenty-two players, from a boy of eleven with a pillow to sit on to a woman in her eighties who had been a regional champion in the sixties and still moved her pieces with surgical precision.

Round one gave me a kind of gift. I was paired with a schoolboy called Anton whose rating was lower than mine, and I played the opening that I always play, a quiet setup with the knight out first. He answered aggressively, pushing his pawns on the kingside, and by move fifteen I could see that he had left a bishop hanging. I took it with a slight cough of guilt. He resigned at move twenty-three, shook my hand, and asked me politely what I would have done if he had played the other knight. I showed him on the board, and he nodded with the grave interest of a future master.

Round two was harder. I met a man with a grey ponytail who spoke only to mutter about the clock. His style was steady and dry, no threats, no errors. We reached a queenless endgame with rooks and pawns, and I spent six minutes of my fifteen on a single move, which is fatal in a rapid game. After that I played on the increment alone, hurrying every move and half hoping he would blunder. He did not. I lost on time in a position that was, according to the analysis afterwards, roughly equal.

At lunch we ate lentil soup at long benches and everyone replayed their games with their hands. The eighty-year-old lady, Gunvor Alm, sat across from me and dissected my loss in three sentences. She said that I had a good instinct for structure and a terrible relationship with the clock, and that the cure was to decide the move within a minute and then check it, not the other way around. She then offered to play a friendly game afterwards. I accepted with some fear.

Round three I drew against a young man in a football shirt, mainly because both of us missed a chance to win in a rook ending. It is a peculiar experience to see the winning idea only when the arbiter is already writing the result on the sheet. He laughed and said the same had happened to him twice this season. Round four I won against a nervous woman who had never played in public, and I found myself feeling so sorry for her that I nearly offered a draw and did not, because the arbiter was watching.

Before the last round I stood at the pairings board with a cup of tea, and Olof came over, looking pleased. I had three points from four, he said, which put me in a group of six players on the same score, and my opponent in round five would be Gunvor Alm herself. There was a small murmur among the spectators. She was on three and a half. I sat down across from her and she gave me a very small smile and adjusted her queen a millimetre to the left.

The game lasted forty minutes and I remember most of it. I played a solid defence and kept to her advice, deciding quickly, then checking. By move twenty, the position was level and the clock time was even. Then she offered a pawn on the queenside as bait, and I took it, because I have never been able to resist. Nine moves later I understood that I had been served, and her knights arrived in the space I had opened up like a pair of very quiet burglars. I resigned with two minutes left and applauded her on the sheet.

The results were read out at half past four. Gunvor Alm won the tournament on four and a half points, the boy with the pillow finished in the top ten, and I ended on three, which was good enough for eleventh place among twenty-two, precisely in the middle. Leif read my name in the same solemn tone as he read the winner's. Nobody minded. Every player received a small enamel pin in the shape of a rook, and the prizes for the top three included a book, a bottle of cordial and a box of fine chocolates.

The lessons are all in my notebook, but I will copy the important ones here. First, watch the clock as though it were an opponent. Second, do not take a poisoned pawn from someone who has been playing since the year I was not born. Third, the pleasure of the day was not in the score but in replaying every game afterwards with strangers who had just beaten me. Olof has asked whether I would like to enter the autumn open in Ostersund. I said I would think about it and then, in the car, I admitted to myself that I already have.

Stargazing weekend at the dark-sky farm near Ammaras, written up on the train home. Mira gave me a voucher for two nights at a farm whose owners have spent ten years persuading the local council to switch off the street lamps on the road. The reward is one of the darkest skies in the south of the country, or so the brochure claimed, and we chose a weekend close to the new moon, when the sky is at its best.

We arrived on Friday afternoon in drizzle, and the host, a cheerful astronomer with a fisherman's beard named Rune, shrugged and said that the clouds always clear by midnight in this valley. He was right, more or less. He gave us tea and a plate of cinnamon buns, walked us round the yard, and showed us the instruments: a big reflector under a sliding roof, two smaller telescopes on tripods and a shed full of folding chairs and sleeping bags.

At ten the rain stopped. Rune turned off every light on the farm, and we stood in the pitch black waiting for our eyes to adjust. It takes about twenty minutes, he explained, and a red torch is the only permitted light, because red does not spoil the sensitivity of the eye. Slowly the stars came out in their thousands. I had never seen the Milky Way as anything but a rumour. That night it stretched across the whole sky like smoke, with dark lanes running through it, and I said something stupid about it that I will not repeat.

Rune took us through the sky with a green laser pointer, naming the constellations, and he told a story about each one. The best was about the Pleiades, a little cluster of stars that appears in the mythology of half the world. He said that most people can see six with the naked eye and that keen-sighted children can see nine or ten. I counted seven on the first attempt and eight on the second, and Mira, who has better eyes, insisted she saw nine.

At half past eleven we went to the big telescope. Rune aimed it at Saturn, which hung low over the trees, and invited us to look. I expected a smudge. Instead there it was, a tiny, clear, golden ball with rings tilted like a hat, so sharp and so improbable that I laughed out loud. Mira gripped my arm. We each looked five or six times and would have gone on looking all night if there had not been a queue of other guests behind us.

Next came a globular cluster in Hercules, an enormous ball of old stars that looks like a handful of sugar spilled on velvet, then a double star with one orange and one blue member, then the Andromeda galaxy, which appeared as a faint oval smear. Rune reminded us that the light we were seeing had left that galaxy about two and a half million years ago, before our species existed. Standing in a cold field with a mug of hot cocoa, I felt both tiny and oddly at home.

We stayed out until three, wrapped in sleeping bags on folding chairs, watching for meteors. We counted eleven, one of them bright enough to leave a trail that hung in the air for a second. On Saturday we slept late, wandered through the birch woods and helped feed the farm's two goats. The second night was cloudier, but we caught a brief clear patch and Rune found us a distant comet, faint as a smear of breath, through the reflector.

On the train home Mira asked whether the trip had changed anything. I said that I would now like to look up more often, and to live somewhere with fewer streetlights. She said she would settle for a good pair of binoculars. We bought them on Monday, an ordinary pair with big lenses, and last night I stood on the balcony and found Jupiter and three of its moons in a line, tiny points beside a glaring disc, exactly as Rune promised.

Pottery kiln firing at the Brannas studio, a long day of watching a fire. I joined the Thursday evening class in January, mostly to have something to do with my hands that did not involve a screen, and over the winter I made a dozen wobbly bowls, three mugs and a jug that leans. Today was the glaze firing, the moment when everything either becomes a real object or is destroyed in the dark, and the teacher, Birgitta, invited us all to help.

The kiln is a huge gas-fired thing built by a previous teacher from firebricks and scrap steel, roughly the size of a small car. It stands in a lean-to behind the studio and takes a whole day to reach temperature. We arrived at seven to load it, working in pairs, placing each pot on a shelf with careful gaps for the flames to pass. Glazed pieces must never touch, or they will fuse into a single lump, so we moved with the exaggerated slowness of people carrying eggs.

My own pots went on the third shelf. I had chosen a pale green glaze for the bowls and a deep blue for the jug, and Birgitta warned that colours in glaze look nothing like the final result. The green I had applied looked chalky and grey, like dried toothpaste. She said that the blue would turn out almost black, and that we had to trust the chemistry. I found this very hard.

By nine the kiln was full and the door bricked up. Birgitta lit the burners and turned the gas to a low setting, and for the first two hours nothing appeared to happen. The temperature climbed by about a hundred degrees an hour, and we were forbidden to hurry it, since moisture trapped in the clay can turn to steam and blow a pot apart. A dozen of us took turns to watch the pyrometer, a dial on the side that Birgitta calls the oracle.

By noon we had reached nine hundred degrees. Birgitta opened a small spy hole and let us peer inside. The pots glowed dull orange against the brick, and the whole interior pulsed like the inside of a lantern. Someone whispered that it looked like a small sun. She adjusted the dampers to raise the pressure, and the flame began to roar. Occasionally a shelf gave a tiny tick as the clay adjusted, and all of us held our breath.

We passed the afternoon with soup, gossip and a game of cards. One of the older students, Rolf, told us about the time in the nineties when a whole firing cracked because someone had loaded a wet pot, and how the studio smelled of sulphur for a week. Another told of a firing that produced a spectacular copper red by accident, which nobody could reproduce. The talk kept returning to luck, and the teacher said that any potter who claims not to depend on luck is either lying or very boring.

By six the kiln had reached its top temperature, about twelve hundred and sixty degrees, and Birgitta held it there for twenty minutes to let the glazes mature. Then she turned off the gas, closed the dampers, and the long cooling began. Nothing may be opened until the kiln falls below two hundred degrees, which takes about a day and a half. We went home tired and full of a low, nervous excitement, as if waiting for exam results.

On Saturday morning we unbricked the door. The first shelf came out, and there was a small collective gasp. The green glaze had turned into a soft celadon with tiny darker specks, far more beautiful than I had hoped, and the jug was a blue so deep it looked like the sea at night. One of my bowls had a pinhole where the glaze had bubbled, and the lip of a mug had chipped, but the rest had survived. Birgitta held the leaning jug up to the light, sighed, and said that it had character, which is the potter's word for a flaw you have decided to love.

Lighthouse open day on the island of Gron, volunteer shift. The old lighthouse on the western point has been automated for forty years, but the heritage society keeps the keepers' house and the tower open for one Sunday every summer, and Mira's uncle, who is the society's treasurer, needed hands. I was given a yellow vest and a station at the bottom of the tower stairs, where my job was to count visitors and stop them from bringing prams up the spiral.

The tower is thirty-one metres high, with a hundred and forty-two steps. I know this because the society's chairman, a retired ferry captain named Sixten, told every single visitor, whether or not they asked. He also told them that the lamp on top used to be lit with paraffin and trimmed by hand, that the keeper's daily routine included polishing the brass until it shone like gold, and that the lens, a great glass beehive of prisms, is worth more than the island's whole school.

The first wave arrived at ten with the ferry, about eighty people, mostly families, plus a group of cyclists in matching jerseys. I counted them up the stairs, ten at a time, and gave each group a small card with a picture of the light and a few facts for children to look for on the way. By eleven the stairwell was a steady stream of puffing adults and shrieking small people, and a woman with a walking frame asked if there was a lift. There was not, but Sixten led her to the keeper's house and showed her a model of the tower and a display of old photographs, which she said she preferred anyway.

At noon I had a break and walked round to the foghorn shed. The horn is a rusting cast-iron monster mounted on a concrete plinth, silent since the sixties, and a boy stood in front of it with his hands over his ears in case it started. Inside the shed the society had laid out a collection of things washed up on the point over the years: a lifebuoy from a wreck, a wooden crate of tin lanterns, a child's shoe from before the war. A handwritten label told the story of each.

The afternoon brought a sudden gust of wind and a scatter of rain, and the crowd drifted into the keeper's house for waffles and tea. I helped serve, which I was not asked to do but preferred to counting. A little girl asked me what the keeper did when it was foggy. I said he rang a bell and lit the lamp, and she asked what he did when nothing happened, and I said that he probably read a lot. She looked very thoughtful and told me she would like to be a keeper when she grew up.

At four the last group came down the stairs and Sixten locked the tower door with an enormous key. The tally at the ferry jetty was three hundred and twelve visitors, which the society said was the best year yet. Sixten poured us each a small glass of something warming and made a speech about the importance of remembering the people who kept the lights. We drank to them, standing on the wet grass, while the automatic lamp above us came on in the dusk, silent and precise, as though it had never needed anyone at all.

The allotment dispute, from the beginning to the shaky truce. Since I took over plot fourteen at the Lindhagen allotments two summers ago, I have been on good terms with almost everyone on the site, and I would like the record to show that I did not start this. What began as a disagreement about a hedge became a nine-week saga of notes, meetings and one bag of manure, and I am writing it down now while the details are clear and my temper has cooled.

Some background for anyone reading this later. The site has thirty-six plots along a gravel path on a slope above the railway, run by an association with a committee of five and a rulebook of eleven pages. Each plot is about two hundred and fifty square metres, and the rules say that hedges between plots may not exceed one metre twenty. My neighbour on the left, a retired engineer named Harald Bergfelt, has a hedge of privet that he claims has been there since before the association existed. It is nearly two metres tall.

The trouble began in April when Harald's hedge, which faces south, started shading my strawberry rows. I mentioned this to him politely by the water tap. He said the hedge was his and had been trimmed every year since 1994, and that if the strawberries wanted sun they could go elsewhere. I said that the rules allowed only one metre twenty. He said that the rules had been written by people who had never grown anything. It was, to be fair, a good line.

I took the matter to the committee, in the person of the chairwoman, Ragnhild Voss, a fierce and fair woman who runs the site with a clipboard. She promised to walk the boundary. She did so in the first week of May, measured the hedge with a folding rule, and wrote a note to Harald asking him to cut it by the end of the month. Harald responded with a note of his own, four pages long, quoting a clause from the founding charter about established features. Ragnhild called an extraordinary meeting.

The meeting took place in the shed by the tool store on a Wednesday evening. Twenty-three plot holders came, more than for the annual meeting, plus a dog. Ragnhild read out the rule and Harald's four pages, which he had insisted on reading aloud himself, and there was an argument. Half the hut took Harald's side on the grounds of tradition and the other half mine on the grounds of light. A woman from plot twenty-two said that shade suits rhubarb, and another that no strawberry should be allowed to divide a community.

I should describe the shed, because it matters. It is a long wooden hut with a tin roof that drums in the rain, one bench along each wall, a stove that has not worked since the flood, and a noticeboard so thick with notices about lost hoses and spare rhubarb crowns that the top layers curl. On the evening of the meeting the rain came down hard and the noise made it necessary for everyone to shout, which did nothing to improve the tone. Ragnhild finally banged a watering can on the bench to restore order, and somebody at the back said that this was the first time the can had been used for its proper purpose.

In the middle of the argument the treasurer, a soft-voiced accountant named Petra Lindqvist, rose to point out that the association had never actually measured any hedge on the site in living memory, and that if the rule were enforced everywhere, eleven plots would be in breach, including the committee's own tool store. This sobered the hut considerably. Ragnhild thanked her, went slightly pale, and said she would take it under advisement.

The vote was postponed for two weeks, and in the interval the dispute got worse. Someone left a bag of manure on my path with a note saying, for your strawberries. I decided this was meant kindly, but Harald took it as a sign that I was gathering allies, and he stopped speaking to me at the tap. I noticed that we had begun to adjust our watering hours so as never to meet. The site, which had always felt like a village, began to feel like a border.

It was Ragnhild who suggested a compromise, after a long telephone call in which she used the phrase adults in their sixties more than once. The proposal was that Harald would cut the hedge down to one metre fifty on my side only, leaving the other sides at their full height, and that I would install a trellis at my own expense for climbing beans, which would soften the border and provide some privacy. Neither of us liked it, which she said was a good sign.

We met at the hedge on a Saturday morning with Ragnhild holding her folding rule, and Harald grudgingly clipped down a two-metre stretch to the agreed line. I watched with mixed feelings. I had won, but the privet looked a bit forlorn, and Harald muttered that it would grow back by August. I held out a hand, which he ignored for several seconds and then shook, briefly. Afterwards he handed me a small jar of his own raspberry jam, without a word, and walked off.

The trellis went up the following weekend. It is five poles and some wire, and I planted runner beans along it in late May. By July they had reached the top, and I could see from the other side that Harald was quietly picking one or two through the gaps. I decided not to mention it. On the last Sunday of the month I left a small bag of my strawberries on his gatepost and, the next morning, found a bundle of rhubarb on mine.

I have thought a good deal about why a hedge of privet became such a battle. I think it was because neither of us was really arguing about height. Harald was defending a piece of history and an idea of himself as the site's oldest resident, and I was defending the belief that rules should apply to everyone equally. Both are worth defending, and neither of us saw the other doing it. The committee is now planning a review of the hedge rule at the next annual meeting, with proper wording for established features, and Ragnhild has asked me to draft it, because, she said, I have obviously been thinking about it.

Small notes for the future. Measure things before speaking. Do not discuss disputes at the water tap, where everyone can hear. Bring a peace offering, ideally something you can eat. And when a neighbour who has not spoken to you for six weeks leaves a bundle of rhubarb on your gatepost, accept it as the sign it is, and write him a message of thanks. I did, on a postcard of the site, and he replied with a single word in square handwriting: sufficient.

Knitting fair stall at the Arvika craft weekend. My aunt Lena, who has knitted since she was six, was invited to hold a stall at the annual craft fair and asked me to come along as porter, cashier and general dogsbody. I agreed on the basis that I would be allowed to sit down. She shook her head slowly and handed me a roll of price stickers and a cash tin.

We arrived at seven on Saturday to a hall already smelling of wool and floor polish. Our stall, number twenty-three, was a pair of trestles under a striped cloth, next to a woman selling hand-dyed skeins and a man who made spoons. Lena unpacked her goods with practised speed: sixteen pairs of mittens, nine hats, a heap of thick socks, four shawls in lace and a stack of small toys in the shape of foxes. She arranged them by colour, moving each item two or three times until the whole stand looked like a sunset.

The first customers came at nine, and by ten there was a queue. I learned that knitting fairs have a rhythm. The early crowd are serious buyers who touch every item and ask what fibre it is. The late-morning crowd are families who want something small. The afternoon crowd are people who have had a long day, have stopped browsing, and buy the first pair of mittens that fits. I sold four pairs of socks to one man who said he was outfitting a whole football team.

Prices were an issue. Lena had priced the mittens at two hundred crowns, which I thought too low given the hours she puts in. Customers sometimes tried to bargain, and she refused with great charm. A woman asked for a discount on the lace shawls, and Lena took her by the hand and showed her the tiny stitches along the edge, explaining that each shawl took forty hours. The woman paid the full price without another word, and I made a mental note.

Lena's method with customers deserves a note. She never pushes. She lets people handle things, remembers what they touched twice, and mentions the price only when asked. She also has a small speech about washing: wool should be rinsed in lukewarm water with a drop of gentle soap, pressed in a towel, and dried flat, never wrung. Three separate customers thanked her for it and one wrote it down on a receipt. A man in a fisherman's jumper came back on Sunday to say that the socks he had bought the day before had survived a night on a wet boat, and bought two more pairs, one for his brother.

During a quiet hour I walked the aisles myself. The hall held about ninety stalls, and I saw felted animals, woven rugs, carved bowls, a woman making lace with dozens of little bobbins that clicked like rain, and a very old man demonstrating a spinning wheel that he had built himself in 1961. He let me try. My thread was thick, lumpy and inexplicably blue, and he told me kindly that I had the makings of an amateur.

On Sunday the fox toys sold out by noon, children clutching them and parents fishing for wallets, and Lena took orders for six more. A journalist from the local paper photographed her at the stall holding up a shawl, and she pretended to hate it. By closing time the tin contained a total takings figure of nine thousand and forty crowns, which she divided into three envelopes marked yarn, rent and treats. I was given a pair of socks in a colour she called mud, and I have not taken them off since.

Change ringing practice at St Olav's, my first month in the tower. I walked into the church one Tuesday in January to ask about the choir and came out having agreed to learn to ring bells, which is not a sentence I ever expected to write. The tower captain, a small precise man named Egil Haugen, was on the steps sweeping leaves and overheard me. He said that the choir had plenty of sopranos and that the bells had none, and he led me up a stone spiral before I had finished apologising.

The ringing chamber is on the second level, a square space with a wooden floor, a clock face on one wall and eight ropes hanging through holes in the ceiling. Each rope ends in a striped woollen grip called a sally, and the effect is of eight fat caterpillars dangling in a row. The bells themselves hang another floor up, in a frame of black oak, and the heaviest, the tenor, weighs nearly nine hundred kilograms. Egil told me that if I ever felt the rope pulling me off my feet, I should let go, and I have decided to take the advice seriously.

The first evening I learned nothing but handling. Egil put me on the lightest bell, the treble, and made me stand with my feet apart while he showed how to hold the rope in both hands, pull down, let the sally rise, catch it at the top of its swing and pull the tail end. A tower bell is hung on a wheel and swings a full circle each time, which is why the rope goes up and down like a magic trick. I managed to ring it about four times before it sailed away from me and clanged out of turn. Everybody laughed kindly.

By the second week I could ring the treble steadily on my own, which sounds simple and feels like patting your head and rubbing your stomach while balancing on a moving train. The real skill is in listening. Each bell rings in a fixed order in a sequence called a round, and change ringing means altering that order according to a pattern, so that each ringer must know when to follow whom. You do not follow the notes. You follow the bell that rang before yours, and try to keep the gap even.

There is a good deal of vocabulary. Handstroke and backstroke are the two pulls. A method is a pattern of changes. A touch is a short piece of one. Plain Hunt is the first method a beginner learns, a weaving movement in which each bell moves one place at a time, up to the back and then down again. The captain drew it for me on a scrap of paper as a zigzag of lines and said that once I understood the picture, the sound would follow. It took me nine evenings.

The band is a mixed group. There is Britt, a retired midwife who has rung for fifty years and has forearms like a docker, two teenagers who came from the confirmation class, a farmer named Sven who arrives smelling faintly of silage, and a Danish exchange student called Freja, who learned in a fortnight what took the rest of us a season. We practise on Tuesday evenings from seven to nine, and after the second hour we walk down the road to the pub where nobody talks about anything but bells.

The high point of the month was the Sunday service on the last day of February. I was allowed to ring the treble in a touch of Plain Bob, with my heart pounding and my hands slick with sweat, while Egil stood behind me calling the changes in a low voice. For the first two minutes I did well. Then I lost my place, rang twice in a row, and heard the whole tower go quiet and start again without a word of reproach. Britt patted my shoulder afterwards and said that everyone makes a noise like that at their first service.

There are small dangers, and the captain takes them seriously. Loose sleeves catch in ropes, and long hair must be tied back. You should never let go of the rope in the middle of a stroke, or a rising sally can hit you in the face. He keeps a first aid box near the door and a list of local emergency numbers beside the clock. In fifty years, he says, nobody has been badly hurt, and he prefers to keep it that way with rules rather than luck.

Egil has asked whether I would like to ring at the midsummer festival, which needs a full band of eight, and I said yes before considering how much I still had to learn. I have set myself a target of ringing a full quarter peal by the end of the year, which is about forty-five minutes without a mistake. It seems impossible, but so did the first four pulls. The rope, now, feels like a part of my arm, and last night I found myself listening to the church bells of another town on the radio and trying to work out which method they were ringing.

A week on a narrowboat, the Lower Kennet route in high summer. Mira's sister Karin and her husband Joel had rented a forty-eight foot boat named Heron for seven days and invited the two of us along, on the grounds that a narrowboat needs a crew of at least four for the locks. We had never been on one before. I imagined a slow, relaxing drift with a glass of wine on the roof. What I got was a masterclass in ropes, mud and patience, and it was the best holiday I have taken in years.

We collected the boat on a Saturday morning from a small yard near Newbury, where a man called Dennis walked us through the controls. The boat has a diesel engine under the rear deck, a tiller instead of a wheel, a galley with a two-ring hob, a saloon with a sofa that becomes a bed, and a washing cubicle so tiny that Joel said he could wash his hair and his feet at once. Dennis spent ninety minutes on instruction and made us each take the tiller for a practice run down the canal. I steered the first hundred metres in an unhappy zigzag that swept across both banks.

The main lesson was that a narrowboat steers like a very long shopping trolley on ice. You turn the tiller to the left to go right, the stern swings out before the bow follows, and the vessel keeps going after you have stopped pushing. Karin, who rides horses, took to it at once and nudged us into the first lock with grace. Joel, an accountant by trade, treated the entire trip as an optimisation problem and kept a notebook in which he logged each lock, the time and the fuel.

Locks were the essence of the week. On the Kennet and Avon there are more than a hundred of them, and each is a small ritual: moor below, open the gate paddles by turning a windlass, wait for the water to equalise, push the heavy beam of the gate, steer in, close the gate, wind the paddles at the other end, let the level drop or rise, open the far gate, and leave. It takes about ten minutes, when done well. Mira and I did the windlass work, Karin took the tiller and Joel walked ahead to prepare the next.

The first lock disaster came on the second day, at a spot called Hungerford, where I forgot to close a bottom paddle before opening the top one. The water thundered in, the boat lurched, and a wave of brown froth rolled over the front deck and soaked Joel's shoes. A man on the towpath with a dog said quite calmly that this happened to everybody, and helped me wind the paddle shut. Mira laughed until she had to sit on a bollard.

The days settled into a routine. We rose at seven, made porridge on the two-ring hob, cast off by eight and travelled until noon, tying up in a village for lunch and a walk. The speed limit on the canal is four miles an hour, roughly walking pace, and it took us about five hours a day to cover eight or nine miles and pass six or seven locks. Herons stood in the reeds, kingfishers flickered by like blue matches, and a swan escorted us for a mile with a look of disapproval.

On the third evening we moored beside a meadow near Kintbury and ate at a pub beside the canal, where the landlord told us that the water level had dropped in the drought and that the boaters were being asked to save water at locks. We had noticed. The next morning we shared a lock with a family on a smaller boat, which lets two vessels use the same fill of water, and the father, a bald man with a wonderful laugh, taught me a way to hold the rope round a bollard so that it takes the strain without burning the hands.

The swing bridges were another lesson. At several points the towpath crosses on a road bridge that must be swung open by hand, and the boat has to wait while cars queue. A car full of teenagers gave us a cheer at one bridge, and at another a farmer on a tractor politely waited while we struggled with a stiff crank. Karin developed the habit of thanking everyone in a formal voice, as if she were an ambassador, and by the fourth day the whole crew was doing it.

The weather broke on the Wednesday. We moored under a willow while a thunderstorm crashed over the water, and spent two hours indoors playing cards and listening to the rain hammer the roof. The stove, which Dennis had shown us how to light, gave a comforting glow and a smell of hot metal. Joel produced a bottle of something he had been hiding, and we toasted the boat, which had not yet run us aground.

It ran us aground on Thursday. Trying to pass an oncoming boat in a narrow section near Great Bedwyn, Karin steered too close to the bank and we slid into the mud, the bow tilting up like a dog sniffing. We pushed with a boat pole, rocked the hull, and eventually reversed off with the help of a passing dredger crew who found the whole scene very funny. Nobody was hurt, and the only damage was to our dignity, and to a shoe.

Food deserves its own paragraph, because a narrowboat galley teaches economy. Karin planned the meals on a single page pinned to the wall: porridge and stewed plums for the mornings, pasta with whatever the village shop had for the evenings, and a running joke about the one tin of peaches that nobody would admit to buying. We shopped at small stores along the route, carrying groceries back along the towpath in a rucksack, and learned that a cold box in a hot summer is a fiction. By Wednesday the butter was soup. Joel solved it by lowering a bag of milk on a string into the canal at night, a trick he swore was in the boater's handbook, and by Friday the water had made us all a little superstitious about it.

The last day brought us to Devizes at the foot of the great flight of twenty-nine locks at Caen Hill, a staircase of water climbing up a hillside like a green ladder. We left the boat at the bottom on the final evening. We had done a hundred and four miles, fifty-one locks and one accidental sunbathing on a mudbank, and none of us wanted to go home. Karin says that next year we should take a boat for ten days. Joel, with his notebook, calculates that this would allow us to reach the Thames, and Mira has already begun to hum a sea shanty in the shower, in a cubicle the size of a wardrobe.

I should note what to pack next time. Waterproof trousers, not just a coat. Rubber-soled shoes for the roof. A proper windlass of my own, because the hire one rusted my hands. A long-handled net for dropped items, since I lost a hat and a torch in the first lock. And a large jar of patience, which Dennis told us on the first morning is the only fuel that never runs out on a canal.

Client visit to the Nordvik shipyard, notes from the site day. Avery and Blake went up on the early train to meet the operations director of a mid-sized shipyard that has been a customer of the studio for about a year. The yard builds small passenger ferries and offshore support vessels and uses our planning product to schedule welding crews across three slipways. The visit was arranged to understand how the software is really used, not how the sales deck says it is used.

We were met at the gate by Kerstin Dahl, the operations director, a woman in a hard hat and a quilted jacket who walks very fast. She issued us with helmets, goggles, ear defenders and boots, and made us sign a safety card before we were allowed near anything. She explained that the yard employs about four hundred people in shifts, that the biggest constraint is the crane, which serves all three slipways, and that whoever owns the crane schedule owns the yard.

The first stop was the slipway where a forty-metre ferry stood in its cradle like a whale on a trolley. The hull was half plated, the steel still bare, and crews in orange overalls moved along it with welding rigs, sparks shooting off in fountains. Kerstin pointed out the paint marks that show which plates are ready for inspection. Each mark, she said, corresponds to a line on a screen in the planning office, and each line has to be updated by hand by a foreman with a handheld screen.

That was the first surprise. The foremen dislike the handheld screen, and not because of the software: it is because their hands are always dirty, and the screen fails to respond to gloves. They have developed a workaround, in which they photograph the plates and give the photos to a clerk who updates the system at the end of the shift. Blake wrote this down with a look of quiet alarm. The result is that the plan in the office is always about six hours behind reality, and the crane is often booked for work that has already finished.

The second stop was the planning office, a low hut with a wall of printed charts and a huge whiteboard. It turned out that the yard uses our product for the official schedule but runs the real one on the whiteboard, with magnetic tokens for each crew. When a crane slot changes, someone moves a token and phones the clerk. Kerstin was frank about it. The software, she said, is good for reporting to the owners and hopeless for the daily chaos, and she wanted to know whether we could fix that.

Lunch was in a canteen decorated with framed photographs of launches going back to 1952. We ate fish stew from steel trays beside a group of welders who had a friendly argument with us about football. Afterwards Kerstin took us up to the crane operator's cabin, a glass box forty metres in the air, where an operator named Torbjorn showed us his own list, a hand-drawn grid taped to the glass. He said he ignored the computer completely, because it never told him when the wind was too strong.

One small exchange stays with me. While we waited for the meeting to start, Siv showed us a folder of paper forms that the foremen fill in when a plate is welded, a pink carbon copy for the office and a white one for the hull file. I asked why the yard kept the forms if the software already recorded the same thing. She said that in eleven years no auditor had ever asked to see the software, but two had asked for the pink copy, and that a hull file is a legal document. It was a useful reminder that our product is one of several records in her world, not the only truth.

The afternoon meeting was a proper working session with Kerstin, her planner Siv and two foremen. We asked what would make the tool useful on the slipway, and the answers were practical and specific. They wanted a way to mark a plate as done with one large button that a gloved hand could press. They wanted the crane list to show wind limits. They wanted the plan to be viewable on a phone in the cold without logging in twice. Nobody asked for new charts.

We left with a list of eleven requests, which Avery sorted on the train into three groups: quick, moderate and expensive. The big-button screen and the offline mode went in the first group, and the wind limits, which need an outside data feed, in the second.
