The third group held a request for the tool to plan steel deliveries from the supplier, which is a different product altogether. Blake suggested that we return in six weeks with a prototype of the big-button screen, and Kerstin, who had said very little about deadlines, agreed with a nod.

On the way home we reflected. The most important lesson, Blake said, was that a plan on paper that is right is worth more than a screen that is wrong. The yard did not need us to be clever. It needed us to be quick, robust and humble. We resolved to bring a foreman to our next planning session and to test every screen with thick gloves on. Avery has already bought a pair of welding gloves from a hardware shop and left them on the desk for anyone who wants to try our own tool in them.

Study visit to the printing museum in Norrkoping, team outing. Nine of us took a Friday off from the studio to see a museum that Avery has been mentioning for a year. It is housed in an old newspaper works beside the river, a brick building with tall glass roofs, and it holds a complete chain of print technology from a wooden hand press to a rotary machine as big as a bus. We were guided by a printer of seventy named Gösta, who worked at the works until it closed and who speaks about the machines the way other people speak about relatives.

Gösta began with type. He showed us a case of metal characters, each a tiny block cast in lead, laid out in compartments according to how often they are used, so that the character e has the largest box and the character q the smallest. He put a composing stick in the hands of Sanna, our designer, and asked her to set her own name backwards. She took ten minutes and produced a line that read perfectly in the mirror. He said that it was the first time in decades that a visitor had got the spacing right on the first go.

Then the press. Gösta inked a small hand press with a roller, laid on a sheet of thick paper, pulled the bar and lifted the sheet to reveal a print of a fishing boat in crisp black lines. He handed it to Blake, who held it like a baby. Everyone got a turn at the bar, and the noise of the metal thud in the quiet hall seemed to wake something in each of us. I have never felt so directly the weight of a page.

The next hall held the typesetting machines that replaced hand setting, a monstrous device with a keyboard of ninety keys that cast a whole line of type in one piece from molten metal. Gösta let us watch it run for a few minutes. Molten lead hissed in its pot, matrices fell in a clattering cascade, and a bright new line slid out into a tray still warm to the touch. He said that a good operator could cast six lines a minute, and that the smell of hot metal and ink never leaves your clothes.

The rotary press hall was the climax. It stood along the far wall, a steel giant three storeys high, with rolls of paper as tall as a person and a maze of rollers that ran the paper up and down through the machine. Gösta explained that in its day, it printed eighty thousand copies of the morning paper between midnight and four, and that the pressmen worked in ear plugs and never spoke. He pressed a button and a small motor turned the great cylinder a single revolution, and even that was enough to make the floor tremble.

We ate lunch at a canteen near the river and then broke into pairs for a scavenger hunt Avery had planned, matching old newspaper headlines from the archive with the events they announced. Blake and Sanna won by finding a front page about the launch of a ferry that nobody else had heard of. The prize, presented by Avery with great ceremony, was a lead slug of type with a capital B, which Blake keeps on his desk as a paperweight.

On the train home we talked about what a studio that designs screens for a living might learn from a museum full of machines. Sanna said that every good interface has the same quality as a good type case: everything you need is in reach, and nothing you do not need gets in the way. Avery said that his favourite object in the whole museum was the humble composing stick, a tool that has hardly changed in five centuries, because nobody could find a way to improve it. We agreed to come back next year with the whole company.

Footpath restoration day on the Ridge Way, team volunteer report. Once a year the studio gives everyone a paid day to help a local cause, and this year the vote went to the walking association that maintains a nine-kilometre trail along the ridge above the reservoir. Fourteen of us signed up. We met at the car park at half past eight on a cold Thursday in October, in the sort of mist that hangs on the shoulders and turns spectacles into frosted glass.

Our host was a warden named Solveig Nyman, a compact woman of sixty with a woollen hat pulled down to her eyebrows and a voice that carried across a hillside without effort. She had a van full of tools, a clipboard and an air of having done this with far worse volunteers. Her briefing was short. The trail had been damaged by two wet summers, and the job for the day was to repair a badly eroded stretch of about four hundred metres near the top, where walkers had worn a trench in the peat and were now widening it by stepping around the mud.

She explained the principle. Water is the enemy of a path. If it runs down the track, it cuts a gully; if you can turn it sideways off the path every few metres, the trail survives. The tools for that are simple: stone steps, wooden water bars set at an angle, and drains that lead the flow away into the heather. She showed us a finished one, a length of split log bedded in the soil at forty-five degrees, its upper end buried and its lower end open to a ditch, and told us that we would build eleven of them before lunch.

We divided into four crews. Mine had Avery, Sanna from design, Tobias from finance and a very quiet intern named Malin. Our job was to dig out a trench across the path, lay a log in it, pack it tight with stones and earth, and check that a bucket of water poured on it would run away sideways. The digging was harder than any of us had guessed, because the ground was a thick clay full of cobbles, and after an hour Tobias declared that he had discovered muscles he would like to return.

Solveig walked between crews with a spirit level and a critical eye. She stopped at our second water bar, prodded the log with her boot, and said that it was too flat and would collect water rather than shed it. We took it out and reset it a few degrees steeper. She said nothing more, which we took to be approval. By ten thirty the sun had burned through the mist and the whole ridge lay revealed, with the reservoir a sheet of pewter far below and a line of pylons striding away to the north.

The stone steps were the crown of the day. In one steep pitch where the path was almost vertical, Solveig wanted a staircase, and she supplied a pile of flat stones that had been lifted in by helicopter the previous winter. Each step had to be levelled, seated on a bed of gravel and wedged in place so it would not rock. She taught us to choose the stone by feel, turning it in the hand until it found its steadiest side. It felt like a slow and very heavy jigsaw, and Sanna named her step Gerald and refused to let anybody stand on it.

Lunch was tea from a great steel flask and sandwiches on a boulder beside the trail. A pair of walkers came by with a dog and thanked us for the work, and one of them remarked that the path used to be so bad that she carried spare socks. We told her it was going to be better. Solveig told us stories about the ridge: the drover's road that once crossed it, the wartime lookout post whose foundations were just visible in the heather, and the local man who walks the trail every morning at six and who had asked her to tell the volunteers that he was very grateful.

In the afternoon we moved to the drainage. The most satisfying task was clearing a culvert under the path that had silted up, so that water had been flowing over the top. Malin, who had barely said a word all morning, climbed into the ditch with a shovel and cleaned it out on her own in twenty minutes, and when the water suddenly gushed through in a brown surge she gave a small shout and the whole crew cheered. Avery said afterwards that it was the best moment of the day.

By four the light was low and gold and we had built ten water bars and fourteen steps. We had missed our target of eleven bars by one, and Solveig said with a straight face that this was excellent, because the eleventh was always a trap for the over-ambitious. She had us walk the finished stretch together, pouring a bucket on each bar to test it, and every one of them sent the water away sideways with a gurgle. It was surprisingly moving to watch it work.

We drove home in a convoy, muddy, tired and cheerful. On Friday morning the office was full of people walking as if they had been horse riding, and somebody had left a bag of biscuits on the desk of every volunteer with a note in Solveig's block capitals: thank you, come back in spring. Several of us have already asked whether the studio can support the walking association in a more lasting way, perhaps by paying for a work weekend every year and buying the tools.

A last thing from the day belongs in the report. During the afternoon a man in his seventies stopped at our section of trail, leaning on two sticks, and watched for a quarter of an hour. Solveig went over and they spoke for a while. It turned out that he had helped to build the original path in the seventies as a young member of the association, when it was a line of duckboards over the bog, and he had come to see what the new generation were doing. He inspected a water bar, tapped it with a stick, and said that his own had been worse and had lasted only twelve years. Then he asked whether he could lay one stone. Solveig handed him a small flat one, and he placed it at the foot of the staircase and pressed it down with a knee that visibly hurt.

The lessons for next year's volunteer day, from the notes I made in the van. Bring gloves that do not come apart, as three pairs did. Wear boots that have already been walked in. Take a change of socks, because Solveig was right about them. Have a proper stretch before the first swing of the pickaxe. And do not name your steps after people, because then everybody feels obliged to walk round them. The final tally, according to Solveig's clipboard, was two hundred and forty metres of repaired path, and she says it should last at least a decade if the walkers keep to the middle.

Fire drill debrief, the first full evacuation of the third floor since we moved in. The building manager scheduled it without warning on a Tuesday at twenty past ten, and the alarm went off while Blake was halfway through a call with a supplier. Everyone in the office stood up, looked at each other, and waited for someone else to move. That pause, about eleven seconds by Avery's reckoning, is the most important finding of the day.

The fire warden for our floor is Yusuf, a job he was given because he was the only person who did not leave the meeting when it was proposed. He put on the green vest, took the clipboard from its hook and began to shepherd people to the stairwell, which is behind a heavy door that sticks. Two colleagues used the lift out of habit, which they should not have done, and had to be retrieved from the lobby by a security guard. Sanna returned to her desk to fetch her bag, and Yusuf sent her out again with a stern look.

We gathered at the assembly point on the pavement opposite, beside a bus stop. The head count took three minutes, and it came out at nineteen against an expected twenty-two. Yusuf checked the visitor sheet, then the list of people working from home, and found that the three missing people were a man on holiday, a woman who had left for a dentist appointment, and a contractor whose name had not been added to the register. After some tense minutes everyone was accounted for.

Mrs Aaltonen also pointed us to a detail that none of us had noticed: the assembly point on the pavement is shared with the dentist's practice on the ground floor, and on the day of the drill their patients had wandered into our head count. Yusuf had spent a minute asking a man in a paper bib whether he worked with us. He did not, and he took the question in good humour, saying it was the most attention he had received all week. We agreed to ask the dentist to hold their own drill at a different hour, and to mark a separate corner of the pavement for our floor with a strip of yellow tape, which Mrs Aaltonen offered to supply.

At the debrief in the lobby the building manager, Mrs Aaltonen, read her notes. The floor had cleared in three minutes and forty seconds, against a target of four, which was satisfying. But she pointed out three problems. The sticky stairwell door had slowed the flow. The two lift users were a risk. And nobody had shut the office door behind them, which lets smoke travel. Her advice was to tape a note on the inside of the door reminding people to close it.

Afterwards Avery went through the floor plan with a pen. Fourteen desks sit within six metres of the stairwell, but the eight at the far end by the blank-walled store have to pass the printers and a row of chairs, and it was two of those people who took longest. Her suggestion, later adopted, was to move the printers back against the wall to widen the route, and to add a small illuminated sign above the store door. It cost very little and is the kind of change that nobody notices until they need it.

We agreed to fix the door with a new closer, to add a laminated card to every desk with the route and assembly point, and to hold a short refresher in the spring. Yusuf asked for a proper hi-vis vest with the word warden on the back, and Avery promised to order one. Blake wondered whether the eleven-second pause could be shortened. Mrs Aaltonen said that the best cure was to run drills so often that nobody hesitates, and that she would be back in six months.

Charity quiz night organised by the team, planning notes and results. Every year the studio hosts a quiz in aid of a local children's hospice, and this year Avery and Blake agreed to run it, which meant writing eighty questions, finding a venue, selling tickets and persuading a local brewery to donate a barrel. The evening took place on a Friday in late November at the upstairs hall of the Two Swans, and forty-two people came.

The planning began six weeks before. We met three times in the small meeting space to decide the format. Avery wanted six rounds of ten questions plus a picture round and a music round, and Blake wanted to add a round on local history, which we agreed to because a quiz that pleases only the people who write it is not much use. We drew up a scoring sheet and chose a tiebreaker: how many steps there are on the town hall tower, a number nobody knew and everybody would guess.

Writing the questions took longer than expected, because good questions are hard. A good question has one answer, a fair difficulty and a little pleasure in it. Bad ones are either impossible or offensively easy. We tested a draft on the two colleagues who joined most recently, both of whom were annoyingly good, and removed nine questions after they answered them in under a second. Sanna made the picture round, a set of famous buildings photographed from strange angles, and the music round consisted of snatches of songs played backwards.

The venue was booked through a friend of Blake's, a landlord called Ove who agreed to give us the hall for nothing in exchange for a share of the bar takings. We set the price of a ticket at one hundred and fifty crowns for a team of four, and sold forty-two seats by the middle of November, mostly to the studio's friends, families and clients. The brewery donated a barrel and three crates of cider, and a local bakery gave sixty cakes for the interval, which was a triumph of goodwill over logistics.

On the night, we arrived at five to set up. The hall smelled of stale beer and floor polish, and we spent an hour dragging benches into rows, laying out pens and answer sheets, and testing the microphone, which squealed. Blake acted as quizmaster in a bow tie that nobody had seen before. He has a gift for it, a warm and slightly sarcastic patter that made even the hardest questions funny, and the audience settled at once into the rhythm of an evening where the answer hardly matters.

The first round was on geography, and the hall was silent except for the scratching of pencils. Team names appeared on the board: Quiz Team Aguilera, The Usual Suspects, Fact Finders and a group of teachers who called themselves Detention. By the third round the teachers led by a point, and by the interval they were four ahead of a bench of engineers from the hospital. During the interval the cakes vanished in about six minutes, and Avery collected donations in a tin, adding up to over two thousand crowns.

The second half went by in a blur of laughter. The picture round split the hall, because half the teams recognised the Sydney Opera House upside down and half thought it was a shell. The backwards music round produced a wild argument about which pop song it was. In the last round, a question about the tallest lighthouse in the country produced a tie between the teachers and the engineers, and Blake announced the tiebreaker: how many steps in the tower? The teachers guessed three hundred and ten, and the engineers, cannily, two hundred and eighty. The real answer was two hundred and ninety-one, so the engineers won by eleven.

Afterwards the two teams shook hands, the engineers took home a crate of cider and the teachers received the wooden spoon, which had been decorated by Sanna with glitter. By half past eleven, we had counted the takings: ticket sales, donations, bar share and a raffle came to a total of eleven thousand four hundred crowns, all of which was handed to the hospice the following Monday in an oversized cardboard cheque. The director thanked us and asked if we would do it again.

We will, but with a few changes. Fewer questions, since eighty proved to be too many for a Friday night. A better microphone. A rule against searching for answers on phones, which some teams ignored. And a written brief for volunteers, because at the peak of the interval three people tried to sell the same raffle ticket. Blake has kept the bow tie, and is talking about hosting a pub quiz on the first Thursday of every month, which Avery says he will attend only if the questions are written by someone else.

Judging the internal photo competition, an afternoon in the small meeting space. The studio runs a photo contest each winter on a single theme, and this year's theme was a place that made you stop. Twenty-three staff and freelancers submitted between one and three pictures each, and Avery and Blake were made the jury, along with a guest, the photographer Ines Vogel, who runs a small gallery on the street behind the office.

Ines brought a method. She printed all sixty-one entries on cheap paper, laid them on the floor in rows, and asked us to walk round them in silence for ten minutes without discussing anything. After that each of us was to pick five favourites on a slip of paper. The system works, she said, because it prevents the loudest person from steering the panel. We tried to obey and only managed to keep quiet for six minutes before Blake muttered that a photo of a bus shelter in the rain was better than it had any right to be.

The slips showed a lot of overlap. All three of us had chosen a picture of an empty swimming pool at dawn, taken by a colleague in Lisbon, and a black and white shot of a fisherman's hut half submerged in a flood. Ines said that a good photograph makes the viewer want to step inside, and both of these did. Then she pointed out something interesting: the pictures with the most people in them were the weakest, because the subjects looked at the lens and the eye went to their faces instead of the place.

Some of the entries deserve mention. There was a picture of a launderette at midnight with a single dryer turning, taken by a developer in Gothenburg, that made all three of us go quiet for a moment. There was a very sharp photograph of a market stall with a heap of oranges, technically flawless and, as Ines said, without a single reason to look at it twice. There was a shot of a church clock stopped at ten past four, and a family of swans walking down a street in a small town, which got a laugh and no votes. Ines kept a tally of what she called the honest ones, the pictures where the photographer had clearly stopped because something moved them, and said that she could always tell.

The debate was polite and lasted an hour. Avery argued for a picture of a rooftop at sunset, very pretty and slightly too neat, and Ines gently observed that it looked like a postcard. Blake liked a blurred image taken from a train, and the panel discussed for ten minutes whether blur is an accident or a decision. In the end the swimming pool won, the flooded hut came second, and third went to the bus shelter in the rain. Ines wrote a comment for each of the winners by hand.

Ines also gave a short talk over tea to whoever wanted to stay. She said the biggest error amateurs make is to shoot from standing height every time, which produces the same picture of the world as everyone else has. Crouch, she said, or climb, or lie on the floor. Hold the camera against a wall. Photograph the light instead of the object. She showed three of her own frames on her phone, an old ferry terminal, a fish stall and a child's boots by a door, each taken from a strange angle, and each obviously right. A dozen people stayed for it, and two asked if she would run a proper workshop in the summer.

The prizes were modest, a gift token, a framed print and a box of pencils. The three winning photographs will hang in the corridor until spring. At the end, Ines said she wished more workplaces did this, since a pair of eyes trained on stopping is a useful asset in any kind of design, and she told the panel that she had learned as much from us as we had from her. Avery took that to be flattery and thanked her twice.

Office recycling audit, a Saturday spent looking through our own rubbish. The building manager sent a polite message in September asking tenants to review their waste, because the block had been fined for contaminated recycling. Blake said that the only way to know how bad we were was to look, so on a wet Saturday Avery and he put on rubber gloves and emptied every bin on the third floor onto plastic sheeting in the loading bay.

The plan was simple. Sort everything into five heaps: paper, plastic, glass, food and residual waste, and weigh each with a hanging scale borrowed from the caretaker. We wanted to compare what people put in each bin with what belonged there. There were sixteen bins, four large ones for recycling near the printers and the rest small ones under desks. The whole floor produced, over the previous five working days, about eighty-one kilograms of waste.

The first hour was mostly disgust. A bin under the meeting space held a half-eaten sandwich, a used tea bag, three cardboard cups with plastic lids, a broken plug and a birthday card. The recycling bins were worse. Nearly a third of the paper bin contained things that did not belong: yoghurt pots, wrappers, one whole packed lunch and, remarkably, a single sock. Plastic was often full of greasy takeaway trays that cannot be recycled and had spoiled the rest of the load.

The scale told the rest. Of the eighty-one kilograms, twenty-two were paper, of which about seven were contaminated; nine were plastic, of which four could not be recycled; six were glass; eleven were food scraps; and thirty-three were general waste. Blake wrote the numbers on the bay wall in chalk. The main finding was that our recycling was polluted by ordinary carelessness, not by malice, and that a person standing at a bin with a sandwich has about two seconds to decide.

Before the changes, though, we asked the cleaners what they thought, which turned out to be the most valuable hour of the project. Two of them, Mirela and her cousin Dragan, have emptied our bins for four years and had a very clear picture. They told us that the floor's biggest problem was not the recycling bins but the general ones: people filled them with paper because it was closer, and the cleaners then had to either sort by hand or tip the whole lot into the general skip. Mirela said that nobody had ever asked them before, and that she had been saving the answer for three years.

She added a practical tip. The bags in the small bins were too thin, and split when someone dropped in a cup of leftover tea, which soaked the contents and made them impossible to sort. Dragan had started carrying heavier bags in his trolley and paying for them himself. We arranged that the studio would buy them from then on, and Blake also arranged a small allowance so that the cleaners could order what they needed without asking. The audit report we later sent to the building manager gave both of them credit by name, which pleased them more than the pastries.

There was a smaller discovery too. In the food heap we found nineteen paper cups with hot-drink lids of a kind that the city's recycling plant does not accept, and the plant's website, when Avery looked it up, explained that the lining of the cup is a thin plastic film that jams the pulping machinery. It was news to everyone, including the person who had bought the cups, who went a little pink. We replaced them with ceramic mugs from the shelf, and Blake, who had been drinking from paper cups for years, admitted that the tea tasted better.

We decided on four changes. Larger labels with photographs of what goes where, since words were ignored. Removing every under-desk bin, so that people walk to a station and think for a moment. A dedicated food caddy near the galley that would be emptied by the cleaners. And a monthly one-page report of the weights, pinned by the lift. Avery drew up the labels the following week, with a picture of a sock on the general waste bin as a joke.

The whole exercise took about five hours, including the wash-up, and left the bay smelling of onions for two days. Mr Lindqvist the caretaker, who came down at noon to see what we were doing, stood in the doorway for a long while and then quietly brought us a bucket of hot water and a mop, with the remark that he had seen many things in this bay but never two grown men sorting yoghurt pots by weight.

We repeated the audit six weeks later on another wet Saturday. The results were better: contamination in the paper bin had fallen from seven kilograms to two, and the total waste had dropped to sixty-three kilograms, mostly because people were no longer refilling small bins with a single tissue. The caretaker, Mr Lindqvist, arrived with a tray of pastries and told us that the block had received a commendation. He said it was the first time in eleven years that anyone had voluntarily read the bin.

Team sailing day on the archipelago, log kept by the person who volunteered to keep it. In June the studio booked a day on the water for all fourteen of us, hired two fifteen-metre sailing yachts with skippers from a small firm on Vaxholm, and warned everyone to bring soft-soled shoes and a sense of humour. I am a poor sailor and a worse swimmer, which was the reason I offered to write things down: a person with a notebook is exempt from the ropes.

We assembled at the jetty at nine, in bright, cold sunshine and a fresh breeze from the south-west. The skippers were a middle-aged couple, Ragna and Arne Lindgren, who run the firm and have crossed the Baltic more times than either can count. Ragna took the first boat and Arne the second. They gave each of us a lifejacket, checked the straps by tugging on them, and delivered a safety briefing that was clear, short and mercifully free of jokes: where the life rings are, how to reach the radio, and what to do if somebody goes overboard.

Blake and I were put on Ragna's boat, called Sunniva, along with Sanna, Yusuf, Tobias and two of the freelancers. We motored out through the channel between wooded islands, past red cabins with white corners, and then Ragna cut the engine, asked us to haul on a halyard, and the mainsail rose with a creak and a flap. The boat leaned, gathered speed and began to hiss through the water, and a shriek of delight went up from the foredeck. I sat down hard on a locker and held on to my notebook.

The first lesson was tacking. To sail upwind a boat has to zigzag, and each time it turns, the whole crew has to duck under the boom, swap sides and trim the sails. Ragna called the manoeuvre in a calm voice: ready about, lee-ho. After ten turns we were doing it smoothly. Tobias, who had been very nervous, took the tiller and steered a tack of his own, and afterwards spoke of nothing else for an hour.

Around eleven we anchored in a small bay for a swim. The water was fourteen degrees, which Yusuf described as a slap from an angry hand. About half the crew jumped in and shrieked, the rest stayed on the deck, and I dangled my feet from the ladder and considered my life. Arne handed round hot chocolate from a flask, and a seal appeared fifty metres off, looked at us with mild scorn and sank from view. I have never seen so many adults so pleased about a seal.

Lunch was on the deck of Arne's boat, which was rafted alongside ours: cold potatoes, pickled herring, hard-boiled eggs, a dill sauce, sliced cucumber and rye crackers, with a dessert of strawberries that somebody had thoughtfully brought. The two crews sat cross-legged on the cabin roofs and talked. It was the longest conversation I had ever had with Sanna, who turned out to have spent her childhood summers on an island very like this one, and could name each bird in the bay from its call.

After lunch we raced. Ragna and Arne had agreed on a course round three islands, with the first boat back to the anchorage winning. The wind had freshened to a stiff breeze and Sunniva heeled until the rail dipped, and water washed along the deck. We sat on the high side with our legs braced, shouting at the sails. Halfway through, a gust hit and the boom swept across, missing Yusuf's head by a hand, and Ragna calmly said that in future everyone should keep an eye on the boom.

We lost by about a minute. Arne's boat crossed the line first, and Arne came up on deck with a wide grin and a ceremonial bow. We consoled ourselves with the knowledge that his boat was lighter and that we had a better story. Ragna said it was the closest finish she had seen from an office crew. She had the good grace to accept a bottle of wine as a bribe for a rematch next year.

On the way back the wind dropped and we motored the last hour through a golden evening, the islands turning blue and then violet, with the smell of pine and seaweed drifting across the water. Nobody said much. Sanna leaned against the mast with her eyes closed. Blake had fallen asleep on a coil of rope. I finished my notes, counted the day in figures and found that we had sailed twenty-six nautical miles, done eighteen tacks, seen one seal and lost one hat and one sandwich to the sea.

Around four, halfway home, a small drama unfolded that deserves its own paragraph. A ferry crossed our bows a little too closely, and Ragna spoke to Tobias, who was at the tiller, in a quiet voice: bear away, now, and hold. He did, and she took the helm again a moment later with nothing worse than a steely look at the ferry captain. Afterwards she explained the rules of the road in a way that even I understood. Power gives way to sail in theory, but a ship the size of a ferry cannot stop, and the sensible skipper never tests the principle. She said the sea is a place where being right is not much of a comfort.

As we motored the last stretch she told us how she and Arne started the business twenty years earlier with a single old wooden boat that Arne had rebuilt in a shed over three winters. The bank had refused to lend to them, so they sold their flat and lived on the boat for two years, taking anyone who asked on day trips to the outer islands. Their first customers were a group of accountants who spent the whole voyage arguing about the price of fuel. Ragna laughed at the memory and said that they were still the best-behaved passengers she had ever carried.

The islands themselves offered a good deal to look at, and I filled several pages with what Sanna told me about them. The low grey one with the single house was a former pilot station where the pilots lived in summer to guide ships through the channel. The tall one with the white daymark had been used in the eighteen hundreds as a quarantine post for sailors with fever. And the little green one with a lone birch had, according to Ragna, a single resident, a retired ornithologist who arrives each April with a tent and a great many binoculars and stays until the terns have fledged.

When we got back to the jetty at seven, the wind had all but gone, and the harbour lay flat as poured glass, with the sunset reflected on it in long streaks of orange. The skippers coiled the ropes, hosed down the decks and handed each of us a small paper bag with a piece of driftwood in it as a souvenir. I kept mine, a smooth grey stick the length of a finger, and it now lives on my desk beside a tin of pens, where it reminds me of a very good day on which nothing went wrong and a hat went missing.

Practical lessons for the next sailing day. Bring sun cream, because the wind hides the burn. Bring a hat with a string. Wear thin layers rather than one thick jacket. Do not leave anything valuable on the cabin roof. And note that the skippers charge less if you book in the shoulder season, which is why Blake has already asked Ragna for a date in early September. The team voted unanimously to make it an annual event, with a bottle of wine at stake and a proper trophy, which Sanna has promised to carve from driftwood.

Restoration Saturday at the tram museum, team volunteer day. The city's tram museum occupies a red brick depot on the eastern edge of town, and it has a collection of eleven vehicles from the horse-drawn era to the nineteen sixties. The volunteers meet every Saturday to repair them, and this month the studio sent eight of us to help with the most ambitious job on the calendar: the restoration of car number forty, a green and cream motor tram built in 1929, which has been in pieces for six years.

We were welcomed by the chairman of the museum association, an elderly man in a blue boiler suit named Folke Ström, who shook hands with each of us and asked what we did for a living. When we said that we design software, he brightened and said that trams and software were quite similar, because both need a great many small parts to work together and both go wrong in the smallest ones. He then gave us tea in enamel mugs and a tour of the depot.

The depot smells of oil, old timber and varnish. Along its three tracks stood the trams in various states of dress, some gleaming, some skeletal. Car forty stood on blocks at the end of the third track with its body panels removed, so that its wooden frame showed like the ribs of a ship. Folke explained that the wood was ash and that much of it had rotted, and that the job for the day was to remove the rotten sections and cut new pieces by hand from templates.

I was put with a retired carpenter named Ake, who has worked on the frame for the last four years. He handed me a chisel and a mallet and pointed at a section of rotten beam above the rear platform. The technique was to cut across the grain in small steps, then split out the waste with the chisel, then pare the surface to a clean line. He watched me for five minutes without a word, then took the chisel and showed me the proper angle, holding it almost flat. After that the wood came away cleanly.

Avery worked on the electrics with a woman named Britta, who explained that the tram's original wiring had been replaced in the fifties with rubber-covered cable that had since become brittle. They spent the morning tracing the circuit from the controller to the motors with a meter and a hand-drawn diagram, finding two breaks and a fuse holder that someone had fixed with a hairpin. Blake sanded and repainted the seats, Sanna researched the original paint scheme in the archive photographs, and Yusuf polished the brass handrails until they gleamed.

At noon we broke for lunch in the volunteers' hut, where a long trestle was laid with sandwiches, boiled eggs, pickles and a rhubarb cake made by Folke's wife. The talk was of trams: the day in 1967 when the last passenger service ran in the city, the crowd that lined the streets, the driver who stopped at every stop for the last time and was given flowers. Folke had been a boy of ten on that day and remembers the smell of the wet street and the sound of the bell.

In the afternoon, I helped Ake fit a new section of beam. We cut it from a length of seasoned ash that the association had bought and stored in the loft for eight years, planed it to shape, checked it against the template and tapped it into place with a mallet. It fitted so precisely that there was hardly a gap. Ake ran his thumb along the join and said, in a voice I could hardly hear, that it was as good as the original. I have rarely been so proud of a piece of wood.

One of the older volunteers, a white-haired retired conductor named Lennart, gave me a short lesson on the tram's controller during the afternoon tea. It is a brass handle on a vertical post, and each notch of the handle switches resistors in or out of the circuit to bring the motors up to speed. He stood with his hand on it and closed his eyes and said he could still feel the vibration through the floor. He then let me move it through the notches on the dead vehicle, and I could hear the tiny click of each contact in the cabinet. He explained that the trick to driving a tram smoothly was to move the handle steadily, never jerking, and to feel for the point where the wheels bit.

Lennart also told me that when the depot closed to the public in the sixties, the cars were nearly sold for scrap. It was the conductors' union that fought to save eleven of them, and it took the museum association ten years of bake sales and appeals to the council to keep the roof over them. The building itself is listed, and the roof leaks in three places, which the volunteers patch each autumn with sheets of lead they beg from a friendly plumber.

By four we were tired, and the depot was full of sawdust and the low sun coming through the skylights. Folke gathered us by car forty and told us that the tram would be finished in about eighteen months, and that on the first day it ran he would like the eight of us to ride on it. We shook hands again. I noted afterwards that a day of chisels and old varnish did more for the team than any away day in a conference hotel, and Avery has already asked whether we can go back monthly.

Visit to the Saltholm brewery, a team afternoon in March. Blake proposed it after somebody left a bottle of their pale ale in the office fridge and the whole floor liked it. The brewery is a small independent one, twelve people in a converted dairy on the edge of town, and it agreed to give the studio a private tour and tasting on a Wednesday afternoon for a modest fee. Eleven of us went, taking the bus to save on a taxi.

Our guide was the head brewer, a big cheerful man named Jonas Frisk with hands like shovels. He began at the malt store, where sacks of barley stood stacked to the roof, and he let us taste the grains: pale malt sweet as biscuit, crystal malt like burnt toffee, and roasted barley so bitter that Sanna made a face and spat into her palm. He explained that beer is simply grain, water, hops and yeast, and that everything else is patience and temperature.

In the brewhouse he walked us through the mash, a warm porridge of grain and water that sits in a copper vessel for an hour while enzymes turn starch to sugar. The air smelled of wet cereal, like a huge bowl of breakfast. Then the liquid, called wort, is boiled with hops. Jonas held out a handful of dried hop cones and let us rub them and sniff. Sharp, resinous, a little like grapefruit and pine, and Yusuf said it smelled like a walk in a very optimistic forest.

Downstairs in the cellar the fermenters stood in a row like silver rockets. Each held two thousand litres and was busy, according to Jonas, doing the only work in the brewery that a human cannot help. He put an ear against one and invited us to listen to the hiss and crackle of the yeast. We took turns. It sounded like frying bacon heard through a wall. He told us that each batch takes two weeks to ferment and another week or two to condition.

The tasting was in a bare hall lit by a single lamp, with six glasses lined up in front of each of us. Jonas took us through them from the palest to the darkest: a light lager, the pale ale, a wheat beer, a brown ale, a porter and a strong stout aged in a whisky barrel. He asked us to smell before we sipped, and to say the first thing that came to mind. Tobias described the stout as a wet campfire, and Jonas said that was exactly what the brewers had been aiming for.

Jonas ended the tour with an unexpected confession. The brewery, he said, had nearly closed in its second year, when a batch of forty barrels turned sour because a cooling valve had stuck overnight. He and his partner poured the whole lot into the yard drain and stood there in silence, and the neighbours complained about the smell for a week. What saved the business was a shipment of their first pale ale to a restaurant in Malmo that had ordered it by mistake and then reordered on purpose. He said that a brewery is a bet on small things going right, and that he has learned to keep a valve wrench on a string around his neck.

We left at six with a case of the pale ale and a good deal of respect for a trade that looks easy until you watch it. On the bus home Blake proposed a team brew, and Jonas had told us that he would gladly host a group willing to spend a day stirring. Avery, who had not touched a drop, pointed out that somebody would need to design the label, and Sanna said she had already begun sketching a fox.

Building the office bike shelter, a project log over four weekends. The studio has eleven people who cycle in, and for two years their bikes lived in the stairwell, chained to the radiator pipes, until the building manager sent a firm but friendly note saying that a stairwell is a fire route and not a parking bay. The landlord agreed that we could put up a covered shelter in the corner of the yard, on condition that we paid for it, built it ourselves and did not touch the drains.

The design came first. Yusuf, who trained as a joiner before switching to software, drew it on a sheet of graph paper over one lunch hour: a three-sided lean-to five metres long and two deep, with a slanted roof of corrugated sheeting, a plank floor raised off the ground and rails to lock bikes against. He worked out that it would hold twelve bikes if they were staggered, with the handlebars at alternating heights so that they would not tangle. Blake, who handles the budget, asked for a materials list. It ran to sixty-eight lines.

The budget was the second stage. We agreed a ceiling of nine thousand crowns from the office fund. Avery got quotes from two timber merchants and a builders' supplier and found the cheapest option was a local yard called Nilsson & Son, who supplied pressure-treated posts, joists, boards and roof sheets for six thousand three hundred, delivered on a flatbed lorry. We spent another eight hundred on fixings, concrete mix, anti-rot paint and a pair of hinges, which left a healthy margin that we then spent, of course, on more fixings.

The first weekend was for the foundations. Yusuf marked out the footprint with string and pegs, and six of us dug holes for the posts with borrowed spades and a hired post-hole auger that sounded like a small aircraft. The soil in the yard turned out to be full of old brick and, at one point, a length of rusted pipe that made us all stop and look worried. The building manager, Mrs Aaltonen, came down with a plan of the underground services and confirmed that it was an abandoned fuel line. She stood over the hole with her arms folded until we filled it back in.

We set the posts in concrete. This is a delicate operation: each post must be vertical in both directions, held with props while the mix goes off, and checked repeatedly with a spirit level. Tobias, the most careful of us, appointed himself the level man and spent four hours checking posts, muttering about half a degree here and there. By four on Saturday, six posts stood in a neat row, and the rain that arrived shortly afterwards did us the favour of demonstrating that the concrete had set well enough.

The second weekend brought the frame. We bolted horizontal beams between the posts, cut rafters with a borrowed saw and fitted them at a slope to carry the water away from the wall. The saw was not sharp, and it took Blake, who is not known for his carpentry, three attempts to cut one rafter to length. Yusuf gently took the saw from him and cut the other nine in half an hour, and Blake declared that he would in future stick to spreadsheets. Sanna painted the wood with a preservative that turned everything a shade called forest.

On Sunday we fixed the roof sheets, which are enormous and awkward and act like sails in a breeze. A gust caught one as it was being lifted and nearly carried Malin over the wall. After that we held the sheets down with sandbags and moved on a slow, deliberate pace. Each sheet had to overlap the next by a full corrugation, and be screwed through the crest of the wave, not the trough, so that water cannot creep in. Yusuf explained that this is the single most common mistake in roofing, and Malin wrote it on her hand.

The third weekend was for the floor and the racks. We laid planks on joists, leaving a gap of a few millimetres between them for drainage, and installed a rail along the back wall at a height of sixty centimetres for locking frames. The rail was a length of galvanised pipe that Yusuf sourced from a scrapyard for the price of a sandwich. We drilled holes for bolts, welded nothing, and tested the result by locking a bike to it and pulling. The bike did not move, and the building manager, who had been watching, nodded once.

The fourth weekend was for the finishing touches: a coat of paint, a small sign reading bicycles, please lock and a hand-painted line marking each space. There was also a lively argument about whether to add a side panel to keep out the wind. Blake felt that a fully enclosed shelter would look like a garage and attract theft, while Sanna thought that a bike in the rain is a sad thing. We reached a compromise with a half-height slatted panel on the windward side, which looks good and keeps most of the weather out.

The final cost was eight thousand four hundred and seventy crowns, comfortably below the ceiling, with two hundred and eleven left over for a bicycle pump on a chain. On the first Monday after completion, eleven bikes were parked in the new shelter, plus a twelfth belonging to a colleague who had not cycled in years and was inspired to start again. The stairwell is empty. The building manager sent a very short message: excellent, please build another.

A word on the neighbours, because the project was not entirely welcome at first. The dentist on the ground floor, whose back walls face the yard, wrote a short and tight-lipped note asking that we not drill before nine. We complied, and to make peace Sanna took a plate of cinnamon buns down the following Saturday. The dentist, a courteous man in his sixties named Dr Lindgren, ended by lending us a set of ear protectors and asking whether the shelter might have a spot for his own bike. We offered him the thirteenth place, a decision that required a rack to be extended, but it solved the entire relationship.

What we learned, for the record. First, measure twice and then let the person with the level measure a third time. Second, anything involving a roof takes twice as long as one imagines. Third, a project of this kind is not really about the shelter but about a small group of people standing in a yard on a Saturday, arguing amiably and passing tools. Sanna has asked whether the next project could be a bench for the yard, and Yusuf has already drawn one.

Open day at the Kyrkoby excavation, a team trip and its afterthoughts. One of our freelancers, Malin's older sister Elsa, works as a field archaeologist, and every summer her team opens the site of a medieval settlement to the public for a single Saturday. She invited the studio, we booked a minibus, and twelve of us drove ninety minutes to a wheat field on a low hill above a river, where a small white marquee and a line of red flags announced the dig.

The site director, a lean man named Dr Anselm Rask who wore a straw hat with a hole in it, met us at the gate. He explained that the field had been known for centuries to have a ruined church on it, and that a survey with ground-penetrating radar the previous year had revealed a pattern of ditches, postholes and foundations that suggested a whole village, occupied between the twelfth and fourteenth centuries and then abandoned. The dig was now in its fourth season, funded by the university and a small regional grant.

We were given a tour by Elsa, who is thirty-four and has the forearms and weathered nose of someone who has spent a decade outdoors. She walked us across the field to the main trench, a rectangular hole about ten metres by six and a metre and a half deep, with straight sides so clean they looked cut with a knife. She explained that each layer of soil is a page of history, and that the trick is to read the colours: a dark band is a floor or a fire, a yellow one is clay brought from elsewhere, and a grey speckled one is ash.

The most exciting feature of the season was a hearth. In the north end of the trench, under a layer of collapsed roof tiles, the team had found a circle of fire-reddened stones with a spread of charcoal and burnt bone. Elsa lowered herself into the trench and showed us a small heap of pottery sherds she had lifted that morning, rough and gritty, with a thumb-pressed rim. She held a piece to the light and said that somebody had made this with their hands eight hundred years ago and left a fingerprint in the clay. She let each of us touch it.

Then we were given trowels. In an adjacent trench, marked out for visitors, the diggers had prepared a shallow square where finds were likely and let us scrape the soil away in thin layers, tipping it into buckets for sieving. It requires patience: you scrape a few millimetres, check what has appeared, sweep it and scrape again. Tobias found a corroded iron nail after ten minutes and held it up as though it were a crown. Yusuf found nothing for an hour and then, with a small gasp, uncovered a curved piece of dark glass that Elsa identified as part of a drinking vessel.

The sieving station was in the shade of a tree, a set of frames with wire mesh where the diggers shook the soil to catch small finds. It was oddly hypnotic. A woman from the university explained that most of what they recover is tiny: fish scales, seeds, beads, fragments of bone, flakes of flint. From the seeds, she said, they can tell what people ate, and from the bones which animals they kept. In the hearth alone they had found barley, oats, peas and the remains of at least four kinds of fish.

At noon we ate lunch on the grass, with sandwiches from a bakery in the village and a flask of tea that the volunteers passed round. A retired schoolteacher who had been coming to the open day for eleven years sat beside me and told me about the first year, when the dig found a skeleton in the churchyard and the whole village came to stare. It had been a man in his forties, tall for his time, with worn knees from a lifetime of kneeling. The local priest, who had not been involved in the dig, blessed him before he was reburied. I found this unexpectedly moving.

After lunch we visited the finds tent, where a young conservator called Ingrid was cleaning and labelling objects. She showed us a tray of bone combs, a bronze buckle, a lead weight from a fishing net and a coin that had been identified as a penny of the king who ruled in the thirteenth century. Every piece has a tag with a number, a context and a date. She explained that the tags are the whole point. An object without its tag has lost nearly all its value, because the archaeologist no longer knows where it lay or what it lay with.

That comment made Blake, who is an incorrigible systems person, ask a string of questions about how the team records everything. It turns out that each find is logged in a database with coordinates from a total station, a surveying instrument on a tripod. Ingrid let him look through the eyepiece and press the button that fixes a point. He was delighted, and spent the rest of the afternoon quizzing her on database structure, until she gently observed that the most reliable system in the field was a waterproof notebook and a very sharp pencil.

The day ended with a talk by Dr Rask in the marquee about what the dig had found so far and what it might mean. He drew a rough plan of the village on a whiteboard, with about thirty houses on either side of a track, a church at the top and a water mill at the river's edge. He said that the settlement had probably been abandoned after a run of bad harvests and a plague, and that what impressed him most was not the dramatic moments but the small evidence of ordinary lives: a child's knucklebone, a mended cooking pot, a worn threshold.

During the afternoon I wandered off to the edge of the field, where a volunteer named Berit was drawing a section of the trench wall on graph paper. She did it in pencil, one square at a time, transferring the shapes of each soil layer to the page with a ruler and a tape measure. It took her three hours for a wall a metre and a half high. I asked why they did not simply photograph it. She said that a photograph shows what the light shows, but a drawing shows what the drawer understands, and that a drawing forces you to look at every centimetre. She had worked on digs for thirty years and had never once regretted the pencil.

We drove home in the evening light, sleepy and sun-burnt. On the bus, Malin admitted that she had spent most of the afternoon thinking about the fingerprint on the pottery. There was general agreement that the day had been the best outing the studio had held. I noticed that the conversation, for once, had nothing to do with work. Elsa has since sent us a small parcel: twelve postcards of the site, each with a hand-drawn diagram of a different find, and a note inviting us back next year to help with the sieving.

Christmas market stall for the hospice, organised by the team. Two weeks before Christmas the studio took a stall at the Saturday market in the old town square, selling homemade goods in aid of the children's hospice. The idea was Sanna's, and it grew from a conversation about what to do with three boxes of leftover conference merchandise. By the end of November the plan had expanded to include jam, candles, wreaths, spiced biscuit and, in a rash moment, a raffle for a signed print.

We had six weeks. Everyone chose a product. Avery made sixty jars of plum jam over two weekends, using a recipe from his grandmother that calls for a pinch of cardamom. Blake, who is not a cook, volunteered to make wreaths from fir branches and was surprisingly good, twisting them on a wire ring and decorating each with a cinnamon stick and a red ribbon. Sanna painted forty spiced biscuit hearts with white icing, and Tobias, without telling anyone, spent three evenings dipping candles in beeswax.

The day itself began at six in the dark, with frost on the cobbles and steam rising from the cider stall next door. We unloaded a borrowed van and set up under a striped canopy: two trestles, a red cloth, a string of lights powered by a battery and a hand-painted sign that said Studio Christmas, all proceeds to the hospice. By eight the market was buzzing, with locals wrapped in scarves, children hauling sledges and a brass band playing carols in the corner.

Sales began slowly and then surged. The jam went first. A woman bought six jars and said she was giving them to her whole street. The wreaths were popular with men, who bought them for their wives with an air of relief at having solved a problem, and the candles sold out by eleven. The spiced biscuit hearts proved harder, because the icing had softened in the damp, but Sanna sold them at a discount to children, who did not care.

A stallholder from the next pitch, a jovial woman who sold knitted socks, gave us the benefit of thirty years' experience. Put the cheapest things at the front, she said, because people buy the small thing first and then feel generous enough to buy a large one. Keep the change in a belt, not in a tin. And smile at the children, since they pull the parents. We rearranged the whole stall on her instruction, moving the jam to the front and the wreaths, which cost the most, to the back where they could be admired from a distance. Within half an hour the takings had visibly improved, and Tobias said that he would like her on the finance team.

The raffle was the star of the afternoon. Tickets were twenty crowns each, and the prize was a signed print of the town hall by a local artist, donated by Ines at the gallery. By two, we had sold nearly four hundred tickets, largely to people who did not want the print but wanted to be nice. At four Blake drew the winning number from a hat, and the winner turned out to be a small boy of six, who looked at the print in confusion and asked if he could swap it for a candle.

Just after three a photographer from the local paper arrived and asked us to stand in a line behind the stall holding jars. Blake, in a bobble hat, held up a wreath and looked so pleased with himself that the picture ran on the front page of the Monday edition with the caption the software team turns to pickles. He has cut it out and taped it to his monitor. The hospice's fundraiser, a soft-spoken woman named Astrid, dropped by at the end of the afternoon with a thermos of mulled juice and told us that stalls like ours made up nearly a fifth of their annual income.

Takings were counted in the van by torchlight. Jam brought in seven thousand crowns, wreaths four thousand two hundred, candles two thousand, spiced biscuit nine hundred, the raffle eight thousand and various donations another three thousand and forty. The total came to a little over twenty-five thousand crowns, which the studio agreed to round up to thirty. We drove home tired and cold and happy, smelling of cinnamon, and Avery admitted that plum jam is a great deal harder to make than to sell.

Team choir experiment, the six rehearsals before the winter party. It started as a joke in the office chat: someone suggested that the studio should sing at the winter party, and Yusuf, who plays the cello, replied that he would conduct if everyone showed up. Fifteen people signed the list, of whom four had ever sung in public. We booked the meeting space on Wednesday lunchtimes, borrowed a keyboard from the school next door and hired a director for six sessions.

The director was a friendly, brisk woman named Petra Holmgren, who leads a community choir on Sundays and treats every group of beginners as a challenge. She began the first rehearsal by making us stand in a circle, breathe deeply and hum. Then she went round the circle asking each of us to sing a single note. It was a horrifying moment. Nobody wanted to be first, so Tobias, who has a big baritone, volunteered and was drowned out by a giggle from the back.

She sorted us into four parts by listening: five sopranos, three altos, three tenors and four basses, with Yusuf doubling as a bass and an accompanist. The first song she chose was a Swedish folk tune in three verses, simple, slow and rather beautiful, which she said would let us get used to holding a line while other people sang something else. We worked on it for forty minutes, phrase by phrase, and by the end of the session it sounded like a choir that had been together for a week rather than ten minutes.

Progress was uneven. Sopranos learned quickly because they had the tune; basses had a harder time because their line was a set of long notes that seem meaningless without the rest. Petra had a trick: she would stop the sopranos and have the basses sing alone, so that everyone could hear what a bass line does. After a few minutes Tobias said with astonishment that the bass line was actually a piece of music in its own right. She smiled and said that this is the best-kept secret of choral singing.

By the third rehearsal a problem emerged. About half the choir turned up late, because of meetings that overran, and by the fourth a quarter had dropped out. Petra suggested moving the sessions to the end of the day, and after some discussion we agreed to hold them at five thirty on Wednesdays, when the office is quieter. The remaining eleven became more committed. We added a second song, a carol in English, and a short piece of unaccompanied harmony which Petra described as the hard one.

One rehearsal deserves a separate note. In the fifth session Petra brought in a guest, an old friend who sings professionally, and asked her to sit in the alto section and demonstrate. The difference was startling. She sang at half volume, barely moving her face, and the sound went straight through the meeting space, and the altos stopped dead to listen. Afterwards she explained that singing in a choir is mostly listening: you should hear the person beside you clearly, and if you cannot, you are too loud. She then sat between Sanna and Tobias and made them sing to each other with their eyes closed. It was the moment when the choir stopped being fifteen individuals shouting a tune and began, tentatively, to be one thing.

There was a small crisis about the dress code. Petra wanted us to wear black, and Blake, who does not own anything black except a single pair of socks, argued for a compromise. In the end everyone wore a plain dark shirt, and Sanna produced a set of red paper poppies that she pinned on us before the performance, one for each singer, so we looked like a slightly eccentric choir from a village that had won a prize.

The party was on a Thursday evening in December in the upstairs hall of a restaurant near the harbour. At eight, after the meal, Petra stood at the front and gave us a nod. We sang the folk tune first, and it went well. There was a slight wobble in the second verse where the altos came in early, but Sanna recovered by holding her breath and glaring at them. The carol was good, and the unaccompanied piece, which we had not managed to sing in tune once in rehearsal, worked on the night, by some kind of miracle.

The applause was warm and slightly astonished. A client who had come to the party said that he would never have expected the people who wrote the software to have voices. Yusuf bowed low. Petra, from the back of the hall, gave a thumbs-up and mouthed a word that I think was adequate. The choir has since agreed to continue on a monthly basis, and there is a proposal from Blake that we sing at the next customer event, an idea that Sanna described as a threat.

Fencing club grading day, my first attempt at a proper assessment. I joined the Vasa fencing club two years ago, at thirty-nine, after a colleague who had fenced in university persuaded me to try a taster night. I have been going on Tuesdays and Saturdays ever since. The club offers a series of grading assessments in each weapon, and I put my name down for the foil assessment with the rash confidence of a man who has never been examined on anything physical.

The assessor was a visiting referee from the national federation, a small elderly woman named Ulla Bergstrom who wore a black jacket and had reading glasses on a chain. She arrived at nine, shook hands with every candidate, and explained the process. There would be three parts: a demonstration of technique, an interview about the rules, and a series of bouts. The pass mark was sixty percent overall, and she warned that she never gives marks for effort, only for correctness.

The technique part came first. I was asked to demonstrate the basic actions in front of a small crowd: the guard position, the advance, the retreat, the lunge and the parry. I had done all of these hundreds of times, but under the eye of the assessor my feet forgot how to move. My first lunge landed with the wrong foot slightly turned, and Ulla, without changing expression, said the word again in a tone that sounded like a warm knife. I tried again and got it right. She made a note.

The interview was gentler than I feared. She asked me who has the right of way in a given exchange, what constitutes a valid hit, what to do if the opponent's mask comes loose and how to signal a halt. She gave scenarios, and I described them out loud. In one, both fencers hit each other at the same moment, and I had to decide who gets the point. I explained the right-of-way principle in about forty seconds, and she nodded, and then asked what I would do if the referee got it wrong. I said I would accept it, and she smiled.

The bouts were the longest part. I fenced four opponents in five-point contests, each for at most three minutes. The first was a nervous student named Mikael, whom I beat five to two, and the second was a girl of sixteen called Lova who was much faster and beat me five to three with a series of quick attacks that I did not see coming. Against the third I lost my concentration and gave away a point by dropping the guard. The fourth bout I won, five to four, on the last touch.

While we waited for the result, the club served tea. I sat with Mikael and Lova on a bench and compared our failures, and Lova said, with the frankness of youth, that I moved well but hesitated too long before attacking, and that the hesitation gave her time to read me. It was fair. I have always been a defensive fencer, and I thought about the way I approach problems at work, waiting until I have seen everything before committing. The parallel was awkward.

Ulla read the results at noon. She called each of us to the front in turn, held out a sheet and said a few words. To me she said that my footwork was sound, my knowledge of the rules was good and my bouts had been erratic, and that the score was sixty-four percent. It was a pass, with four percent to spare. I had done it. She shook my hand and added quietly that if I attacked one beat earlier I would be a very good fencer.

In the changing area afterwards, an older fencer named Torsten, who has competed since the seventies, sat beside me and unlaced his shoes. He told me that in his own grading, in 1978, the assessor made each candidate fence in a suit jacket to prove they could stay composed, and that he had passed with ripped trousers. He said the real test of a fencer is whether they come back the week after losing, and that in forty years he had lost more bouts than he could count and had kept coming. He took my foil, weighed it in his hand, and told me that mine was a fraction too light in the tip, which explained why I always felt slightly behind the blade.

Ulla's parting speech to all the candidates, gathered on the mats, was short. She said that a grading measures one afternoon and not a person, and that she had failed a future national champion when he was fifteen for sloppy footwork. Several of the younger candidates looked stricken, but she went on to say that he had come back a month later and passed with the highest score she had awarded that year.

The certificate is a small card with a stamp. I have pinned it above my desk, beside a photograph of the club. I called my partner from the car park and could not stop talking. It is a curious thing to be forty-one and thrilled by a piece of card, but I think that after years of work in which the results are invisible, there is a rare pleasure in a test that a person can pass or fail with their body. On Saturday I go back to the club, and I shall try, for once, to attack one beat earlier.

Cider pressing day at my father's orchard, and the six weeks after. My father, Anders, has an orchard of about forty trees behind his house in the hills near Kivik: old apple trees, mostly, some pears, a stubborn plum and a quince that he says has never produced a decent fruit. Each autumn, as long as I can remember, the family has gathered on a Saturday in October to pick, press and drink the first juice. This year I proposed to go further and turn some of it into cider, and he agreed on the condition that I did all the work.

The pressing day began with picking. My father, my sister Britta, her two children and I spent the morning with ladders, canvas bags and wide hampers fetched from the shed, shaking branches and gathering windfalls. Different trees give different fruit: the big green cooking apples are sharp and thin, the small red-streaked ones are sweet and sour, and an old russet has a nutty taste that my father claims is the best. We filled forty-two crates, and my father worked out with a pencil that this would yield about three hundred litres of juice.

The press is a beast that lives in the barn. It is a cast-iron and oak contraption on wheels that my grandfather bought secondhand in the fifties, with a hopper on top, a grinder below that crushes the apples into a pulp, and a big wooden screw that squeezes the pulp between slatted trays. The pulp is called the pomace, and it smells wonderful, sweet and winey, with a hint of autumn rot. My nephew Elis, who is nine, was put in charge of the handle and turned it with tremendous solemnity.

We ground the fruit in batches, wrapped the pomace in squares of cloth, stacked them between trays like a giant layer cake and cranked down the screw. The juice ran in a golden stream into a stainless tub, foaming and pale, and I tasted it from a ladle and nearly wept. It was cold and dry and sweet all at once, with a faint bitterness at the back that my father says comes from the russets. We drank a great deal of it, and by lunch everyone had a sticky face.

My father had set aside a share for cider. He believes in simplicity: no added sugar, no cultured yeast, just juice in clean containers left to ferment on the wild yeast that arrives on the apple skins. I was less convinced and had bought a packet of cider yeast and a hydrometer, a floating glass instrument that measures density. We compromised by dividing the juice into two batches. He would take one, using the old way, and I would take the other, using the yeast and the hydrometer, and we would compare in the spring.

My batch came to a hundred and ten litres, poured into two big fermentation buckets with airlocks, which are small plastic devices that let gas escape while keeping air out. The hydrometer reading was one point zero five zero, which by the chart in my book meant that the finished cider would be about six and a half percent alcohol. I stirred in the yeast, fitted the lids and carried the buckets to a cool corner of the cellar under the house, where the temperature is a steady eleven degrees.

For the first few days nothing seemed to happen, and I fretted. Then on the fourth evening the airlock began to blip, a slow tick every few seconds, and by the next morning it was bubbling like a small kettle. The cellar smelled of fresh dough and apples, and my father, sniffing at the trapdoor, said that this was the smell of the whole year turning into something new. I checked the temperature and the readings every day for a fortnight, in a notebook with columns and a rough graph that Britta mocked.

Racking came after three weeks. That means siphoning the cider off the sediment at the bottom, called the lees, into clean containers, to stop it developing off flavours. I used a length of plastic tube, sucked to start the flow and got a mouthful of cider in the process. The liquid was cloudy and yellow and tasted rough and yeasty, but under the roughness I could taste the shape of the apples. My father tried some, made a face and said that it was going to be all right.

A frosty morning in late November brought a visit from my father's neighbour, a man named Sixten who used to make perry from the pear trees along the lane. He sniffed at both batches and told me the yeast batch was too clean for his taste, and then, seeing my face, added that clean was not a criticism but merely a difference of religion. He said that the trick with cider is to leave it alone, and that most disasters he had seen were caused by a person who could not stop fiddling. I resolved to stop fiddling, and I lasted nine days.

Bottling was in early December. I had collected about a hundred and fifty beer bottles from friends and neighbours, each of which had to be washed, sterilised and rinsed. I added a small spoonful of sugar to each bottle to give a light sparkle, capped them with a hand capper that pinched my fingers twice and stacked them in crates in the cellar. The labels I designed at home in a dull evening, a small drawing of a tree with the words Kivik orchard and the year. Britta said they looked like a tin of soup.

We held the comparison tasting on a Sunday in March at my father's stove-side counter, or rather at the workbench beside the stove, with both batches in unlabelled glasses. Eight of us tried them. The old-fashioned batch was cloudy, tart and strange, with a slightly funky smell that half the guests loved and half politely avoided. Mine was cleaner, drier and more fizzy. The vote was five for mine and three for his, although two of the three said that his had more character. My father took this with a shrug and said that he was not competing with his son, only with the apple.

One thing I had not planned was what to do with the pomace, the pressed pulp left in the cloths. My father hates waste and has a whole system. Half goes to the neighbour's pigs, who arrive at a run when they hear the barn door. A quarter goes on the compost heap, and the rest he spreads under the plum tree, which he says keeps the wasps away in August. He has a theory, unproven, that the quince has never fruited because it resents being ignored, and he insisted that I tip a bucket of pomace round its roots. We will see next autumn.

For the record I wrote a page of lessons. Use only sound fruit, and discard anything with rot. Sterilise everything twice. Keep the cellar cool. Rack early and often. Record everything, because the numbers turn out to be the most useful part in the second year. And when my father offers advice while you are working, listen, since half of it will be wrong and the other half will save you a batch. He has already asked me to help him plan a larger press day next October, with twice the trees and a second barrel.

Amateur radio field day on the hill above Ostra Torp. I got my licence a little over a year ago, after a slow winter of studying for the exam in the evenings, and this was my first field day: a twenty-four-hour event, held every June, in which radio clubs set up temporary stations in the open air and try to contact as many other stations as possible, as far away as possible, using only battery and generator power. Our club, the Ostra Torp group, entered with nine members and a very old caravan.

We assembled at noon on Saturday on a grassy hilltop with a wide view over fields and a distant wind farm. The team leader was a retired telecoms engineer named Gunnar Peterson, who is seventy-three and calls everyone by their call sign. He handed out tasks as we arrived. Two of us were to erect the antennas, three to build the operating tent, one to run the generator and the rest, including me, to set up the transceivers and the logging computers inside the caravan.

The antennas were the heart of it. Gunnar had brought a long wire dipole for the lower bands, strung between two telescopic masts about eleven metres high, and a small beam antenna for the higher frequencies, mounted on a mast that had to be raised by four people with guy ropes. Raising the mast was the tricky moment. It rose slowly from the ground, wobbled and leaned, and Gunnar bellowed instructions in a voice that I imagine he used in his working days, until it stood upright. We staked the guy lines and stepped back.

The station was a pair of transceivers on a shelf, each connected to a laptop running logging software and to a small amplifier. The generator, a quiet inverter model, sat forty metres away under a tarpaulin to keep the noise down. We had a folding desk, three chairs and a kettle, and a thermos of soup for the night shift. At two, on the stroke of the start, Gunnar switched on the first radio and tuned up the band, and the speaker crackled with the whistles and warbles of a hundred stations calling at once.

Contacts are made in a simple pattern. You tune to a frequency, listen for a station calling, reply with your call sign and exchange a short message: your station name, your category and your signal report. Then you log it, move on and repeat. In the early afternoon I had my first go at the microphone, calling cq field day for what felt like ten minutes before a station in Poland answered. I read off the exchange in a wobbly voice, and the operator said that it was a good signal, and I nearly fell off the chair.

By six in the evening we had made two hundred and thirty contacts. Gunnar pinned a map on the caravan wall and coloured in each country we had reached with a felt pen: Germany, Poland, Finland, Italy, Spain, Croatia, Latvia, and a single very faint one from Iceland, which produced a small cheer. We ate sausages grilled over a camping stove and drank tea from tin mugs, and the sun set in orange streaks behind the wind farm, the turbine blades turning slowly like the hands of a slow clock.

The night shift began at midnight, and I was on with a young member called Sofie, who was seventeen and could tune a receiver faster than any of us. We took turns to call and log, and she taught me to listen for the tiny difference in tone that reveals a distant station under the noise. It was an odd pleasure, sitting in a dim caravan with a headset on, while the antenna hummed above us and the stars appeared through the door. At two in the morning we reached a station in Turkey and both of us clapped.

There were small pleasures in the middle of the night that I want to record. Sofie brought a flask of hot chocolate and shared it, and Gunnar, who had been sitting in the caravan doorway in a camp chair, told us how he had first been licensed in 1967 and made a contact with a fisherman on a trawler in the North Sea, using a radio he had built from a kit in his parents' shed. He still had the log, with the date and the name of the boat, and he said that he had tried in vain to find the boat since. It was the sort of story that grows in the dark, in a caravan, with the hum of the antenna above.

At some point we tried an experiment.
