Gunnar wanted to know whether a weak signal from a distant station could be dragged out of the noise using a slower kind of transmission, in which messages are sent as a series of tones that the computer decodes. We tried it with a station in Norway, exchanging a few short lines that appeared on the screen in a scrolling stream, character by character, an eerie echo of the telegraph. Sofie said that she felt like a ghost in a machine, and Gunnar added that this was a very good description of amateur radio.

Morning brought a thick mist that made the wind farm vanish and left the caravan floating on a white sea. We opened the door to the smell of wet grass and heard a cuckoo somewhere in the field. Gunnar ordered scrambled eggs on the camping stove, and we ate them from our knees while listening to a faint station somewhere in the Balkans repeating its call sign again and again, as patient as a lighthouse.

The low points were real. Around four the generator coughed and died, and it took twenty minutes with a torch to find that we had run out of fuel. The dew soaked the tent, and the tea, or rather the soup, went cold. A gust of wind brought down one end of the dipole, and Gunnar and I climbed a ladder in the dark to re-fasten it, watched from below by a sceptical rabbit. Yet none of this seemed to matter, since every station we contacted was another small victory over distance.

At two the next afternoon, the contest ended. Gunnar announced the final tally in the caravan: four hundred and eighty-six contacts in twenty-four hours, spread over thirty-one countries. It was a good total for a small club, he said, and better than the previous year by about eighty. We dismantled the antennas in an hour, wound up the cables, folded the tent and drove home in convoy. I have never been so tired and so pleased. On Monday morning I went to work with a sunburnt neck and a log full of call signs, and I found myself, on the bus, reciting phonetic words under my breath.

Afterwards we did a debrief over beer. The main lessons were logistical: bring more fuel, a second lamp, a sturdier mast, and a proper rota so that no one operates for more than three hours at a stretch. Gunnar proposed a mobile station for the autumn, and I offered to build a better logging sheet, since the software glitched twice and one contact was recorded with a date from the year before. He gave me a nod and said, in the flat voice of a man who has heard a hundred good ideas, that I might have found my role.

Model railway exhibition in the town hall, a Saturday with the layout club. My uncle Nils has belonged to the Kalmar model railway society for thirty years, and every autumn the society rents the main hall for a weekend to show off its layouts. This year he asked me to help with the display of his own, a small branch line called Bergsbo, which he has been building in the attic for eleven years and which had never been seen by the public. I said yes before asking what I was in for.

The layout is four metres long and one wide, set on a frame of plywood and pine, modelled in a scale where one millimetre on the track stands for eighty-seven of the real thing. It represents a country halt on a Swedish branch line in the early fifties, with a wooden station, a goods shed, a signal box, a small dairy, a level crossing and a mountain of coal. There are eighteen trees, made of twisted wire and painted sponge, and a river with a bridge that Nils built from balsa and matchsticks over a whole winter.

We carried it into the town hall on Friday evening in three sections, wrapped in blankets, and spent two hours joining them with bolts and connecting the wiring. Nils checked every join with a small brass gauge, a rail-to-rail measure that he says he takes to bed with him. When we finally switched on the power, the little locomotive on the siding jerked forward, went halfway round the loop and stopped dead. Nils muttered, took out a screwdriver, crawled under the frame with a torch and emerged four minutes later with a satisfied grunt.

Doors opened at ten on Saturday, and by half past there was a queue. The hall held twenty-eight layouts, from a huge American one with a mountain and a mining town to a tiny circular track in a suitcase. Ours stood in the corner beside a layout of a Swiss alpine railway with a real waterfall, an awkward neighbour, but Nils said that modesty was the essence of the branch line. He sat on a stool behind the layout in a railwayman's cap with a small controller in his hand, and greeted each visitor with a nod.

I was given a job, to manage the queue and answer questions. The most common were: how long did it take, is it real, and can my son press the button. The answer to the last was yes, but only once. Nils had installed a single button by the level crossing that set off a small bell and lowered a barrier, and children lined up to press it. One boy of about four pressed it twenty-one times in a row, until his mother gently removed him, and asked if he could come again on Sunday.

An older gentleman in a tweed jacket spent half an hour at the layout without saying anything and then remarked to Nils that the signal box was in the wrong place. Nils, who is normally the most peaceable of men, stiffened and asked for the evidence. The man produced a photograph from his wallet, an original, showing the real signal box at a real halt, on the opposite side of the track. They looked at it together for a long time. Nils said quietly that he had never seen that photograph, and that he would move the box in the winter.

By the end of the day we had counted over four hundred visitors, and a member of the society who was judging the exhibits awarded Bergsbo the prize for best small layout, a brass plaque that Nils accepted with a modest cough. He has hung it in the attic, next to the wall where the tools are kept. On the drive home he was silent for ten minutes and then said, without looking at me, that it had been worth every winter. I said I thought so too. Then he asked whether I would help him build the signal box again.

Archive diary, Saturday at the Hollin Green parish archive. The village history group has been promising for three years to scan the collection ahead of the damp gets it, and this month a small grant finally arrived, so eight of us turned up at the old vestry with two flatbed scanners on loan from the county library, a laptop, and a roll of grey archival tape. I volunteered because my great-uncle appears somewhere in the baptism registers and I wanted to see his line for myself.

Our lead is Mrs Okonkwo-Hayes, a retired records clerk who runs the vestry like a very polite naval operation. She began with a short talk on handling: clean dry hands, no pens anywhere near the volumes, pencil only, and never turn a brittle page by the corner. She showed us how to support a spine on foam wedges so the binding is never forced past a hundred and twenty degrees. Anyone who has watched a stitched signature come loose will understand why this matters.

The collection itself is modest and lovely. There are eleven baptism and burial registers running from 1723 to 1911, a churchwardens' account book that records the price of every candle, two bundles of tithe maps, and a box of school logbooks in which the head teacher of the 1890s complains about mud, measles and the vicar in roughly equal measure. Mrs Okonkwo-Hayes had already numbered every item with a soft pencil on the inside cover so that the scans could be named consistently, using the shelf order followed by a three-digit sequence.

I was put on the second scanner with a man called Tobias, who teaches woodwork at the comprehensive school and turned out to be extremely good at the cradle, a V-shaped book holder he adjusted with a spirit level. We settled into a rhythm: he turned, I checked focus and exposure on the laptop, and we swapped every forty minutes so that neither of us developed the scanner stare. The resolution was set to 400 dots per inch in colour, which produced files of about forty megabytes per double page. By lunch we had done the first register, 212 images, and a very long list of small discoveries.

The best was a marginal note in the 1798 burial register, where a curate wrote that the deceased miller had been carried to the churchyard through snow up to a man's knee, and that the bearers were given a jug of warm ale afterward at the parish's expense. Someone else found a pressed violet between two pages of the 1850s, brown and flat as paper. We photographed it in place and left it where it was.

Lunch was soup in the church hall, made by a woman named Fenella who brings a tureen to every working party and refuses to let anyone wash the ladle. Over the soup we argued about file formats. Mrs Okonkwo-Hayes wants uncompressed TIFF masters kept on two separate drives, one of which will live in the county record archive, and small JPEG copies for the website. Tobias worried about the cost of the drives; the grant covers two, at about ninety pounds each, and he proposed to build a wooden case for them that would keep the dust out.

The afternoon was harder. The tithe maps are folded into eighths and cannot be flattened on the scanner without cracking along the creases, so we photographed them on the floor of the vestry under a raised camera stand, in sections, with a scale bar and a grey card in each frame. A stitched image will come later, when someone with the right software has an evening free. It took nearly three hours to do four maps, and my neck hurt from bending, but the field names are wonderful: Long Dole, Cuckoo Pen, Hangman's Acre, and a small triangle of land simply labelled Nobody's.

At half past four we did the tidy-up, returned each volume to its acid-free box, and ticked the log sheet. The total for the day was 1,846 images from six items. Mrs Okonkwo-Hayes reckoned that at this pace the whole collection would take another five Saturdays, plus one for re-shooting anything blurred. She asked each of us to take home a small task: mine is to type up the index pages of the churchwardens' book, which have never been searchable, into a spreadsheet, so that a visitor could look up a surname without turning every leaf.

On the way home I stopped at the cemetery gate and looked for my great-uncle's family plot. I did not find it, but the sexton's hut had a hand-drawn plan pinned inside, and I copied the row numbers down. Next Saturday I will bring my own gloves; the cotton ones from the box had a hole in the thumb, and I want to keep my hands the way Mrs Okonkwo-Hayes taught us.

Beekeeping season log, kept from the first inspection in April to the last feed in October. I took over two hives from my neighbour Cornelius when his knees gave up on the stairs to the orchard terrace, and he insisted on teaching me for a full season until he would let me touch anything unsupervised. This is my record of the year, mostly written in the shed on wet evenings with the smoker still smelling of pine needles.

April. The first proper inspection was on the ninth, a mild still morning with bumblebees on the willow catkins. Cornelius handed me the hive tool and said only, keep your hands slow. Hive one, the older colony, had a full brood nest on six frames and a queen with a blue dot on her thorax, marked two seasons ago. Hive two had come through the winter thinner, with about half the stores gone and a scattering of dead bees on the floorboard, but a cluster was alive on the sunny side and there was a patch of eggs, so we left it alone and fed it a light syrup, one part sugar to one of warm water, in a rapid feeder.

May. The willow gave way to dandelions and then to a great rush of blossom from the cherry orchard belonging to the Lindqvist family, who keep the field behind the terrace. By the middle of the month hive one had built up so much that Cornelius warned me swarming was near. We looked for queen cells along the bottom bars of the frames and found four, capped. The standard answer is to split the colony, so on the twentieth we moved the old queen and three frames of brood into a small box, a nucleus, with a frame of stores, and left the queen cells to raise a new one in the original hive. The nucleus went to a corner of the terrace, three metres away, with the entrance turned in the opposite direction so that foragers would not mix.

June. Two things went wrong and one went right. The wrong ones: a heavy rain kept the bees indoors for eight days in a row, and the nucleus, cramped in its box, almost robbed itself out from hunger until I fed it again. Also, I dropped a frame on a hive stand and squashed perhaps thirty bees, which I still think about. The right thing: the new queen in hive one emerged, mated, and was laying by the twenty-sixth, a pale gold creature whom I could not find for ten minutes and then saw walking calmly across a frame of capped brood as if she owned the place.

July. The main honey flow came from lime trees along the lane to the school, and the smell of the hives changed to something almost minty. I added a super, a shallow box with ten frames of foundation, to each hive. Cornelius taught me the rule for whether honey is ready: hold the frame sharply and shake it over the hive, and if no nectar sprays out, the cells are ripe and capped. We took a first small harvest on the nineteenth, four frames, which produced eleven jars of pale summer honey. I labelled them by hand with a date and the word terrace.

August. The wasps arrived. I reduced the entrances with a strip of wood so that the bees would have less to guard, and hung two wasp traps on a fence post well away from the hives. Hive two, the weak one, recovered so well that it needed a super of its own. In the third week I ran the standard test for varroa mites by sprinkling powdered sugar on a cup of bees, rolling them gently and counting the mites that fell through a mesh. Hive one had four mites in a cup of about three hundred bees, hive two had eleven. The second is above the level where treatment is recommended, so Cornelius brought a strip treatment that I laid across the brood frames according to the label.

September. The second harvest came from heather that a friend of Cornelius moved his own hives to on the moor, and we were given three frames of dark, thick heather honey that does not run from a spoon. It needs pressing rather than spinning, so we squashed the comb in a muslin bag over a bucket. The whole business was sticky and glorious, and the wasps came in through the shed door as if invited. The season's total was thirty-eight jars, of which I have given away twenty-two.

October. Last feed on the fourth, a thick two-to-one syrup. I put mouse guards over the entrances, strapped the roofs with a ratchet strap because of the winter gales, and thanked both colonies out loud, which Cornelius said was perfectly normal. He will come by every fortnight to hold a hand to the hive side and listen for the hum. I have ordered a book on bee diseases, and next spring I want to add a third colony, if my wife allows it and if the split from hive one survives the winter.

Regatta write-up: the studio crew at the Kingsmere Autumn Regatta. When the rowing club at Kingsmere invited local firms to enter a fun eight in their charity race, Blake said yes until anyone had checked who could actually row. The invitation was for a Saturday in the second week of October, a 1,000-metre sprint on the river reach below the boathouse, with a barbecue afterwards to raise money for the club's junior scheme. This is a record of how we got from a crowd of enthusiastic amateurs to a boat that finished the course upright.

Recruitment took a week. Of the volunteers, exactly one, Sami, had ever held an oar, in a school pond at fourteen. Avery agreed to cox because she is the lightest and has the loudest voice. Blake took stroke, Meera bow, and the middle seats went to Yusuf, Colm, Deepa, Ilse from finance, Wenzel from the backend team, and Marguerite, who joked that the only muscle she used was the one in her jaw. We had nine people and a sunny outlook.

The club proposed two training sessions on the Tuesday and Thursday evenings ahead of the race, at half past six, with a coach called Ottoline Barr. She is a former national squad rower in her fifties, gentle but ruthless about timing. The first session took place entirely on land, in the boathouse, on rowing machines, where she set each of us to hold a steady twenty-four strokes a minute and told us that the most important thing in an eight is not power but being early on nothing and late on nothing. Half of us spent the hour making the sound of a dying seal.

On the water on Thursday we were put in the club's old training boat, a heavy wide eight named Marigold, with a crack in the bow that had been repaired with fibreglass. Ottoline rode alongside in a launch with a loudhailer. The catch was our greatest problem: some people stabbed the blade in too early, others dragged it out of the water in a way that made the boat lurch. The word she used again and again was square, meaning that the blade must be turned flat prior to entry. After forty minutes we managed ten strokes in a row without anyone crabbing, which is to say catching the water wrongly and having the handle punch them in the ribs.

The morning of the race was cold, with mist lying on the river. We arrived at nine for a briefing. The rules were simple: a single heat, six boats, and a rowing club representative in each launch to police lane discipline. Ours, drawn as lane four, was a novice eight from the estate agents on Bridge Street, a pair of dentists and their friends, three mixed crews from a supermarket, a council team and, alarmingly, a team of sixth-formers who all seemed to be over six feet tall.

At the start we were held by a man kneeling on the pontoon. Avery, sitting facing the stroke seat, had a small microphone taped to her collar and a cox box that made her voice crackle. When the flag dropped, Blake set a rate of thirty, higher than we had ever attempted, and for twenty strokes the boat felt astonishing, as though it were flying. Then Yusuf caught a crab at the 400-metre mark, the boat lurched, and we lost two lengths. Avery shouted, sit up, breathe, and by some miracle the boat settled and we recovered to third. At the finish the sixth-formers were first, the dentists second, and we were three seconds behind them.

Afterwards, we carried Marigold back up to the boathouse on our shoulders, which took ten minutes and was much harder than the race. Ottoline gave each of us a small tin cup with the club crest, and the barbecue produced very good sausages. The regatta raised 2,340 pounds in total for the junior scheme, of which our team's sponsorship pledges came to 610. Blake handed over the cheque, and the club chairman, a large gentle man in a blazer, made a short speech that mentioned our seal noises with what I chose to interpret as affection.

The barbecue deserves its own paragraph. It was run by the club's veterans, who stood in a row behind a long trestle in aprons that read Old Boys' Eight, 1974. One of them, a man named Torvald who is now eighty-one, told us that in his day the club owned a single boat and that the whole membership walked it to the river on their shoulders every Saturday. He asked Sami what he did for a living and, on hearing the answer, said that in his day a computer was a woman with a pencil, which was met with the approval of everyone in earshot. Blake spent twenty minutes with him examining a framed photograph of the 1974 crew, all with moustaches, taken after they won a cup at Henley-on-Thames.

The post-mortem in the car park was more useful than the coaching. Wenzel, who had said almost nothing all morning, pointed out that in the last 300 metres everyone had stopped looking at the back of the person in front and started looking at the river, which is why the blades lost their rhythm. Deepa said she had counted, and that by the end the crew was only rowing at nineteen strokes a minute, not thirty. Ottoline heard this and nodded gravely. She added that most novice crews start too fast and finish too slowly, and that a rate of twenty-six held for the whole course beats a sprint of thirty that collapses. It was the only technical advice she gave all week that I could repeat without a diagram.

There was also a small administrative matter. The regatta committee asked each entrant to submit a crew list with dates of birth for insurance, and Marguerite, who was in charge of paperwork, discovered on the Friday that one of us, whom I shall not name, had listed a birth year that made him three years older than he claimed. The committee did not mind. The entry fee was 180 pounds per boat, paid from the team events budget, and the club supplied waterproof jackets in a rather loud shade of orange that Colm now uses for cycling.

The follow-up. Ilse discovered that she had a blister the size of a coin and had no complaint about it whatsoever. Sami has, since then, joined the club as a social member and has been out in a single scull twice, once ending in the water. Colm proposed that the studio enter next year with a plan, meaning practice sessions from August, and I made a note to ask the studio to bring a first-aid kit for the next outing. We took a team photograph on the pontoon, all of us in damp fleeces, and Blake has pinned it above the printer.

What I would change. First, we should not enter a boat in a race without a full session together on the water beforehand, and one Thursday is not enough. Second, the person calling the stroke rate must be told it in advance; Blake's sudden thirty was heroic but foolish. Third, nobody should agree to be the cox unless they are certain they do not mind being shouted at by the other boats' supporters. Avery says she minded very much, and would do it again.

Piano tuning saga, or the upright in the hall. My grandmother left me her piano, a dark walnut upright made in Leipzig in the 1930s, and for eleven years it stood in my parents' hallway collecting family photographs and slightly out of tune. When we finally moved it to our flat in April it took four men and a hired trolley, and on the first evening every note I played sounded to me like a wet finger on a glass.

I called a tuner recommended by the music shop on Storgatan. His name was Mr Adeyemi-Lund, a slow, spectacled man of about seventy who arrived with a leather roll of tools, a fork, and a small torch. He lifted the lid, played a single note, and sighed audibly. The piano had dropped a good deal below concert pitch, he said, and a tuning that far adrift has to be done in two stages, because pulling the strings up all at once would put dangerous stress on the frame and likely snap a few.

His first visit lasted three hours. He began with what he called a pitch raise, quickly bringing every string up roughly a semitone toward A at 440 hertz and letting the piano settle, then tuning it properly a fortnight later. During those two weeks it drifted sharply, as he had promised it would, and I heard the bass strings groan when the heating came on. He had also removed the front panel and shown me the action, the row of felted hammers, and pointed out that six of them were worn to a flat shape with grooves cut by the strings. Those would need reshaping, which he did with a sanding tool the size of a nail file.

The second visit revealed the actual troubles. Three keys, in the middle octave, stuck when pressed softly. The cause turned out to be humidity: the wooden key bushings had swollen in the damp of our north-facing living space. He eased them with a thin blade and a pinch of powdered graphite, and warned me not to leave the piano against an outside wall or above a radiator. I had done both. We dragged it a hand's width from the wall, put a small hygrometer on top, and I now keep it between forty and fifty per cent, which sounds fussy but is easily done with a bowl of water in winter.

There was also the matter of a buzz on the top F sharp that neither of us could locate for twenty minutes. He tried every trick, pressing the soundboard, tapping the frame, and eventually found a lost coin, a tiny silver five-krona piece, lying in the bottom of the case where it had presumably fallen decades ago. It was black with age. He gave it to me, and it now sits in a saucer on the shelf, and I like to think it was my grandmother's.

The bill, all told, was 1,450 kronor for two tunings, plus a modest fee for regulating the action. Mr Adeyemi-Lund advised me to have it tuned twice in the first year, then annually, ideally in the same month each time, since pianos like habit. Since then I have played it most evenings, mainly the small pieces I learned as a child, and Noor has started to pick out a tune with one finger.

What I learned. A piano is not a fixed object but a living tension of about eighteen tonnes spread across a cast-iron frame, and it wants gentle handling. I also learned that the sound of a properly tuned upright is much warmer than I remembered, and that my grandmother had left a small treasure in the case. Next month I will ask about replacing the hammers on the top octave, though he says there is no hurry.

Volunteer day report: the tram museum restoration, Blake's account. The studio agreed at the spring planning session to give every employee two paid volunteering days a year, and eleven of us chose to spend one together at the Ashgrove Tram Museum, a former depot that a trust of pensioners and enthusiasts has run for thirty years. They were restoring a green and cream double-decker from 1927, car number twenty-nine, which had lain in a field as a chicken shed for half a century ahead of the trust rescued it.

We arrived at half past eight to a tea urn and a health and safety talk by the trust's chairman, Mr Pettigrew, a lean man in a blue boiler suit. He explained that the depot floor has three inspection pits, none of which we were to enter without a supervisor, and that the tram itself was on jacks and not to be touched where the yellow tape was. Then he split us into teams. I was in the woodwork crew with Sami and Deepa; Avery, Meera and Colm went to the electrical bench; Yusuf and Ilse joined the painting team; and the rest were sent to the archive, where the trust keeps five thousand photographs.

The woodwork task was replacing a lower panel on the staircase. Trams of that era had platforms at each end and a curling stair to the upper deck, and the wood, teak and ash, had suffered from a century of damp. Our supervisor, Gwendolyn, a retired joiner with the biggest hands I have seen, showed us how to trace the shape of a broken panel on to a sheet of paper, transfer it on to a new blank, and shape it with a spokeshave. She let us do the fine work ourselves, but held our wrists when we cut too deep. I made one panel in three hours, and it fitted on the second attempt.

Meanwhile, on the electrical bench, Avery and Meera were rewiring a set of reproduction lamps. The originals, of course, had been lost, and the trust has been making copies from photographs. The wiring was all in cloth-covered cable, which they cut, stripped and crimped under the eye of a retired signal engineer called Harold. Colm reported that he had never enjoyed a screwdriver as much.

The paint team did a surprising job with a very small area. The livery of car twenty-nine required fourteen layers, according to the trust's paint chart: primer, undercoat, three colour coats, lining in gold leaf, and then transfer numerals and varnish. Yusuf spent the morning masking a two-inch strip along the waist panel with tape so that the cream could meet the green in a perfectly straight line, and he was told he had a future.

Lunch was sandwiches on the platform, where the trust runs a short loop of track about two hundred metres long. We were allowed a ride in one of the working cars, an open-topped tram from Blackpool with wooden slatted seats. It rattled and swayed, and the bell was operated by a foot pedal that Blake, meaning me, was invited to press at the end of the line. I pressed it like a child.

In the afternoon, the archivists taught the archive group how to scan and caption old glass negatives without touching the emulsion. Ilse discovered a portrait of a conductress from 1943, standing on the platform of a tram in a tight-fitting uniform and a peaked cap. A note in ink said her name was Doreen, and the trust is still looking for her family.

At four o'clock the trust presented us with a certificate and an invitation to return in June for the reopening of the upper deck. We had contributed eighty-two hours in total, and Mr Pettigrew calculated that the panel work alone had saved the trust about three weeks. He also asked whether the studio could make a small website for them, and after some discussion Avery and I agreed to do it as a further favour, on the condition that it be simple, mobile-friendly and kept updated by the trust's own volunteers. Meera has volunteered to write the first draft of the copy.

A word on the depot itself. It stands on the site of the old horse-tram yard, and the brick walls still carry iron rings where the animals were tethered. The trust owns four complete cars and the remains of six more, stored under tarpaulins at the back, and pays for everything from a shop that sells postcards, tea towels and a very good enamel badge. Mr Pettigrew told us the annual running cost is about thirty-one thousand pounds, of which the shop covers a third.

Loose ends. The trust needs a sponsor for the gold-leaf lining, which costs about 900 pounds, and Blake will raise it at the next finance meeting. The new panels will also need staining, and Gwendolyn has kindly proposed to show us how to match the old wood on a Saturday in May. I went home smelling of linseed oil and with a splinter in my thumb, and the children at my door asked whether I had been building a boat.

Glacier hike write-up, the day on the ice above Fjaerland. It had been on my list for a decade, since a colleague showed me a photograph of a blue ice cave, and this July, with Mira's blessing and a cheap flight to Bergen, I finally booked a guided walk on an arm of the Jostedal glacier. This is my account of the day, written on the ferry back with sunburned ears.

The preparation was more involved than I expected. The tour company sent a kit list of eleven items, including stiff-soled boots, waterproof trousers, a warm hat even in summer, and sunglasses with side shields, since glare on the ice can burn the eyes. I borrowed crampons from a friend of a friend, which turned out to be unnecessary because the company supplies them, and I bought a pair of liner gloves that I did not use. I also did four training walks on the hills north of town, each about ten kilometres, in the same boots, to avoid blisters on the day.

We met at eight in the morning at a car park near the glacier museum. Our guide was a woman in her thirties called Solveig Rasmussen, who had been leading groups on the glacier for eleven summers and had a dry humour that put everyone at ease. The group was nine people: an elderly Dutch couple, a family with two teenagers from Manchester, two nurses from Glasgow, a solitary Japanese engineer, and me. Solveig checked our boots, gave us harnesses and helmets, and made us practise walking in crampons in the car park like ducks.

The approach was a forty-minute walk along a glacial river, past a lake the colour of milky turquoise. The silt in the water, she told us, is rock flour, ground fine by the moving ice, and it reflects only the blue-green part of the light. We crossed a moraine ridge made of boulders the size of cars, then a slope of loose scree, and at last stood at the foot of the ice. It rose in a great blue-white curve and was quite a bit dirtier than in the photographs, streaked with black at the edges where the rocks fall in.

Putting on crampons was the moment the trip became real. Solveig taught us the walk: feet wide apart, knees slightly bent, a stamp with each step so that the spikes bite, and never to cross one foot in front of the other because it catches the points. She also told us how to use the ice axe as a walking stick with the pick facing backwards, and what to do if someone falls, which is to shout, drop flat, and dig in the axe. We roped up in groups of four, with me between the Dutchman and a nurse.

The first hour was a steep climb of a hundred and fifty metres, over ridges of blue ice polished by melt. Water ran in tiny channels and disappeared down holes called moulins with a deep glugging sound. We passed a crevasse, narrow at the top and darkening into black blue below, and Solveig had us lie on our stomachs to peer in. The cold that rose out of it was a pure clean chill, and there was a drip echoing a very long way down.

At noon we stopped on a flat shelf for lunch. I had brought a pack of dark rye sandwiches and a bar of chocolate, which Solveig said was the correct food for altitude. She also passed round a flask of hot blackcurrant juice and pointed to a distant ridge where, in 1750, according to a church record, the glacier had reached the valley floor and overrun two farms. Since then it has retreated about three kilometres, and the marker stones the local authority has placed show the steps of the retreat, one every decade or so.

The highlight was the ice cave, a cavity sculpted by meltwater under a thick overhang. We ducked through a low entrance, one at a time, into a chamber about five metres high, and the light changed to a deep sapphire. The walls were rippled like the inside of a shell. Nobody spoke. The elder Dutchman put his glove to the wall, and the teenagers, who had been sullen all morning, forgot to take photographs.

Before the descent Solveig gathered us on the shelf and gave a short talk about the glacier's health that I found more sobering than anything else. Every year the tour company measures the position of a red-painted stake, hammered into the ice near the flat shelf. In 2009, she said, the stake had been placed at the edge of a wide white plateau; today the same spot stands twenty-eight metres lower, and the edge of the ice has crept back so far that the company has had to move the whole approach path twice. She was not gloomy about it. She said the glacier had been shrinking for a century and that guiding was a way of being honest about what is happening while there is still something to show.

The Dutch couple, Joost and Marieke, then told us that they had walked on this same glacier in 1986 on their honeymoon, and that they remembered the ice reaching almost to the road. Marieke had brought an old photograph in a plastic sleeve, and Solveig held it up beside the view so that we could compare the two. The difference was so large that the teenagers, who had said nothing all day, asked to hold it. It is a small thing, but I will remember the way the boy from Manchester turned the photograph over to read the date on the back.

Practicalities I would pass on to anyone else: the tour cost 118 pounds for the day, food not included, and the company will not take anyone under the age of ten. The crampons pinch on the ankle bone if the boots are laced too loosely, and a pair of thin liner socks under wool ones prevented any blister. I also learned to keep my sunglasses on a cord, because Kenji dropped his and it slid a long way down a smooth slope until Solveig retrieved it with the axe.

The descent was harder on the knees than the climb. We reached the car park at half past four and returned the crampons. On the ferry, the Japanese engineer, who turned out to be called Kenji, showed me his photographs and proposed to send them, and I gave him my address. At the museum by the car park I bought a postcard for Mira and a small jar of glacier mint sweets, and stood for a while in front of the exhibition on how the ice moves, a huge slow conveyor that flows about a metre a day in the middle and much less at the edges. My legs ached for two days, and my face peeled, but I would go again. Next time I would pick a cooler day, bring a stronger sunscreen, and stay a night in the village to see the ice at sunset.

Chess club tournament diary, the Ridgeway Rapid, Sunday. I joined the Thursday club in Ridgeway in January, mostly to get away from screens, and by June I was asked to play in the annual rapid tournament, a one-day event with six rounds of twenty minutes each per player. My rating is a modest 1,340, according to the club's list, so I entered the lower section, for players under 1,600.

The event took place at the community hall, which had been set up the previous evening by the arbiter, a former maths teacher named Mr Kowalczyk. There were thirty-six players in my section, two to a board, with digital clocks that beep at the last ten seconds. The hall smelt of floor polish and stewed tea. I brought a flask, a banana, and my late father's leather wallet, which I keep in my pocket in tournaments for no logical reason.

Round one I was paired with a boy of about eleven called Felix, who played the Sicilian defence with astonishing confidence and nearly beat me on time. He was a pawn up in the endgame, but he used his clock so carelessly that I got a draw by repetition with eleven seconds left. His mother, who was sitting behind him, looked more shaken than either of us.

In round two I had white against an older man, dressed in a sports jacket, who played very slowly and hummed. I opened with the Queen's Gambit, a system I know well, and he responded in a way that was unfamiliar. After the twelfth move he sank into thought for six of his twenty minutes. I calmly used that time to plan a knight manoeuvre and won a piece around move twenty. He resigned and shook my hand for a long time, still humming.

Round three was a disaster. I was black against a woman named Priyanka who had a rating of 1,580, and she played fast, sharp chess with a bishop pair that cut through my position. I blundered a rook to a simple fork on move nineteen and resigned immediately. In the break, I ate the banana and read the pairings, and decided I would put the loss behind me.

Rounds four and five went better. In round four I won a long endgame, a rook and four pawns against a rook and three, through patient technique I had practised on the Thursday evenings. In round five I drew with the tournament's second seed, who proposed a draw on move thirty with a slightly better position because he had a train to catch.

Going into the last round I had three and a half points out of five, which put me in the top ten. My opponent was Felix's older brother, aged fourteen, who had the same nose and the same aggressive style. He sacrificed a pawn for the attack, which I accepted, and then he sacrificed a piece, which I declined. By move thirty I had the better endgame, and I won a rook ending with twenty-two seconds to spare. The final score was four and a half out of six.

I finished seventh, and the prize for the top six was a small trophy, so I missed by half a point. Mr Kowalczyk shook my hand and said that a seventh is the most dignified place because it is the position of someone who will be back. The winner was Priyanka, with five and a half. The club's chairman announced that the raffle had raised 118 pounds for the junior chess fund.

Lessons. First, my clock management needs work, and I should practise playing on increment in the evenings. Second, I need to study the Sicilian, because it appears in every second game. Third, I should not eat a banana at half time, as it made me sleepy. On the drive home I replayed the game against Priyanka three times in my head. I have written the moves in a notebook and shall show them to Mr Kowalczyk on Thursday.

Science fair jury notes, the Northfield district school fair. Ilse in finance knows the head of science at Northfield Junior School, and when the fair asked for three outside judges, she volunteered Meera, Deepa and me. It was a Wednesday afternoon in February, and we were released from the studio at half past twelve, which Blake described as the best use of billable time this quarter.

The fair was held in the gymnasium, where forty-one projects stood on folding boards along the walls. We were given a clipboard each with a one-page scoring sheet: questions asked, method, results, presentation, and a final box marked curiosity. The head of science, Mr Adisa, told us that the children were aged nine to twelve, that each project was worth a maximum of twenty points, and that the winners would go to the regional final in March. His only request was that we be kind. Most of the exhibitors were already close to tears from nerves.

My first stop was a boy named Ravi, who tested which brand of paper towel absorbed most water. He had tried five brands, measured the water in a beaker from start to finish, and repeated the test three times, which impressed me more than the results. I asked what he would change if he did it again, and he said, use a syringe instead of pouring, because his hand shook. It is the kind of answer that ought to earn extra marks.

Two girls in matching lab coats had a project on the temperature at which chocolate melts, and it involved a hairdryer, a ruler and a very sticky bench. Another child had built a small hydraulic arm from syringes and cardboard and could lift a tennis ball, and a sombre boy in a tie explained the growth of cress under different colours of light, with photographs of every day for a fortnight.

Meera and I disagreed on one project, a wobbly working model of a volcano, because it copied a design from the internet. Deepa pointed out that the child, a shy girl named Tuva, had modified the recipe and could explain each step with total clarity. We gave it fourteen points.

The best project by a distance was by a girl of twelve called Amara, who asked whether plant growth was affected by music. She had grown bean seedlings in three boxes, one with classical music, one with heavy rock, and one with silence, and measured them every two days for three weeks. Her result was that all three grew at about the same rate, which she reported honestly and with a slight air of disappointment. She noted that her boxes stood at different distances from the radiator, which she thought might have confused things. I gave her nineteen out of twenty and a note that the honest report is the mark of a scientist.

After an hour of walking, the three of us met in the staff area, where a tray of orange squash and oat biscuits awaited. We compared our sheets, averaged the scores, and settled on winners in three age bands. Amara won the older group, and Ravi's absorbent towels won the younger. A boy whose project on paper aeroplanes flew across the gym and struck the principal was given a special prize for enthusiasm.

At the end Mr Adisa asked whether the studio might run a workshop on spreadsheets and graphs for the older pupils. Deepa agreed to run one in April, with sample data on the rainfall in Northfield. We went home slightly dazed and happy, and Meera has since proposed that the studio make the judging an annual habit.

Stargazing weekend diary, two nights at the dark-sky camp above Tarn Moor. I had wanted to see the Milky Way properly since a school trip to a planetarium, and Mira gave me a place on a weekend course run by the Pennine Astronomical Society for my birthday. It took place in the last week of September, when the nights are long and the moon was a thin crescent that set by ten. This is my record, written by red torchlight in the back of the car and tidied up at home.

Friday. We were asked to arrive by four to pitch tents on a sloping field beside a stone barn that serves as the society's observatory and meeting place. The course leader was a retired optician named Lawrence Ferreira, tall, quiet and inclined to speak of galaxies as if they were relatives. There were fourteen of us, including a father and his ten-year-old daughter, two sisters from Leeds who had never touched a telescope, and a taciturn man in a waxed jacket who turned out to have built his own mirror. Lawrence gave everyone a red cellophane sleeve for a torch and forbade white light after sunset with the seriousness of a lifeguard.

Before dark he taught us to find our way around by eye. The Plough is the hook, he said, and from its pointers you jump to Polaris, which is not the brightest star but is the one that does not move. From there we learned the W of Cassiopeia, the great square of Pegasus rising in the east, and how a hand held at arm's length covers about ten degrees of sky. He drilled us until we could point to any of a dozen objects without looking at the chart. I was pleased to be quicker than the sisters, and less pleased to be slower than the ten-year-old, whose name was Isla.

Dusk arrived slowly and then all at once. By nine the sky over the moor was black and crowded, and I stopped talking. The Milky Way was not a smear as in photographs but a structured river with dark lanes running through it, and when I looked at the Summer Triangle I could see the faint rift that splits the band toward Cygnus. Lawrence said that a site like this is rated about two on the Bortle scale, where a city centre is nine, and that most of the people in Britain have never seen a truly dark sky.

Then the telescopes. The society had six on the field, from a small refractor on a wobbly tripod to a huge Dobsonian with a mirror thirty centimetres across, standing on a plywood rocker like a cannon. We queued at the big one for Jupiter, and I had my first proper view: a small creamy disc crossed by two dark belts, with four tiny bright points of light in a line on one side. Lawrence said these were the moons Galileo had seen in 1610, and that if I came back the next night they would have moved. I did, and they had.

The Andromeda galaxy is a faint grey smudge to the eye and only a slightly bigger smudge in a telescope, but Lawrence explained that the light I was seeing left it two and a half million years ago, prior to our species existed. The taciturn man, who I now learned was called Bernard, showed me the mirror he had ground over two winters in his shed, a disc of glass with a curve so slight that he could only detect it with a knife-edge test. I asked how long the polish had taken and he said, four hundred hours, and did not smile.

Saturday brought a clear day and a talk in the barn on astrophotography. Lawrence showed how to take a long exposure with an ordinary camera on a tracking mount, and why the images from a fixed tripod streak into trails after about twenty seconds. He also demonstrated stacking, in which dozens of short frames are combined so that the noise averages out. In the afternoon we made pinhole projectors from cardboard tubes and looked at a few sunspots, which were visible as two tiny dots on a white disc.

On Saturday night the sky was even better. We went out at half past nine, dressed in every layer we owned, and lay on groundsheets with our heads propped on rolled fleeces. Around eleven a meteor, a long slow one, crossed almost the whole width of the sky, and the ten-year-old shouted a word I will not repeat. A little later Lawrence found the double cluster in Perseus in binoculars, two knots of jewels side by side, and I could not stop looking. It was minus one on the field, and my breath made the eyepiece fog, so I learned to hold the tube out to the side and breathe the other way.

One more thing from Saturday deserves a place here. After the talk Bernard, the mirror maker, took four of us out to the back of the barn and let us look through his home-built telescope at a globular cluster in Hercules, a ball of several hundred thousand stars that appeared as a small fuzzy snowball with a sparkling edge. He explained that the cluster is about twenty-five thousand light years away and that its stars are among the oldest in the galaxy, some of them nearly twelve billion years old. He said all this in the flat tone of a man reading out a bus route, and it was the most moving thing I heard all weekend.

There was a practical lesson too, which I record for next time. Cold saps batteries, so the spare set for my red torch should live in an inside pocket, and a hot water bottle wrapped in a scarf is worth more than a second jumper. Dew forms on lenses within an hour, and the society's telescopes each wore a small heated strap, powered by a car battery, that stopped the glass misting up. The sisters from Leeds made do with a hair dryer on a long cable, which Lawrence pretended not to see. I also learned to let my eyes adapt for twenty minutes prior to expecting to see faint things, and that even a glance at a phone screen resets the clock.

On the Sunday morning we packed up in a low bright mist. Lawrence gave each of us a printed sheet listing the twelve easiest deep-sky objects for the autumn, with a small box to tick beside each one, and I have so far ticked seven. He told the group that the commonest mistake of beginners is to buy a huge telescope until they have learned the sky, and the second commonest is to give up after the first cloudy month. I will remember both.

We finished at one in the morning with cocoa from a flask, and I lay awake in the tent listening to sheep. On Sunday morning the society's chairman drew a prize from a bucket, and a book about the moons of Saturn went to Isla. I drove home with the car heater on, thinking that I would buy a pair of binoculars, a seven-by-fifty, which Lawrence said is the best first instrument. I have already ordered a red torch and a planisphere, and I have put a note in my calendar to book the November session for the Leonid meteors, which he says will peak in the early hours of the eighteenth.

Team outing report: the open day at Skerry Head lighthouse. Avery arranged this one after seeing a poster at the harbour, and eight of us from the studio, plus two partners and a dog, spent a Saturday in August on the headland forty minutes from the studio by minibus. The lighthouse is opened to the public on two days a year by the local heritage trust, and the trust's volunteers had promised the full experience, including the lamp chamber and the fog signal.

We arrived at ten to be met by a keeper's daughter, now in her sixties, called Agnes Thorsen, who grew up in the cottages at the foot of the tower. She led us in through a green door in a whitewashed wall and told us the tower is thirty-four metres tall, was lit in 1868, and has 147 steps, which she said she knew exactly because she counted them every night as a child on her way to bed. The dog stayed below with a volunteer who gave him a bowl of water and a great deal of attention.

The stair is a spiral of iron and stone, with a small landing every twenty steps, and the walls are painted a glossy cream that shows every fingerprint. Meera, who is afraid of heights, climbed the entire flight with her eyes on Sami's boots. On the fourth landing there was a tiny museum in what had been the oil store, with a brass barometer, a keeper's log open at a page for a stormy night in 1902, and a row of glass lamp chimneys in a wooden rack. Agnes read out the entry: gale from the north-east, seas breaking over the gallery, all lamps burning, two vessels seen in distress and lifeboat called.

The lamp chamber at the top was smaller than I expected, and full of light. The original Fresnel lens, a beehive of glass prisms taller than a person, still stands in the centre, though it was replaced in 1985 by a modern beacon on the roof of the outbuilding. The trust polishes the lens once a month with soft cloths, and a volunteer, a plumber called Winston, explained that the prisms bend the light of a single lamp into one strong beam, so that a flame of only a few hundred candlepower could be seen for twenty miles. He let us turn the lens by hand on its mercury bath, which is now filled with oil, and it swung round as if it weighed nothing.

Out on the gallery the wind was so strong that Colm's cap went over the rail and was retrieved later by a boy on the rocks below. The view was tremendous: a long grey sea, a ferry the size of a toy, a line of white where the current meets the reef, and, to the south, the low smudge of the mainland. Agnes told us that the reef, called the Widow's Teeth, has claimed at least eleven ships since records began, and that the last keeper left in 1991 when the light was automated.

Down at the foot we were taken to the fog signal house, where a compressed-air horn the size of a small barrel is kept in working order. At noon the trust sounds it once for visitors. We were warned to cover our ears and everybody did, and still the note came up through the soles of our feet, a low, sorrowful bellow that made the gulls lift off the roof in a body. Ilse said it sounded like a cow with a grievance.

Lunch was a picnic on the rocks behind the cottages, and the trust's tea stall sold slabs of fruit cake for a pound. In the afternoon we joined a short talk on how the trust raises money, mostly from open days and a small shop selling tea towels and postcards, and how a new roof for the oil store needs 14,000 pounds. Avery suggested that the studio contribute the price of a day's lunch budget, and we agreed to pledge 400.

The dog, meanwhile, had made friends with everyone and had been fed three biscuits. On the minibus home, Yusuf wrote a small poem about the horn, and Colm, whose cap had been lost, found it in the lost property box, having been returned by the boy. It was the best team day I remember.

Pottery diary, the kiln firing at the Alderbank studio. For eight months I have been going to a Tuesday evening class at Alderbank, a converted mill where a potter named Greta Nakamura teaches twelve of us the basics of throwing and glazing. This week, for the first time, our pieces were to be fired together in the big gas kiln, and Greta asked the group to help load and watch it. I have kept notes because I want to remember how it feels to open a kiln after two days of waiting.

Some background. My own work is mostly bowls, with three mugs, a small jug, and one plate that has a permanent tilt. I threw everything on the wheel in a rusty red stoneware clay, dried it slowly under a sheet of plastic for a week, and had it fired once already, in the bisque firing, to about a thousand degrees. That made the clay hard but porous, a chalky pale brown, ready to take glaze. The second firing, the glaze firing, melts the glaze to glass and takes the clay up to twelve hundred and sixty degrees.

The glazing itself took two evenings. Greta keeps a wall of test tiles, each glued with a card that lists the recipe: a celadon, a tenmoku that goes almost black, a shiny cobalt, a milky white she calls oatmeal, and a matte green with copper in it. She taught us that glaze looks nothing like its finished colour. Applied to the bisque it is a pale pink or grey powder, and its final shade depends on the thickness, the atmosphere in the kiln and even where the piece stands. I dipped my bowls in celadon, brushed tenmoku on the mugs, and used a wax resist on the foot of every piece, so that the glaze would not run and stick the pot to the shelf.

On loading day, a Thursday, we arrived at five. The kiln is an old brick beast, a cube about a metre and a half in every direction, with a door that is bricked up each time. Greta showed us the shelves, called batts, and the short posts that hold them apart, and explained that every piece must sit at least a finger's width from its neighbours. She placed the taller pots at the back and the small ones near the burners, and refused to let me put my tilted plate on the top shelf because, she said, glaze may run and the top shelf is the hottest. It went on the second, on a small disc of alumina.

Everything was packed by seven. She sealed the door with a fresh row of bricks and clay, lit the burners, and turned the gas to a low blue flame. The first stage is to bring the temperature up very slowly, at about a hundred degrees an hour, so that any remaining moisture leaves the clay quietly instead of exploding it. She said, without smiling, that every potter has a story about a shattered pot taking three others with it.

We took turns to watch through the evening, a strange kind of vigil. The controller on the wall showed the temperature in red digits, and Greta had told us to write it in a log every thirty minutes. Around nine hundred, the peep hole at the top glowed a dull orange, and by eleven it was a bright yellow with a hint of white. At about 1,100 she reduced the air so that the flame turned smoky, which starves the glaze of oxygen and coaxes the copper in the green towards red. I stayed until one, and drove home smelling of hot brick.

While the kiln climbed, Greta told us stories, which I found as instructive as the technique. She trained for two years in a village pottery in Japan, where the wood-fired kiln was tended day and night by shifts of apprentices and the glaze of each piece depended on where it had stood in the ash. She recalled a firing in which the whole village stood outside at four in the morning to watch the last stoking, and a master potter who could judge the temperature by the colour of the flame alone, within ten degrees. She keeps a small stone from that kiln on the shelf above the controller.

She also showed us how to read pyrometric cones, small ceramic pyramids that bend at a known temperature. Three of them stood on a shelf at the front of the kiln in view of the peep hole: one that bends at 1,220, one at 1,240 and one at 1,260. When the first curled over like a tired flower, it meant the glaze was almost mature, and when the third bowed its head the firing was done. The controller is more precise, she said, but the cones show what the pots actually felt, and she trusts them more.

The peak came at four in the morning, when Greta, who had slept on a camp bed by the door, shut the gas off at 1,260 degrees. Then began the wait. A kiln cannot be opened until it is below a hundred degrees, or the sudden chill will craze the glaze, and cooling takes about thirty-six hours. Greta called it the longest fortnight of the week. She also said that during cooling you can sometimes hear the pots ticking, as tiny cracks form in the glaze, and that a good ring is a sign of a good fit.

On Saturday afternoon we opened the door. The bricks came down one by one, and warm dry air rolled out. My celadon bowls were beautiful, a smooth grey-green with a slight blue pooling in the base, and two of the mugs had come out a deep brown with rust streaks at the rim. The plate, on the other hand, had stuck to its disc, and there was a small crack running through the bottom. Greta said it was probably a fault in the clay and told me I could keep it as a lesson.

I brought seven pieces home in a cardboard box lined with newspaper. Mira picked the biggest bowl and has claimed it for the fruit. One of the mugs has already become my favourite, and I have used it every morning since, though the handle is a little too small for my fingers. Greta told me this is the commonest fault of a beginner, who makes a handle for a hand that is not their own, and suggested I trace my fingers on paper prior to pulling the next one. The classmate next to me, a retired bus driver called Emmanuel, had three pots come out with pinholes in the glaze, and Greta explained that these are tiny bubbles that burst and fail to heal, usually because the glaze was too thick or the firing too quick to finish. We spent ten minutes on the hearth discussing it like doctors.

Next term Greta wants us to try a wood ash glaze, which she says is hard to predict but lovely. I am already sketching a teapot, and thinking about the shape of the spout, which is the hardest part.

Knitting fair stall diary, the Saturday market in Wickerby. My neighbour Ingeborg has knitted for sixty years and sold nothing, so when the parish council announced a winter craft fair in the assembly hall she said she was too old to bother, and I heard myself saying I would run a stall for her. We agreed to share the takings, of which there would apparently be none, and to bring wool, a card reader, and a plastic sheet in case the roof leaked.

Preparation took three weeks. Ingeborg dug out seventy items from a cupboard: mittens in Fair Isle patterns, a dozen pairs of thick wool socks, six hats with pompoms, a blue cardigan for a child of about four, and eleven dishcloths that she said were her best sellers in 1983. I sewed neat paper labels with the price, and we settled on a simple scale: socks twelve pounds, mittens nine, hats fourteen, and the cardigan thirty. I made a sign with a needle and thread drawn on it.

The fair opened at ten. Our stall was the third from the door, between a man who sold handmade candles and a family with a stand of jam. Ingeborg sat on a folding chair with her needles going, knitting a sock without looking, and told me that her stall would attract more customers if she stayed and was seen to be working. She was right. By half past ten an audience of six had gathered, and one of them was a teenager who asked how to cast on.

The first sale was a pair of mittens to an older woman who claimed she had a grandson in Norway. The second was two pairs of socks to a man buying gifts for his sisters. By noon we had sold twenty-two items and made 212 pounds. I had not counted on how sociable it is: a stall is a sort of open door, and strangers stop to tell you about their own grandmothers' patterns. A woman told me about a jumper in the pattern of her village's coat of arms, and Ingeborg listened as if it were the first she had heard of such a thing.

At one o'clock the pipes in the hall's ceiling began to drip, and I got the plastic sheet out. We covered the stock and moved to the other side. At about half past one a girl of eight, holding her father's hand, asked Ingeborg how many stitches there were in a sock. Ingeborg thought for a moment and said, about six thousand, and the girl's mouth fell open. She then let the girl hold the needles and knit one row, guiding her hands, and the girl went away with a half-finished piece of grey garter stitch that she carried through the hall like a flag. I mention it because it was the best moment of the day, and it earned nothing.

Ingeborg, unruffled, went on knitting through the whole business. The candle man lost a third of his display to a puddle, and we shared our tea with him.

By the end of the day we had sold fifty-three items and the cardigan, and made 517 pounds. The parish council took a five-pound stall fee, and Ingeborg insisted on giving the whole balance to the roof repair fund, which seemed only fair. She kept the eleven dishcloths and said she would try again in the spring, and I have agreed to join her, on condition that she lets me pay for the wool.

Canal working party report: clearing the lock at Fenwick Cut. The studio's community group signed us up for a volunteer day with the Fenwick Canal Restoration Society, a small charity that has been reopening a mile of derelict waterway since the year 2001. Eleven of us gathered on a cold Saturday in November at the old lock keeper's cottage, a squat brick house with a chimney that leans, where a man in a fluorescent tabard called Desmond was handing out gloves. He is the society's works studior, and for that day he was our boss.

The plan was simple in outline and awful in practice. The lock chamber, a brick-lined rectangle about twenty-two metres long, had been filled by decades of leaves, silt and rubbish, and the society needed it empty by the winter so that a specialist team could repoint the walls in the spring. The pound above the lock had been drained a fortnight earlier, and the chamber was down to a foot of black water and a great deal of mud. Our job was to shovel the mud into buckets, pass the buckets up the wall by hand, and tip them into a skip.

Desmond began with the safety brief. Everyone wore waders or wellingtons, a hard hat, and a life jacket, though the water was barely thigh-deep. Nobody was to work alone in the chamber, and nobody was to lift anything heavier than they could carry easily. He demonstrated the correct way to shovel, with the knees bent and the load kept close to the body, and noted that the last group of volunteers, from a bank, had done it in patent leather shoes.

The first hour was slow. The mud was as thick as porridge and stank of rotting leaves, and every bucket weighed about twelve kilos. Meera and Yusuf worked on the lower gate, cutting away a mat of tangled roots, while Colm, Sami and I formed a bucket chain up a set of stone steps. Ilse, who had brought a flask of ginger tea, took the role of tally keeper and counted out loud each time a bucket came up. We reached two hundred by half past ten.

Then the finds started. Among the mud we pulled out a rusted bicycle frame, several traffic cones, a car battery, three shopping trolleys, a pram wheel, a mangled teapot, and a length of iron chain that Desmond said was very likely from the working days of the canal. Wenzel found a small glass bottle with a stopper and a paper label that read, in a copperplate hand, Fenwick Mineral Waters. Desmond stared at it for a minute and said it should go to the society's museum shelf.

At noon we stopped for soup from a van. The society's chairman, Prudence, came down from the cottage and told us about the history of the cut. It was built in 1794 to carry coal from the pits on the hill to the river, she said, and it closed in 1956 after a breach in the bank. There are eleven locks in the whole flight, and only two have so far been restored. The society hopes to reopen the entire mile in six years at a cost of about 1.2 million pounds, most of it from grants.

In the afternoon we finished the last third of the chamber. By half past three the floor of the lock showed the original brick for the first time, and Desmond, in the chamber with a long brush, pointed out the marks of the old barges on the walls. The skip was full by then, and the volunteer driver hauled it away. We had shifted, by the count, 486 buckets, about six tonnes of mud.

One of the trust's volunteers, a quiet retired engineer named Cuthbert, spent the afternoon with a clipboard beside the lower gate, measuring the gap between the gate and the sill with a steel rule. He told me the leakage at that point was the main reason the pound above never held its water, and that the gate's oak beams were still sound after more than two hundred years, a fact he took as a personal compliment from the eighteenth century. He drew me a small diagram of how a paddle gear works, with a rack, a pinion and a windlass, and I was astonished that such a simple machine could move a wall of water.

We handed in the waders at four and drank tea from a flask at the lock side. Everyone was tired, muddy and content, and Sami said that he had never enjoyed being filthy so much. Desmond invited us back in the spring for the repointing. Avery has set up a rota, and Meera has volunteered to organise a sponsored walk along the towpath in June.

Minutes of the Oakhurst village hall roof committee, taken by Blake as one of two co-opted members from the studio. Present at the meeting on Tuesday evening at the vestry: Mrs Adelheid Brandvold (chair), Mr Percival Osei (treasurer), Mrs Rukmini Das (secretary), Councillor Hugh Tallis, Blake, Avery, and two members of the congregation, Mr and Mrs Lowry. Apologies were received from the vicar, who was at a diocesan conference in Lincoln. The meeting opened at seven fifteen with the reading of the previous minutes, which were approved with one correction to the spelling of a surname.

Item one: the state of the roof. The chair reported that the hall, built in 1934 with money raised by the village's farmers, has a slate roof that has been failing for years. In March, after heavy rain, water came down through the ceiling above the stage and ruined a set of curtains. A structural surveyor from Lincoln visited in April and produced a nine-page report. In summary: about forty per cent of the slates are cracked or slipped, the timber battens along the north slope are rotten, the lead flashing around the chimney has perished, and the gutters are blocked and leaning. The surveyor advised against patching, saying that piecemeal repairs would cost as much in the end as a proper re-roof.

Item two: costs. Mr Osei presented three quotations. The first, from a firm in Grantham, was for 68,400 pounds to strip the roof and re-slate it with reclaimed Welsh slate. The second, from a local builder, was for 54,900 using new imported slate. The third, a larger firm from Peterborough, quoted 71,200 including scaffold, which the others treated as an extra. Mrs Das pointed out that the reclaimed slate would be more in keeping with the village, but Councillor Tallis said the parish planning studior had already indicated that either would be fine. After discussion the committee resolved to invite the local builder to a second meeting to negotiate, and to ask the Grantham firm whether a lower quote is possible if the work is phased over two summers.

Item three: funding. The committee has 19,350 pounds in the hall's roof account, of which 6,800 was raised at last year's summer fete. Mr Osei has made an application to the county community fund for 20,000, a decision on which is expected within six weeks. The heritage lottery scheme was discussed, but Blake pointed out that the deadline for the small grants round had passed and that the next round opens in January. Avery proposed, on behalf of the studio, to draft the application, and to prepare a simple budget spreadsheet. She was thanked.

Item four: fundraising events. It was agreed that a sponsored walk will be held on the second Saturday of June, starting at the hall and following the old railway path to the reservoir and back, a distance of eleven kilometres. Mrs Brandvold will ask the school to take part. Mr Lowry proposed a quiz night in October at the village pub, and proposed to set the questions himself. There was a short debate on whether to allow phones, which was resolved in the negative. The studio agreed to donate a hamper for the raffle, and Blake will produce a poster.

Item five: a proposal to sell a plaque. Mrs Das suggested that donors giving over two hundred pounds might have their name on a slate in the new roof, which would be inscribed and fixed inside the porch. The idea was welcomed, though Councillor Tallis raised a concern that it might delay the work if the plaques were late. It was agreed that names would be collected until the end of the year and that a local mason would be asked for a price per slate.

Item six: safeguarding the building in the meantime. A bucket brigade has been arranged to check the roof after each heavy rainfall, and Mr Osei will place three tarpaulins in the loft space. The hall is booked on Thursday evenings for the badminton group, who were asked to move away from the leaking corner.

Item seven: the fete. Mrs Lowry reported that the summer fete this year raised 6,800 pounds, but only after the weather turned at two o'clock, and that the tea tent lost a third of its trade to rain. It was proposed that the next fete be held in the hall itself, weather permitting, with stalls on the stage. Mr Osei disagreed, pointing out that the stage is the very part of the ceiling that leaks. After some good-humoured argument the committee decided to hold the fete on the school field as usual, with a marquee hired for 350 pounds as a precaution.

Item eight: volunteers with skills. The chair asked whether any villagers might offer labour or materials in kind. Mr Lowry said that his cousin runs a scaffolding hire firm in Newark and might give a discount. Blake mentioned that the studio has a colleague, Yusuf, who is a keen amateur roofer, and could advise on the flashing, though not do the work. Mrs Das said that the church's insurance broker had warned that any volunteer working at height must be covered, and that the committee should not, in any circumstances, allow amateurs on the scaffold. This was agreed without dissent.

Item nine: communications. Mrs Brandvold proposed a fortnightly bulletin in the parish magazine and on the notice boards, with a thermometer drawn on it to show the sum raised. The secretary will keep a mailing list of interested households. Councillor Tallis suggested that the council's website carry a donate button, and Avery proposed to check whether the parish's bank can accept card payments. It was noted that about a third of the village is over seventy and that paper forms remain important.

Any other business. Mrs Lowry reported that the vicar's wife has proposed to donate a piano, and that the committee would need to decide where to store it. The secretary asked for a volunteer to keep the minutes next month; Blake proposed. The next meeting was fixed for the first Tuesday of next month at seven fifteen, with the local builder to attend at eight. The meeting closed at nine ten.

Action points. Mr Osei: chase the county fund and arrange a second visit by the builder. Avery: draft the lottery application by the end of the month and circulate the budget. Blake: design the sponsored walk poster, book the reservoir car park, and confirm the hamper. Mrs Das: contact the mason. Mrs Brandvold: write to the school. It was noted with appreciation that a farm family had left an envelope of cash on the vestry desk with a note that said only, for the roof.

Bell-ringing taster session, a team event at St Anselm's tower. Meera saw a notice in the porch of the church near the studio and asked the local ringing band whether a group of novices could visit. The captain of the tower, a schoolteacher named Rosalind Achebe, agreed to give us two hours on a Wednesday evening in March, with the warning that bell-ringing is not a spectator sport and that we should wear flat shoes.

Eight of us climbed the narrow stone stair to the ringing chamber, a square wooden-floored space about halfway up the tower with eight ropes hanging in a circle through holes in the ceiling. Each rope has a soft woollen grip, the sally, in red, white and blue stripes. Rosalind explained that the bells above us weigh from about two hundred kilos for the lightest to nearly nine hundred for the heaviest, and that they are hung on wheels so that they swing right over and back rather than merely tolling.

We began with handling on the silent bells, a technique in which the clapper is tied. Rosalind taught us to hold the rope with both hands, to let the sally rise and catch it on the upstroke, and to pull the tail end at the right moment. Sami's first attempt was wild, and the rope leapt up and wrapped round his arm. Rosalind untangled him without comment and told us that the most important rule was never to let go, and the second rule was to keep our feet clear of the loops of rope on the floor.

The first time I rang a bell I was astonished by how light it felt. The weight rises on the backstroke, then falls on the handstroke, and the timing is a curious tugging rhythm, more like a conversation than an effort. Each of us managed a slow sequence of five strokes until we lost the pattern. The band's ringers stood behind us, calling out, look at the rope in front of you, watch the one after you, listen for the bell you follow.

At the end they rang a short touch of rounds and call changes with the full eight bells, and it was thrilling to stand in the centre of the chamber while the sound rained down through the ceiling. Rosalind said the band rings for services on Sundays and for weddings, and that they always need new recruits. Two of us signed up for the practice night on Fridays. Rosalind told us about the terminology on the way down the stair. A touch is a short piece of ringing, a peal is a performance of at least five thousand changes, and a method is a pattern such as Plain Bob or Grandsire, named after ringers who died ahead of the Napoleonic wars. The band has twelve members, the youngest fifteen and the oldest eighty-three, and the tower has been in continuous use since 1793, when the bells were cast at a foundry in Loughborough. She said the hardest part of ringing is not the pulling but the listening, and that a good ringer hears the whole sound as one instrument.

On the way out Blake noticed a board on the wall listing a peal rung in 1911, which took three hours and ten minutes without a single mistake.

Allotment dispute diary, the shed on plot 14. It began in April with a small message on the notice board at the Hartley Fields site, from a man named Everard Pym on plot 15, accusing me of allowing my shed to overshadow his beans. I read it standing on the gravel path with my spade in one hand and my flask in the other, and felt the sort of indignation that only a very small matter can provoke. The shed is two metres by two and a half, with a lean-to roof. It has stood in the same spot since 2016, when I took over the plot from a woman who moved to Spain.

I wrote back a polite reply and pinned it under his. He responded in a longer note, on graph paper, with a sketch showing the sun's angle at the summer solstice and a measurement of the shadow's length at eleven in the morning: three metres eighty. He asserted that this violated rule nine of the site's tenancy conditions, which states that structures should not impair the growing conditions of neighbouring plots. I looked up rule nine, which does say that, and then rule four, which says that sheds should not exceed six square metres, and mine is five. I began to feel that I would win, and did not much like the feeling.

By May the dispute had spread. Two other plot holders took sides, and someone left a bundle of bean poles on my path, either as a gift or as a taunt. The site secretary, a brisk retired nurse called Winifred Okafor, called a mediation meeting for a Sunday morning at the trading hut, with tea and a plate of ginger biscuits, and gave each of us five minutes to speak. Everard arrived with a clipboard. I had a photograph.

Everard's case was that his runner beans, which he grows every year for the autumn show, had grown thinner and later since my shed was repainted, in a dark green that he said absorbed heat and cast a colder shadow. I said this was absurd, that the shed had not moved, and that the colour did not alter a shadow. There was a silence, and then Winifred said, gently, that she had noticed the beans were sparse this year, and had assumed it was the wet spring.

We resolved it in an unexpected way. Winifred took a tape measure and paced the plots, and found that Everard's bean rows ran in a north-south line that put them in shade in the morning, as any shed would. She suggested he turn the rows east to west, and I proposed to cut back a small elder that hung over my fence and had been adding to the shade. We shook hands, and I promised him a jar of my honey-coloured onion chutney.

Afterwards Winifred took me aside and said that in nine years as secretary she had dealt with disputes over compost heaps, a bonfire, a scarecrow that frightened a child, and a swan that someone claimed was a duck, and that in every case the trouble had started with a note. I have thought about that since. A note pinned to a board has no tone of voice, and so a mild remark reads as a charge. She said she now walks round every month and simply says hello to each plot holder, and that it has cut the complaints by half.
