He moved the rows in mid-May, planted a fresh sowing, and by August the beans were fine. He won a second prize at the show for a plate of nine pods, and put the rosette on my shed door without a word, which I took as a peace treaty. Winifred has since put a new rule on the notice board, asking that any complaint be discussed in person before it is pinned up.

Amateur radio field day, Blake's log from the hill above Marsden. I got my foundation licence in the spring after a six-week course in a school hall, and the local club, the Marsden and District Radio Society, asked new licensees to join their annual field day, a twenty-four-hour contest in which stations set up in the open with battery power and try to contact as many others as possible. I signed up as an operator and a general pair of hands, and brought a flask, a folding chair, and far too many socks.

The site was a farmer's meadow on a ridge at 310 metres, which the club has used for nineteen years in return for a crate of beer at harvest. We arrived on Friday evening at six to build. The club's contest manager, a wiry man in his sixties called Reginald Mbeki, had drawn a plan on the back of an old calendar. Two tents, one for the high-frequency station and one for the VHF; a generator set well downwind; and three antennas, one of which was a long wire strung between a pair of fibreglass poles, one a small directional beam on a mast, and one a vertical whip fixed to the roof of a van.

Building the mast took most of the evening. It was a telescoping aluminium pole twelve metres tall, guyed in three directions with ropes and pegs, and the way to raise it, Reginald said, was slowly, with someone at each guy line and nobody standing beneath. Six of us walked it up hand over hand while he called the instructions like a ship's mate. The beam on top weighed about eight kilos and tried to swing us round like a weathercock. We staked the guys at forty-five degrees and Reginald tightened each one until the mast hummed in the wind.

The contest began at two on Saturday afternoon, and the first thing I learned was how strange a radio sounds when it is used for competition. There is no small talk. The operator says the call sign, the other side replies with theirs and a signal report and a serial number, and the whole exchange takes about eight seconds. The skill is in hearing a faint voice in a crowd of loud ones, in what Reginald called the noise. He put me beside a veteran named Philippa, who wore a headset with one ear uncovered so that she could keep up a running commentary.

My first contact was with a station in Norway, and I remember it exactly because my hands were shaking. I said the call sign twice, the reply came back in a thin, rushing voice, and I wrote down the number wrongly, so I had to ask for a repeat, which Philippa said is nothing to be ashamed of. By four I had made eleven contacts. By seven, when the band opened to the west, I was making one a minute and my handwriting had turned into a scribble that only the logging computer would forgive.

The evening shift was quieter and more absorbing. As the sun set the higher frequencies faded and the lower ones came alive, and the long wire began to catch faint stations from very far away: a man in Poland, a woman in Portugal, and after ten a very weak signal from Madeira, which took three attempts and a lot of concentration. The generator ticked in the dark, and someone brought a tray of tea and sausage rolls. At midnight the wind rose, the tents flapped, and a moth the size of a mouse blundered into the lamp.

At three in the morning I took my turn on the graveyard shift with Reginald himself, and he told me a great deal about the hobby. He said that most of the joy is in the antenna, that a poor radio with a good aerial will beat a good radio with a poor aerial every time, and that a fine sunrise contact with a stranger is worth ten long conversations. He also confessed, as the sky lightened, that he had spent the previous winter building a radio from a kit and had not yet dared to turn it on.

Dawn came at five, grey and cold, with dew on everything. We logged the last hours in a haze. By two on Sunday afternoon the contest was over, and the total was announced: 612 contacts in eleven countries, a modest but decent result. Reginald said that the club's best had been just over eight hundred, in a year with better conditions. We took down the mast in the same order as it was put up, and the farmer came out to inspect the meadow and shook everyone's hand.

What I take from the weekend is a strange kind of gratitude. I had wondered what the hobby was for, given that a phone can reach anybody in an instant. But the radio has a different quality, that of being dependent on weather, sunspots and skill, and it feels earned. I have ordered a second-hand beam and a roll of wire. Reginald has agreed to help me set up a modest station in my parents' yard, and next month I sit the intermediate exam.

Moth trapping diary, a warm night in late June at the Kettleby reserve. A naturalist I met at a village fair, Dr Adaeze Hollis, invited me to a moth night run by the county wildlife trust, a Saturday evening with lamps, sheets and a great many little jars. I had thought of moths as brown things that eat jumpers, and I came home with a much better opinion.

The trust puts out about eight traps on a night like this, at different points around the reserve, a mix of woodland edge, wet meadow and a small chalk bank. A trap is an ingenious device: a bright bulb on a stand over a plastic bucket or box containing egg cartons, so that moths drawn to the light spiral down and settle in the crevices, where they sit quietly until dawn. It does no harm. The next morning the moths are counted and released. I was put with Adaeze at the trap beside the woodland edge, and she taught me how to hold a small clear pot over a moth and coax it inside with a card.

We started at half past nine, when the light was going. Adaeze spread a white sheet on the grass and hung a lamp over it, a mercury vapour bulb that gives off an eerie violet-white glow. Within ten minutes moths arrived out of the dark, first a few, then dozens, whirling around the light and settling on the sheet. There were pale ones the colour of driftwood, tiny ones no bigger than a grain of rice, a fat brown one with feathery antennae, and one the size of a wren.

The names were half the delight. Adaeze called them out from memory as they landed: a Buff Ermine, a Heart and Dart, a Common Footman, a Small Elephant Hawk-moth, which is a bright pink and olive thing that looks as though it has been dipped in raspberry sauce, and a Peppered Moth, whose speckled wings had famously turned darker in the smoky cities of the nineteenth century. I wrote a list in a notebook with a red torch, and by eleven there were forty-one species, which she said was a good total for June.

At midnight we went round the other traps. The one by the wet meadow had caught a Poplar Hawk-moth, chunky and grey, that sat in the palm of my hand and refused to go away. At the chalk bank a young volunteer called Thabo had counted three hundred individuals of one species of tiny brown moth and was still counting. I learned that identification often depends on small details, such as the pattern on the outer edge of a forewing or the shape of a spot, and that some species can only be told apart by looking at their genitalia under a microscope, a fact that was delivered with great enthusiasm.

At half past one the air grew cold and the moths thinned out. We had tea from a flask, and a young owl called from the wood. Adaeze told me that the trust keeps records of every trapping night going back to 1996, and that they show a steady decline in the numbers of moths, about a third fewer than at the start. She blames the loss of hedgerows, more pesticide and, she said, more light at night, because the bulbs of streetlamps confuse the insects and draw them away from feeding.

There is a second tradition of the night which I nearly forgot: the breakfast count. At six the volunteers reassemble, light a small camping stove for tea, and go round the traps in the low light, emptying each one gently into a large white tray and identifying everything ahead of the sun warms the moths and sends them flying. This is when the sleepy ones can be photographed. A Privet Hawk-moth, as big as a small bird, sat on my sleeve for ten minutes, and Thabo got a picture of it that he says he will print for his mother. The tray at the wet meadow held two rarities, a Marsh Oblique-barred and a scarce moth called the Reed Dagger, and the trust's recorder was so delighted that she poured more tea for the whole group without being asked.

A word on ethics, because I asked about it. Adaeze says moths are handled as little as possible, never with fingers on the scales of the wings, and always released at dusk in the shade of a bush, since a released moth in daylight will be eaten by a robin. Every record goes into a spreadsheet with a grid reference and a date and is sent to the county recorder, who passes it to the national database. A single pair of eyes at one trap, she said, may count a thing that no one else has seen.

We packed up at two, leaving the traps to run until dawn, and I slept in the car for an hour prior to driving home. In the morning the trust's records show that the reserve caught 1,204 moths of ninety-eight species. I have decided to buy a book, and I am going to make a small trap of my own with a bucket and a lamp, and keep a diary on my balcony.

Sponsorship review: the Harbourside Brass Band and its spring concert. The studio was approached in January by the secretary of the Harbourside Silver Band, a community ensemble of thirty-one players who rehearse in a Methodist hall on Thursdays. They asked us to sponsor the printing of programmes for their spring concert and the hire of a larger venue, in return for our name on the poster. Blake asked me to write up the meeting and the decision, since I attended both the rehearsal and the concert.

Background on the band. It was founded in 1889 by the dockworkers of the old Harbourside shipyard, and has been playing without interruption, except during the two wars, for the whole of that time. The present players include a retired postman on euphonium, three teenage cornetists, a nurse who plays tenor horn, a pair of brothers on trombone, and a conductor named Mr Oyelaran, a music teacher from the grammar school who took over five years ago. The band competes in a regional contest each March and usually finishes in the middle of the third section.

The request came with a budget. The band needs 2,150 pounds for the concert: 700 for the hire of the concert hall in the town centre, 480 for printing, 350 for a guest soloist, 320 for insurance and licences, and 300 for a reception afterwards. It has 900 in a fund, some of which came from a raffle, and the members pay a subscription of two pounds a week. The secretary, a soft-spoken man named Godfrey, explained that they would not ask for anything more from us than the programme costs, and that a contribution of 500 pounds would be a real help.

Discussion in the studio was short. Blake said that the studio has a small community budget of 3,000 pounds a year, of which about 1,400 remained, and that the band was a good fit because it is local, has volunteers rather than staff, and does not solicit from large firms. Meera asked whether we would be expected to give a speech. Ilse asked whether we were covered by their insurance if a tuba fell on someone. It was agreed to commit 500 pounds, on condition that the studio's logo appears on the front of the programme and on the poster at the same size as any other sponsor.

I went to a rehearsal on the Thursday ahead of the concert to see what we were paying for. The hall was cold and smelled of damp coats. Thirty musicians sat in a horseshoe under strip lights, tuning in a haphazard chorus that gradually became a single note. Mr Oyelaran, a quick and cheerful man, raised his baton and they played the opening of an arrangement of a Grieg piece. It was flat in the middle, ragged at the edges and extraordinarily moving, and I thought that this is what sponsorship is for.

The concert itself was held on a Saturday evening in April. The hall seats 420, and there were about 380 people in it, mainly older, with a knot of children in the front row. The programme began with a march, then a selection from a musical, a solo by the guest cornetist Marguerite Aubin, who had come from Lyon, and a piece for the whole band in which the percussion section dropped a cymbal on the stage. The audience laughed, and the conductor turned round and bowed as if it had been planned.

At the interval, the raffle was drawn, and a woman in a green coat won the studio's donated hamper. In the second half the band played a jazz medley and a hymn tune. As an encore they repeated the march at a faster speed, and the trombones stood up. The last note was greeted with the kind of applause that fills a hall like a warm bath.

The accounts afterwards show that ticket sales brought in 2,266 pounds, so the band made a small surplus of 116, which Godfrey has put aside for new music stands. Our name appeared on the front of the programme, in a modest box, as agreed. Godfrey wrote to thank us and sent a photograph of the band with the sponsors' banner.

A small complication came up in the run-up. The venue hire agreement asked for a certificate of public liability insurance covering the band, and the band had let its policy lapse in January. Godfrey was mortified. Ilse spent a morning on the phone to a broker and found a policy for community groups at 186 pounds a year, and the band agreed to pay half if we paid the rest as part of the sponsorship. It was a good example of why a sponsor should ask questions prior to signing anything, and I have added a line to the studio's sponsorship checklist to ask every applicant about insurance and licensing.

Another small matter was the licence for performing copyrighted music. A concert that includes works still in copyright needs a licence from the performing rights society, and the band had assumed the hall's own licence would cover it. It did not cover live performance by a visiting group, and Mr Oyelaran had to submit a list of every piece with its composer and length. The fee was 64 pounds. He did it in an evening at his study desk, he told me, with a pot of tea and a great deal of muttering, and afterwards he was rather proud of the spreadsheet.

One more detail from the accounts: the printing bill came in at 452 pounds, not 480, because the printer, a family firm on Quay Street that has done the band's programmes since the seventies, rounded down and would not be argued with. The saving went towards flowers for the guest soloist.

The percussion incident deserves a final note. The cymbal that fell was borrowed from the Salvation Army band, and the percussionist, a young woman named Eleni who is only sixteen, was so upset that she cried in the interval. Mr Oyelaran took her aside, told her that every drummer in history has dropped a cymbal, and gave her the bass drum solo for the encore, which she played without a flaw. I saw all this from the back of the hall, and it was as fine a piece of teaching as I have watched.

Recommendations. The studio should sponsor the band again next year and think about a small in-kind gesture, such as designing their poster, which they clearly need. We should also propose that members of the team, in turn, attend a concert, rather than send a cheque and stay away, since the gesture means more when someone is in the audience. Blake agrees, and Meera wants to learn the cornet, which the band has proposed to lend her.

Fossil hunt diary, a low-tide morning on the Jurassic shore at Ravenscar Bay. My father-in-law Gunnar turned seventy in the autumn and asked for a day out that involved digging in something, so we booked a guided fossil walk with a local geologist, and I brought the notebook, a small hammer, a hand lens, and a box of newspaper for wrapping finds. The tide charts gave low water at ten past eleven, which meant an early start and a slow walk along the base of the cliffs.

Our guide was called Perpetua Mwangi, a woman in her forties who runs the small geology museum in the harbour village. She has been collecting on this coast for twenty-five years and her first words were about safety. Do not go near the foot of the cliffs when the clay is wet, she said, because the slope collapses without warning. Do not hammer at the rock face itself. Wear a hard hat, check the tide constantly, and turn back if she blows the whistle. Nobody asked for a second explanation.

The rocks of this bay are about a hundred and eighty million years old, dark grey shales full of the remains of an ancient sea. Perpetua showed us how the layers are stacked like a book, with each band a different chapter, and how the storms of winter pull blocks out of the cliff and roll them along the shore, where the sea splits them and reveals what is inside. The best place to look, she said, is not the cliff but the pebbles of the beach, particularly the round grey nodules called concretions, which crack open like eggs.

The first hour brought nothing except a good deal of laughing at my father-in-law, who had selected a rock the size of a suitcase and was bashing it with a mallet. Then Perpetua showed us a coiled shape in a pebble at her feet. It was an ammonite, she said, the shell of a squid-like animal that swam in this sea, and this one was about the size of a coin, with fine ribs running round the spiral. She pointed out that the animal lived in the outer chamber, and the inner coils were filled with gas to give it buoyancy. She let me hold it. I am not embarrassed to say that I felt a lump in my throat.

Gunnar's suitcase split open at last, and inside, to his astonishment, was a faint imprint of a fern-like leaf, black against grey. Perpetua said it was a piece of a plant from the age of dinosaurs, washed out to sea from the land. In the next half hour I found a belemnite, a bullet-shaped fossil that was once the internal skeleton of another squid relative, and a piece of fossil wood that had turned to jet, black and light, which the people of Whitby once carved into brooches.

The tide turned at noon and we moved higher up the shore, where Perpetua showed us a large flat slab with a trail of small footprints. She thought they were the tracks of a small dinosaur, a plant-eater, crossing what had been a muddy river bank. The prints were three-toed, about the size of a man's palm, and there were eleven of them in a line. She said the slab had been discovered the previous winter and the museum had photographed it and applied for a permit to keep it.

At one o'clock we sat on a rock and ate sandwiches. Perpetua examined each of our finds with a hand lens and told us what they were. The best was Gunnar's, which she said would make a good exhibit in a small cabinet at home. She also gave us a rule of the shore: you may keep what you find on the beach, but you may not dig into the cliff, and anything unusual should be shown to the museum. It was a sensible rule, she said, and it kept the hobby alive.

Perpetua also set us a small task in the final hour, a kind of fieldwork exercise. She drew a square metre on the shale with a stick and told us to record everything we found in it: the number of fossils, their type, and their condition. Gunnar took charge of the count with an old pencil stub and produced a neat tally on the back of a receipt that he was very proud of: seventeen ammonites, nine belemnites, four fragments of wood, and a single tooth, probably from a fish. It is the kind of exercise that geologists do to compare one place with another, she said, and it made us look at the beach in a completely different way. In a single square metre, a hundred and eighty million years lay in a heap.

We walked back along the sand as the water rose, and Gunnar carried his fossil wrapped in my scarf. In the museum's small shop I bought a pocket guide, and Gunnar bought a postcard. He has since told me that he plans to give the leaf slab to his granddaughter, and I saw that he had already written a label for it in pencil.

Orchard pressing day, report on the studio's volunteer outing to Holm Farm. The community group of the studio spent a Saturday in October at a working orchard on the edge of the city, where a cooperative of neighbours picks, presses and bottles apple juice each autumn to raise money for the village school. We joined about thirty other volunteers. It was a mild, bright morning, and the trees hung heavy with fruit.

The orchard has some ninety trees, most of them old varieties that few shops sell: Ashmead's Kernel, Blenheim Orange, Egremont Russet, and a very sour cooker called Bramley's Seedling that nobody would ever eat raw. The person in charge was a farmer named Mrs Sigrid Loveday, a short, energetic woman of about seventy, who greeted us at the gate with a tray of mugs and a whistle. She divided us into pickers, sorters and pressers, and said that the morning's aim was two tonnes of fruit.

I joined the pickers with Avery and Sami. The method was simple. A ladder against the tree, a canvas bag hung round the neck, a gentle twist of the apple until the stalk parted, and never to pull. Windfalls on the ground, we were told, could be used but only if they had not lain for more than two days, since a bruised apple ferments and spoils a whole batch. We were also asked to leave every fifth apple on a tree for the birds and the wasps, an old custom, and to leave the highest fruit for the tree spirit, which Mrs Loveday said with a straight face.

By eleven we had picked forty crates. They were carried by wheelbarrow to the press shed, an old brick barn with a slate floor and a great oak press in the centre, dating from 1920. The first step was to wash the apples in a trough and tip them into a grinder, a hopper with rotating steel teeth that turned them to a coarse mash, called pomace. Ilse and Meera ran the grinder and complained bitterly about the smell of fermenting fruit.

The second step was the pressing. The pomace was ladled into square cloths, folded into parcels and stacked between wooden racks, and a screw was turned by hand until the juice ran out and down a channel into a stainless steel tank. It is a slow business: each stack of ten parcels gave about thirty litres, and pressing took twenty minutes. Colm and Yusuf took turns at the screw and by lunchtime they were both red with exertion, and Mrs Loveday said they had done better than the vicar.

Lunch was a huge leek and potato soup, with baked potatoes and cider vinegar chutney, eaten on trestle benches under a tarpaulin. Over the meal Mrs Loveday told us the history of the orchard, which was planted in 1898 by her great-grandfather and nearly grubbed up in the nineteen-sixties when the price of apples collapsed. Her mother saved it by starting the juice business, and the cooperative now has forty members. The school gets 60 pence of every bottle sold.

In the afternoon the freshly pressed juice was pasteurised in a large stainless pan at seventy-five degrees for twenty minutes, then poured into bottles with a funnel and capped. The labels were hand-stuck, and Avery, who has a steadier hand than I, did a hundred without a wrinkle. By five o'clock, the count was 1,480 bottles, and the volunteers were allowed to take home two each. The rest would be sold at the school Christmas fair.

During the lunch break Sami asked how much juice the cooperative makes in a good year, and Mrs Loveday answered with a precision that surprised us: last year, 9,400 bottles, of which she had sold about 8,100. The rest went to friends, teachers and, she suspected, a badger. She then gave us a short lesson on blending. The best juice, she said, is never made from a single variety. A sweet apple gives sugar, a sharp one gives acidity, and an old russet gives what she calls the finish, a faint nutty warmth at the back of the tongue. She had a tasting tray of six small glasses and asked us to guess the proportions of the day's blend. I guessed three parts Blenheim to one Bramley and was told that I was close, but that I had forgotten the russet.

She also explained why the pressing must be done within two days of picking, and why every apple is inspected prior to it going into the grinder. One rotten apple, she said, can taint a whole tank with a musty note, and an expert nose can tell within seconds. She let Ilse smell a bad batch, and Ilse said it was like a wet dog. A good press day has a warm smell, she said, like baking, and by the end of the afternoon the whole barn had that smell, so strong that I could still taste it on the drive home.

Meera has proposed that the studio buy a hundred bottles as gifts for the year-end, and Blake has agreed, and asked whether the label could carry a small note about the cooperative. Mrs Loveday has invited us back for the wassail in January, when the trees are blessed with cider and a lot of noise, to drive out evil spirits and encourage a good crop.

Dinghy repair diary, a winter in the shed. In September I bought a wooden sailing dinghy for 350 pounds from an elderly man in Deal who said he could no longer bend his knees. She is a 12-foot clinker-built boat named Wren, built in 1962, with a sprung mast and a rotting transom, and I intended to have her in the water by the following June. This is my log of the repair, kept in a notebook in the shed and typed up in spring.

The survey, which I did with a torch and a screwdriver on a cold Saturday, revealed the extent of the trouble. The hull planks were mostly sound, with two exceptions on the port side below the waterline. The transom, the flat piece at the stern to which the rudder is attached, had gone soft with rot around the pintle fittings. The centreboard case had a split along one side, and the paint, four or five layers of it, was peeling like a sunburn. I made a list of eleven items and put a price beside each; the total came to about 420 pounds, which suggested I had not been entirely honest with myself when I paid the 350.

I joined the community boatyard at Faversham, a warehouse where twelve people restore their boats in pens beneath a shared roof, under the eye of a retired shipwright named Ambrose Ndlovu, a large and quiet man who charges nothing but expects to be listened to. He looked over Wren for a long time and said, this is a good boat with a bad bottom. He suggested that I begin with the transom, since nothing else could be fitted until it was sound.

The transom took three weekends. First I unscrewed the fittings and removed the old timber, which came away in wet brown crumbs. Ambrose showed me how to make a template from cardboard, transfer the shape to a plank of iroko, and cut it with a jigsaw, then plane the edges to the bevel of the hull planks. The trickiest part was to fit the new piece so tightly that no light showed through the joint. I spent an entire Sunday shaving off fractions of a millimetre with a block plane, and when it finally sat home, Ambrose put his palm on it, nodded, and walked away, which was the highest praise he gave.

The planks came next. I scarfed in two new sections of larch, cutting a long, slanting joint of about eight to one, so that the old and new timber overlapped for a hand's length and glued with epoxy. Each was clamped with bits of wood and a great deal of improvised weight, including a bag of sand and a bicycle. Then I fastened them to the ribs with copper rivets, a process that needs two people, one to hammer from outside and one to hold a heavy iron dolly against the head inside. Ambrose's partner, a woman called Philippa who builds violins, agreed to hold the dolly, and we riveted forty-one in a single afternoon.

The centreboard case was repaired with a strip of marine plywood and more epoxy. I sanded the hull for two weeks. Every evening I came home with sawdust in my hair and epoxy on my elbows, and my flatmate began to leave notes on the fridge asking me to shower prior to touching the sofa. The stripping of the old paint with a heat gun was slow and smelled of burning toast, but it revealed a lovely honey-coloured wood under the layers.

In March I painted her. The recipe, from Ambrose, was one coat of primer, two of undercoat and three of gloss, with a light sanding between each. I chose a dark blue for the hull and cream for the inside, and a strip of red under the gunwale. It took eleven days because the shed was cold and the paint would not cure below eight degrees, so I hung a heater from the beam and watched the thermometer as though the boat were a patient.

In the last week of May I made the running rigging: a main sheet of eight-millimetre polyester rope with a spliced eye, a halyard with a whipped end, and a set of tiny wooden cleats that Ambrose cut for me from an spare piece of ash. The sail, an old tan Terylene one that came with the boat, had a tear along one seam, and Philippa taught me to sew it with a sailmaker's palm and a waxed thread, using a stitch that looks like the rungs of a ladder. It took an evening, and it is the piece of work on the boat of which I am most proud.

The launch was on the second Saturday in June at Faversham Creek, on a rising tide. Ambrose stood on the slipway with his arms folded. Wren went down the ramp on her trailer and floated with only a whisper of water at the garboard, which we watched with breath held for ten minutes. She was dry. I stepped aboard, stepped the mast, hoisted the sail and, with a light westerly filling it, moved silently out into the creek. It was the best moment of the year.

There were setbacks, and I should record them for my own instruction. In January I discovered that the copper rivets I had bought were the wrong gauge for the plank thickness, and half of them flattened instead of clenching. Ambrose said nothing while I drilled them out one by one, and then said, that is how you learn. In February the shed heater failed and the epoxy would not go off, so that a joint I had clamped on a Saturday was still gummy on Sunday night and had to be scraped back. And in March I put the first coat of gloss on a damp day and it clouded, and I sanded it off and started again. The single most important lesson of the winter was patience, in the form of a rule that Ambrose repeats: do not do the next thing until the last thing is finished.

The boatyard itself was a source of unexpected friendship. On Thursday evenings the twelve of us stopped work at seven and ate a shared supper, usually a stew, at a long trestle by the wood stove. There was a retired teacher who was rebuilding a Mirror dinghy for her grandson, a young couple restoring a canal boat with a leaking roof, and a widower named Tobias who was making a small rowing boat entirely with hand tools, in memory of his wife, who liked the river. I learned more about rot, glue and human patience in those suppers than in any manual.

Total cost, in the end, was 1,146 pounds including the boat, timber, epoxy, paint, rivets, boatyard membership and a new set of sheets and blocks. Ambrose says she will last another sixty years if I keep the bilge dry. I have sailed her nine times since and capsized once, the day I tried to go about in a squall, and been rescued by a man in a canoe. Next winter I plan to make a new rudder.

Dry-stone walling day, a team report from the Cotswold edge. For the studio's autumn volunteer day, Meera suggested something practical and out of doors, and after a few phone calls she found the Stonewall Trust, a small charity that repairs field walls in the hills above Painswick. They needed helpers on a Saturday in September to rebuild a collapsed section beside a footpath, about twelve metres long, and had agreed to teach us how.

We arrived at nine in a lane between two hillsides of rough grass and stood in a circle round the gap. The wall had been there since the 1780s, said our instructor, a retired farmer named Emrys Ogunbanjo, and it was built without mortar, with about a tonne of stone in every metre. He had a weather-beaten face and hands like shovels. He also had four rules: never lift a stone twice, never put a small stone where a large one will fit, always face the best side outward, and be kind to your back.

He showed us the structure of a wall. It has a broad base of big stones, two faces that slope inward, a fill of small rubble in the middle called hearting, and through-stones that span the whole width every metre or so to tie the two faces together, and finally a row of cope stones set on edge along the top. The batter, as he called the slope of the faces, is important: the wall should be about a fifth narrower at the top than at the bottom. To check it we used a wooden frame called a template, which we moved along the wall as we built.

The first job was to take down what remained of the ruined section, sorting the stones by size into piles: footings, walling stones, through-stones, hearting and copes. It took an hour and a half and some serious grunting. Ilse discovered that, in ten years of studio life, she had lost her sense of how heavy a rock can be. Sami discovered a small snake, which was a slow-worm, and Emrys picked it up with his spade and put it under a hedge, saying it did more for the farm than any of us.

We laid the footings in a trench about thirty centimetres deep, with the heaviest stones at the bottom. Then we began to build up in courses, working from the two ends toward the middle, and checking the line with a string stretched between two posts. There was much talk of one over two and two over one, meaning that each stone should sit across the joint between two stones below it, so that no vertical line ran through the wall. Deepa turned out to have an eye for this, and Emrys called her the best beginner he had had in a year.

Around noon we stopped for tea from a great flask and a packet of oat biscuits, in the lee of the wall. Emrys told us that there are about 120,000 miles of dry-stone wall in Britain, and that a good waller can lay six or eight metres in a day. He said that when he learned, in 1969, his father used to knock down his work if it was not tight enough and make him do it again. The skill, he said, is in selecting the right stone at first glance, and it comes with practice, like reading.

By four o'clock we had built the wall up to knee height along nine of the twelve metres. Emrys said that the rest would take a further morning, and that the cope stones would go on last, by his own crew. He looked over our work, kicked the wall gently in a few places to test it and pronounced it sound. Colm asked whether it would last a hundred years, and Emrys said that it would last as long as nobody leans on it.

In the afternoon there was a short talk about the wildlife of a wall. Emrys pointed out that a dry-stone wall is a habitat in itself, with hundreds of small crevices used by wrens, stoats, lizards, spiders and beetles, and that a section rebuilt too tightly, without any gaps in the hearting, is worth less to the creatures than an old ruinous one. He showed us a lichen, pale grey and crusty, that grows only on stone that has been exposed for over a century, and said that it would take fifty years to appear on the wall we had built. He also told us about the small openings called smoots, or hogholes, left at the base of a wall to let sheep pass through from one field to the next, and he made us build one, a neat square gap spanned by a lintel of flat stone.

The last hour was spent selecting cope stones from the pile at the roadside. Emrys said that a wall without copes is like a house without a roof, and he taught us to choose stones of about the same width and to set them on edge, leaning slightly, with a small stone underneath to wedge them. Colm had a knack for it. He laid eleven copes in ten minutes and then admitted he had played with building blocks for hours as a child.

We finished with a photograph. Meera has asked the trust whether we could return in November, and Emrys has said that he would welcome us. I went home with bruised fingers and the deep pleasure that comes from having made something that will outlive the person who made it.

Scything course diary, a Saturday on the meadow at Long Barrow farm. A friend told me that a good scythe, properly set up, is faster and much quieter than a strimmer, and I signed up for a one-day course taught by a woman named Odalys Freeman at a farm in the downs. I have a small unkempt meadow behind the flat that I share with my neighbours, and I dreamed of mowing it in silence at six in the morning.

Odalys began with the equipment. A scythe has a long curved blade, called the blade, and a snath, the wooden pole with two handles that must be set to fit the height and arm length of the user. She measured each of us and adjusted the grips and the angle of the blade with an allen key until it felt natural. The blade's edge is not sharpened with a file but hammered thin with a small anvil and hammer, a process called peening, and refreshed every twenty minutes in the field with a whetstone.

The stroke itself is a graceful, swinging movement of the whole body, the arms almost still and the hips turning, so that the blade sweeps in a low arc close to the ground and lays the cut grass in a neat row at the left. I made a poor start. My blade dug into the turf, then flew up and sliced nothing, and Odalys came over with a grin to correct my stance. Feet apart, knees soft, weight moving from the right foot to the left, and let the blade do the work. After an hour I had managed a few clean swathes.

She told a story at this point about the mower she once beat. In a village competition, a man with a petrol strimmer challenged her to cut a strip of meadow twenty metres long, and she finished eleven minutes behind him with a tidier edge and, she added, a clear conscience.

Odalys explained the case for the scythe with real passion. It is silent, she said, so that a mower can hear birds while working; it uses no fuel; it does not throw stones; it cuts the grass cleanly rather than tearing it, so that the plant recovers faster; and it leaves the grass in rows, which makes raking easy. She added that there is a physical benefit: a whole day's mowing works the shoulders, back and legs, and if one is doing it right, it feels like a slow dance, not labour. She herself is fifty-eight and has never had a back problem. I noted the last claim with hope.

By noon the group of eleven had cleared a rectangle about the size of a tennis court. I learned to whet the blade with quick strokes, a sound like a small bell, and to check the edge by feeling it with a thumbnail across, never along. At lunch Odalys told us she could mow an acre in a day, a claim we found hard to believe until we watched her cut in the afternoon, walking steadily down a line of long grass, the blade hissing and every stem falling in a perfect row. The grass smelled of summer, and skylarks sang overhead. I bought a second-hand scythe from her for eighty pounds, along with a whetstone, a small hammer and a folding anvil. On the bus home I held the blade wrapped in a sack between my knees, and the man across the aisle asked, without a trace of humour, whether I was planning to reap. On Sunday morning I mowed a strip three metres long behind the flats in the dew, and a neighbour leaned out of a second-floor casement to ask what the lovely sound was.

Bird ringing morning at the estuary hide, notes from the studio's nature day. Ilse's brother-in-law volunteers with the Severn Mouth Ringing Group, a licensed team that catches, measures and rings wild birds to study migration, and he found the studio a morning at the group's autumn station. Six of us went, on a Saturday at the start of October, meeting at the car park by the sea wall at a quarter to six, in the dark, wearing every warm garment we owned.

The lead ringer was a woman named Henrietta Sowande, a wildlife biologist by trade and a bird ringer for thirty-one years. She holds a licence from the national ringing scheme, which is granted only after a long apprenticeship, and she explained the purpose of it while we walked along the sea wall with torches. Every ring carries a tiny unique number, and when a ringed bird is caught again, or found dead, the number reveals where it has been and how long it lived. A willow warbler ringed on this marsh has been recovered in Ghana; a sedge warbler, in Spain; and one oystercatcher had reached the age of thirty-four.

The station consisted of a row of fine nylon nets, called mist nets, strung between poles along a line of reeds and scrub. A mist net is almost invisible, a soft pocket of mesh that holds a bird gently without harming it, and it must be checked every twenty minutes, because a bird left too long can become stressed or cold. The nets are closed altogether in rain or high wind. Henrietta showed us how to walk to a net, look for the dark shape of a bird in the mesh, and lift out the bird by working it free from the feet up, using only fingertips. She would not let us touch anything on the first round.

The first bird of the morning was a blue tit, small and cross, which she extracted in under a minute and dropped into a cotton bag to calm it. Back at the ringing hut, a shed with a single bench and a heater, she took it out, held it between two fingers in what is called the ringer's grip, and fitted a tiny aluminium ring around its leg with special pliers. She measured the length of the wing with a steel ruler, weighed the bird in a cone on a balance, read its fat score by blowing gently on the belly feathers, and checked the moult of its wings. Then she opened her hand, and it flew away with a shriek of what sounded like indignation. The whole process took perhaps two minutes.

The morning was busy. By half past eight we had processed thirty-six birds: goldcrests, a wren, two dunnocks, a greenfinch, three chiffchaffs, and a great tit that bit Colm on the thumb and drew blood. Henrietta let us record the data on printed sheets, and I was entrusted with the pencil. She taught me the shorthand for age and sex, based on the wing feathers. A young bird has pale fringes on the coverts; an adult has a distinct moult limit; and a male reed bunting can be told from a female by the colour of the head. I made mistakes, and she corrected them without fuss.

The highlight came at nine, when Sami, walking the nets, called out, hush, come and see. In the bottom of the far net was a bird about the size of a small pigeon, streaked brown and cream with a striking barred tail. It was a sparrowhawk, and it had caught a chaffinch in the mesh and was now itself tangled. Henrietta, in her thick leather gloves, freed it swiftly, holding it firmly with its talons pointing away. She ringed it, a female weighing 262 grams, and then, prior to releasing it, held it up so that each of us could see the yellow eyes and the fierce look. It flew off low over the reeds like an arrow.

By ten the sun had cleared the mist and the birds were wary. We took down the nets, folded them into bags, and sat on the sea wall with tea and a packet of digestive biscuits. Henrietta gave us the total for the morning, sixty-one birds of fourteen species, and explained that the group does the same thing every Saturday in autumn, and that over the years the totals had changed. Fewer willow warblers, more chiffchaffs, a steady decline in the birds that winter in Africa. She thinks the marsh is drying out slightly, and she shows the data at the county bird club every winter.

She also told us a story that I will repeat. In 2011 the group caught a bird with a ring that had been fitted in Latvia. It was a bluethroat, a small robin-like bird with a bright blue bib, and it had stopped for a few days on the marsh on its way south. To Henrietta it was the equivalent of receiving a postcard from a stranger, and the entry for the ring is still framed on the wall of the hut.

Blake has asked whether the studio could sponsor a set of new nets, which cost about 340 pounds, and Ilse agreed to raise it at the next community budget review. We also took a photograph of the whole party on the sea wall, and Henrietta signed a card for each of us with the name of the bird we had ringed together. Mine says, blue tit, adult female, 11.2 grams.

Woodturning evening class, six weeks, notes by Blake. In the spring I bought a small lathe at a farm auction for forty pounds, mostly because it was so beautifully made, a cast-iron machine from the nineteen-fifties with a foot pedal that no longer worked, and it stood in my garage for four months doing nothing. Then a colleague mentioned that the adult education college on Marlow Road runs an evening course in turning, and I signed up, half in the hope of learning to make the lathe useful.

The class met on Wednesdays from seven to nine in a workshop that smelled of pine resin and machine oil. There were ten of us at ten lathes, a mix of retirees, a young apprentice electrician and a woman who wanted to make a rolling pin for her aunt. The tutor was a small, precise man in his sixties called Mr Ishikawa, who had spent thirty years making furniture for a firm in High Wycombe and now taught turning for pleasure. His first words were about the dangers. Long hair tied back, no loose sleeves, no rings, no gloves, because a glove can snag on the spinning wood and draw the hand in. He showed us the emergency stop button on each machine, and said that if we ever used it, we should tell him afterwards without embarrassment.

Week one was about the tools. A turner's kit is a small set of long-handled chisels, each with a different job: the roughing gouge, which takes a square block round; the spindle gouge, for coves and beads; the skew chisel, for smooth finishing cuts; the parting tool, which cuts a narrow groove; and the bowl gouge, for hollowing. We were told to hold each tool firmly on the rest, with the bevel against the wood, and to let the wood come to the tool rather than pushing. Mr Ishikawa demonstrated by taking a plain square of ash and turning it into a cylinder in about three minutes, with a fine spray of shavings arcing behind him.

My first attempt was a disaster. The block was mounted between centres, and I held the roughing gouge at too steep an angle, and the tool caught, and the wood leapt out of the lathe and struck the ceiling. Nobody was hurt, but the whole class was silent for a moment, and then Mr Ishikawa said, lightly, that was the most instructive thing that could have happened, and asked me to tell everyone what I had done wrong. I did. He nodded and gave me another block.

By week two I was making passable cylinders, and in week three he introduced us to the first project, a small mallet, with a round head and a handle turned from a single piece of beech. The trick, he said, was to mark the tool rest with a pencil to show where to cut. I made a handle that was too thin at the middle, and discovered that a thin handle vibrates and buzzes. I was pleased, however, by a bead I turned near the end, a small half-round moulding that caught the light.

Week four was bowls, the reason most people had come. A bowl is turned from a disc of wood held on a faceplate, first shaping the outside and then hollowing the inside, and the risk is much greater because the wood is not supported at both ends. Mr Ishikawa spent the whole lesson watching over us, in the manner of a lifeguard. I used a blank of sycamore, about twenty centimetres across, and shaped a curve on the outside that I liked. Then I began to hollow, taking thin, controlled cuts, and felt the wood peel out in long curling ribbons. The bowl was finished, in the end, at about five millimetres thick, and I sanded it through five grades of paper, from 80 up to 400.

The finishing was the part that surprised me. Mr Ishikawa showed us how to burnish the surface with a handful of the wood's own shavings, which polishes it to a soft shine, and then to apply a thin coat of oil, wiping off the excess with a cloth. When I lifted the bowl to the light, the grain shone like water. I put it on the shelf at home, and my mother, who visited on Sunday, picked it up and asked me where I had bought it.

In week five we made a pair of candlesticks by turning two pieces on a pin chuck, and in week six the class made a top, a spinning toy, which everyone raced across the workshop floor. Mr Ishikawa gave each of us a certificate, and a piece of advice: buy a good set of chisels and a small grinder, and sharpen often, since a dull tool tears the wood. I have since bought a six-piece set for 96 pounds and am working on a fruit bowl.

The old lathe, which I have now repaired, has a new belt and a working pedal. I made a wooden handle for it out of walnut, and it purrs. My first project is a set of four goblets, and I have a plan for a small stool.

Hedge-laying day, a team report from the Chiltern foothills. The studio's community group has adopted a rural volunteering day each year, and this year Deepa proposed a hedge-laying course run by a local rural skills charity, the Wychwood Landscape Trust. It was held on a cold, bright Saturday in January, at a farm north of Thame, in a field where a hedge of hawthorn and hazel had grown gappy and tall. There were fourteen volunteers from three companies, and our instructor was a lean man in his fifties named Callum Yeboah, who had laid hedges in eleven counties and whose thumbs were scarred from fifteen years of billhooks.

The point of laying a hedge, he explained at the gate, is to renew it. An overgrown hedge is thin at the bottom and leafy at the top, and gaps open where the stems have grown apart. If you cut it back hard to stumps, it will regrow, but it takes years to become stock-proof. Laying is the older and better method. Each stem, called a pleacher, is cut part-way through near the base and bent over to lie almost horizontally, still attached to its root, so that it continues to grow, sending up new shoots from the cut, and making a dense living barrier. A well-laid hedge can keep sheep in for thirty years.

He then demonstrated the regional style, called the Midland bullock, which uses vertical stakes, called stakes or uprights, driven into the line at intervals of about a metre, and a binding of hazel rods woven along the top. The pleachers are laid at about thirty degrees, in the same direction as the slope, and the whole hedge looks like a long, dense woven braid at the end. Callum stood a hazel rod on end and swung it to show how flexible the wood is when it is green. He said that ash and hawthorn are best, hazel and field maple are good, and that elder is useless, since it snaps.

We began with safety and tools. Each of us was given a pair of thick leather gauntlets, a hard hat and eye protection, and a billhook, a heavy curved blade with a wooden handle, and Callum walked round tightening the handles. The rule with a billhook, he said, is to cut away from the body, with the free hand behind the blade, and never to strike downward when the wood is close to the leg. Then he took us to the first stretch of hedge, about twenty metres, and marked with a spray can where the stakes should go.

The first task was to clear the ground. We trimmed off the side growth with slashing strokes, and pulled out brambles and dead wood, and Callum showed us how to save the straight hazel stems for binding and stakes. Colm found a rusted horseshoe in the ditch, and Yusuf found a dead mole, and we put both on the fence post as a tribute. By eleven the tangle had become a line of bare stems, looking oddly lonely, and Callum said this was the moment when everybody's confidence drops.

Cutting the pleachers is the delicate work. The idea is to make a slanting cut down the stem, about two-thirds of the way through, close to the ground, so that a thin strip of bark and sapwood remains to carry the sap. Callum called it a pleach. Too shallow, and the stem will not bend; too deep, and it will snap. He showed us the sound of a good cut, a soft crack, and the feel, a slight give. I broke two in a row, and he came over and told me that he broke a dozen in his first week, and that every one is a lesson.

We laid the pleachers along the line, each overlapping the last, and drove the stakes in with a heavy wooden mallet, Meera swinging with a determination that alarmed the crows. Then came the binding, the weaving of long hazel rods in and out of the stakes along the top in a rope-like pattern, which locks everything in place. It is like plaiting, Deepa said, and she was the fastest. By half past two, the first ten metres stood: a low, neat, tightly woven hedge, with bare stems slanting at an angle and the new binders pale against the dark.

Lunch was baked potatoes with chilli and a large iron pot of tea, on straw bales in the lee of a barn. The farmer, Mrs Bhattacharya, told us that she had inherited the hedge from her father, who laid it in 1974, and that the last time it was done, there were partridges. She hoped they might come back. She also said that a well-laid hedge is worth about twelve pounds a metre in grants from the countryside scheme, and that the labour would have cost her three times as much.

In the afternoon we finished the twenty metres. Callum walked slowly along the line, testing each stake, and lifted the whole hedge with one hand to prove its strength. He said it would leaf in April, that within three years the stems would send up thick new growth, and that after ten years a person would not know it had been touched. We had laid, by his count, twenty-two metres in one day, which was three times what a beginner team usually manages.

One of the younger volunteers, a sixth-former named Tobiah on a work experience week, asked Callum why anyone bothered with all this when a flail cutter on a tractor could trim a hedge in ten minutes. Callum stopped, wiped his hands on his trousers and gave an answer that I wrote down that evening. A machine, he said, cuts the hedge into a box, and a box has no bottom and no berries, because the flail takes the flowers off until they set. A laid hedge is a home. In one long hedge, he said, there may be sixty species of bird, thirty of them nesting, and hedgehogs, dormice and bats along the base, and the local dormouse survey found two nests in a hedge he had laid in 1998. He added, with a small smile, that he did not dislike tractors, only the people who use them badly.

He also told us about the old hedge-laying competitions, which are held every winter in the shires and where the judges walk the line with a measuring stick. Marks are given for the angle of the pleachers, the straightness of the line, the tightness of the binding and the neatness of the cuts. Callum has won the county cup three times, and he keeps the latest, a silver quaich, on the dashboard of his van. Colm asked how the judges could tell a good cut from a bad one, and Callum said that a good cut is clean and slopes away so the rain runs off, and that a bad one is ragged and holds water and rots. He said he could recognise the work of his old teacher, a man named Gideon, from a hundred metres away.

A final note on the practical side. The trust charged 35 pounds per person, which Blake paid from the community budget. The billhooks, gloves and hard hats were supplied, and the studio has been asked to return in autumn for a second stretch. Avery is arranging a rota, and we have discussed making a small display for the studio with a photograph of the hedge from start to finish, and the horseshoe.

Model railway exhibition diary, a weekend at the Eastfield Hall show. My uncle Ferdinand has built the same layout in his attic for thirty-six years, a fictional branch line called the Little Barrowdale, in a scale of one to seventy-six, and this year, for the first time, he agreed to show it at a public exhibition. He asked me to help transport it, set it up and operate it for two days, and I said yes without asking what that involved. This is what it involved.

The layout, in its present form, is a rectangle of four boards, each two metres long and a metre wide, which bolt together to form a single scene of about four by two metres. On it stand a country terminus with a stone station, a goods yard, a small engine shed, a river with a viaduct of seven arches, a village of thirty-odd buildings, and a mountainside of plaster and painted netting where the line vanishes into a tunnel. There are eleven locomotives and about sixty items of rolling stock, most of them scratch-built from brass, and every one has a name in tiny gold script.

Loading day was Friday. My uncle had decided that the boards would fit into a hired van, but forgot to take account of the viaduct, which is detachable but fragile, and it needed its own padded crate. We packed everything in blankets, foam and bubble wrap, and carried each board down the attic stairs with the tension of a bomb disposal team. It took four of us three hours. The van travelled the forty miles to Eastfield at twenty-five miles an hour, which the driver, a cousin, described as the most miserable drive of his life.

The exhibition took place in the Eastfield Town Hall, in a space shared with forty-one other layouts, from tiny scenes the size of a tea tray to a sprawling American mainline that took up half a wall. Ferdinand's was in the north corner, between a Swiss mountain railway and a model of a gasworks that emitted a small puff of smoke every two minutes. We set up on Friday evening by bolting the boards together, levelling them with shims, connecting the electrics through a single control panel, and testing the track with a small locomotive that ran perfectly on the first try, to our surprise.

Saturday opened at ten with a queue in the rain. I stood behind the layout, at the operator's side, with a controller in each hand, and watched the visitors. There were families with small children who pressed their noses against the boards, retired men who asked pointed questions about the gauge of the track, and one gaunt, silent man who stood for an hour, watching each train arrive and depart, and then said, to nobody, that the signalling was wrong. Ferdinand went across and they had a long, happy conversation about the block system.

Operating the layout was more difficult than I had imagined. My uncle runs it to a fixed schedule of nineteen trains, which he keeps on a card, and each has to leave the terminus, cross the viaduct, pass through the tunnel and return, and the goods train has to shunt wagons in the yard while the passenger service is waiting. If two trains meet, or if one stalls in the tunnel, it means reaching in from the back with a long-handled tool, which I did once and knocked a chimney off the village bakery. Ferdinand said he would repair it that evening and that in thirty-six years he had knocked off the same chimney eleven times.

The children were the best part. A girl of about six asked to press the button that sounds the whistle, and did so twenty times in a row. A boy asked why there were no people on the platform, and Ferdinand answered that the passengers were all inside, having tea. One of the older visitors leaned over the boards and said, in a soft voice, that the model reminded him of a branch line in Wales that had been closed in 1963, and that he had been a fireman on it. He stayed for a whole hour and named every locomotive.

On Sunday morning, the judges came round for the annual prize, and paused at our layout for about ten minutes. They asked how the trees were made, and Ferdinand said, from wire and lichen, and showed a pot. They asked about the weathering of the track, and he said he uses a mixture of powdered chalk and old tea. They asked about the tunnel, and he confessed that it is a hollow-cored cardboard tube. The award, announced at four, went to a Swiss layout, but ours was given a commendation for craftsmanship, a certificate that Ferdinand has hung, after a long pause, over the mantelpiece.

A few words about the man behind it, since the weekend taught me things about my uncle I had not known. Ferdinand was a ticket inspector on the railways for forty years, and began the layout in 1988 the year after his wife died, because, he said, it gave him a small world in which everything ran on time. He built the first locomotive from a kit and the last from a sheet of brass and a set of drawings he made himself. His handwriting is on every label under the boards: the date each building was finished, the paint used, and a small note in the corner such as, chimney redone, again. Visitors who peered underneath were often more interested in these labels than in the trains.

On Saturday evening after the hall closed we ate fish and chips on the steps of the town hall, in the last of the rain, and he told me how he had once refused a bid of eight thousand pounds for the layout from a collector in Zurich. It was not for sale, he said, in the tone of a man discussing a member of the family. I asked what would happen to it after him, and he said that he had left it to me in his will. I did not know what to say, and stood on the steps with a vinegary chip in my hand, and he changed the subject to the price of brass.

Lessons, for anyone doing it again. Bring a spare motor, spare fuses, a can of contact cleaner, a bag of assorted screws and two extension leads. Set up a low stool for the operator, because standing for eight hours will destroy a person. Put a small notice on the front with the name and history of the layout, because visitors ask. And bring sandwiches, because the exhibition's own catering consisted of one urn and a tray of flapjacks.

We took down the layout on Sunday evening, and the boards went back into the van in half the time it took to unload them, because we were tired and had learned the manoeuvre. At Ferdinand's house, we set them against the wall, and he brewed a pot of tea. He says he is now thinking about a bigger layout, with a second station, and I have volunteered to help with the wiring, on condition that he draws a diagram.

Visit to the tide mill at Shepperton Quay, a working-day report. The studio's operations lead, Ilse, has a friend who is a trustee of the Shepperton Tide Mill Trust, and on a warm Friday in May the studio closed for half a day so that fourteen of us could visit the mill, watch a milling session and stay to lunch. The mill is a big white weatherboarded building on the edge of a tidal creek, with a great brick pond behind it, and it has been grinding grain, on and off, since the year 1745.

We were met by the head miller, a tall, sunburnt woman named Ottilie Sesay, who wore a floury apron and had a small brown dog called Bran that followed her everywhere. She explained the principle at the water's edge. When the tide comes in, it fills a large pond behind a sluice gate, held shut by the pressure of the rising water. At high tide the gate is closed and the pond is full. As the tide falls away, the water in the pond is released through a channel, and it turns a wheel. The mill therefore works for about four hours on either side of low tide, twice a day, and Ottilie's working day is set by the moon, not the clock.

Inside, the mill is a tall, dim, warm space that smells of dust and warm grain. There are three floors, and everything is made of oak and elm and iron. The wheel is on the lower floor, an undershot wheel of about four metres in diameter, its paddles dripping and creaking. From it a great vertical shaft rises through the floors, and on the upper floor it drives two pairs of millstones, each about a metre and a half across, made of French burr stone and mounted one above the other. The lower stone turns while the upper one is stationary, and the grain is fed between them from a hopper through a wooden shoe that shakes it down in a steady trickle.

Ottilie showed us the art of dressing the stones, which means cutting a pattern of shallow grooves in the surface to direct the flour outward. Every few weeks she lifts the runner stone with a crane and re-cuts the furrows with a steel pick called a mill bill. She let Sami try, and he chipped a groove that made her raise her eyebrows and say, gently, that it was too deep. A good millstone, she said, lasts for twenty or thirty years, and this pair had been cut in 1889.

Then we went upstairs to watch the grain being fed in. It was a batch of soft wheat from a farm three miles inland, about two hundred kilos in sacks, and she poured it into the hopper with a wooden scoop. Within minutes there was a rumbling sound and a fine warm flour began to fall into a wooden bin below. She caught some in her palm and showed us the texture: soft, creamy, and warm to the touch. The stones grind so slowly, she said, that the flour never overheats, which is why it keeps its flavour.

A fascinating point was the sound. A working mill makes a particular hum, and the miller listens to it as one listens to an engine. If the hum rises to a whine, the stones are running dry. If it drops to a groan, the feed is too fast. Ottilie could tell from the floor below whether the stones were exactly a hair's width apart, and she said that in the old days a miller went deaf in old age but never lost this sense, because it lived in the feet.

The mill also has a small museum on the top floor, and Ottilie let us climb the ladder to the loft to see the machinery of the sack hoist, a rope and pulley worked by a lever that raises a full sack of grain from the ground floor in about fifteen seconds. Deepa noted that it was, in effect, the oldest lift in the building. A wall of the loft is covered in pencil marks, the initials and dates of millers over two centuries, and Ottilie showed us the earliest, a scratched H.W. 1751.

We ate lunch in the mill's small tea shed, a plate of cold ham, pickles and rolls made that morning with the mill's own flour. The trustee, a man named Bertrand Nwosu, told us the history: the mill was almost demolished in 1970, but was saved by a group of local people who raised 40,000 pounds, and today it produces about eleven tonnes of flour a year, sold at farmers' markets and to three local bakeries. He said the trust would like to install a small turbine to generate electricity, and to make a visitor gallery on the upper floor.

At two o'clock the tide turned and the sluice was closed. We stood on the quay in the sun and watched the water begin to creep back across the mud, bringing with it a line of seaweed and a heron. Ottilie said that, for her, the end of the milling day was the best part, because the whole building went quiet, like a ship coming to rest. Bran went to sleep in a patch of sunlight on the flagstones.

The studio has since decided to buy twenty kilos of the mill's wholemeal flour as gifts at the end of the year, and Ilse has proposed an annual donation of 250 pounds, which Blake has approved. I bought a small bag of stoneground flour and a tea towel, and on Sunday tried to bake with it and made a solid, delicious brick.

Kite festival at Sandybank, a Sunday with Noor's cousins. My sister's children, Elias, aged nine, and Zora, aged six, have talked about nothing else since they saw a poster at the library: a kite festival on the beach at Sandybank, with a competition for the best home-made kite, and a prize of thirty pounds for the child with the highest flyer. We spent the previous Saturday in my sister's shed building two kites from thin bamboo canes, a roll of bin bags and a ball of twine.

The design was a simple diamond. Two canes, one longer than the other, tied at a cross with twine, and a frame of string stretched round the outside. We cut the plastic to shape with a margin, folded it over the string and taped it down, and attached a tail of knotted ribbon that Zora had cut from an old dress. The bridle, the loop of string to which the flying line is attached, needs to be fixed at the right point, which we found by holding the kite up and seeing where it balanced. Elias insisted on painting a shark on his, in green paint that would not dry, and Zora drew a lot of hearts.

The beach was crowded when we arrived at ten. The wind, a steady breeze from the south-west at about twelve miles an hour, was perfect, and the sky was full of kites: box kites, delta kites, a huge blow-up octopus, a dragon thirty metres long, and a team from a club in Blackpool flying a matched set of sports kites in a routine, swooping and looping, on four lines. It was as loud as a fair, with a crackling of plastic and cries of children.

Elias's shark went up at once. He held the reel and I stood behind him and released the kite gently, with a small run into the wind, and it climbed with a smooth tug until it was a small green dot high above the beach. Zora's kite was less fortunate. It spun twice and crashed into the sand, and she wept until I found a strip of gaffer tape, mended the frame and lengthened the tail. The second flight took it up to about thirty metres, where it swung from side to side and made her shriek with joy.

The competition was judged at noon by a woman from the organising committee, who walked among the children with a clipboard. The measure of height was a guess, based on the length of line paid out, and the kites were also judged for looks. Elias's shark was awarded a rosette for the most original design, and Zora's heart kite a certificate for effort. The thirty-pound prize for the highest flyer went to a girl of about twelve who had a huge line and a delta kite, and who flew it, as far as I could tell, beyond the limits of visibility.

We spent the rest of the day on the sand, eating chips from a paper cone, and Elias fell asleep in the car on the drive home with the rosette pinned to his jumper. There was one small crisis. Around one o'clock the wind veered and gusted, and Elias's shark, at the end of its line, began to dive and swing so violently that he could no longer hold it. It tore the reel out of his hands and trailed across the sand, a hundred metres of twine flapping behind it, and half a dozen strangers, without a word, ran after it and one of them, a very large man in a red anorak, brought it down with a diving tackle. The shark was undamaged and the man got a round of applause.

I learned that the best kite is not the fanciest but the one with the balance right, and I promised the children another building day next month.

Rehearsal notes for the community choir's midwinter concert, taken by Avery as a new bass. The studio has a small choir, formed by Deepa two years ago, which meets on Tuesday lunchtimes in the church hall opposite the studio, and this year we were invited to join the Riverside Community Choir for its annual midwinter concert at the parish church. About twenty of the choir's regular singers would be joined by eleven of us for a programme of seasonal music. This is a record of the last three rehearsals ahead of the concert.

The conductor, Mr Lindgren-Okafor, is a professional choral director in his forties who comes to the hall on Thursday evenings from the cathedral school, where he teaches. He has an unusual habit of giving each rehearsal a single theme, and the first of the three was breathing. He had us stand with our feet apart and hands on our ribs, and breathe in through the nose for four counts, out for eight, and then hold a single note on a hiss for as long as we could. I managed twenty-three seconds, and Sami managed eleven.

The programme had eight pieces. There was a Gaudete arrangement in Latin, a sixteenth-century carol; a setting of a poem about snow by a living English composer; a lullaby for two parts; a spiritual that had the tenors and basses in a call-and-response pattern; and a fast, rhythmic piece from South Africa, sung in Zulu, which everyone had trouble with. We were also to sing a well-known carol with the audience, and a final piece called The Turning of the Year, which the choir commissioned in 2019.

The Zulu piece caused the most difficulty. The pronunciation of the clicks was beyond the studio's members, but a choir member, Nomvula, who is from Durban, took the tenors aside for twenty minutes and showed them how to shape the consonants with the tongue against the roof of the mouth. It was chaotic and hilarious, and at the end of it Yusuf could produce a decent click. Mr Lindgren-Okafor said he had never heard a piece improve so quickly, and hummed the melody down the corridor.

The second rehearsal was about dynamics, the loud and soft of the music. Each piece has a shape, he said: a start, a swell, a peak and a quiet resolution, and a choir that sings at one volume is a machine. He had us practise a crescendo over eight bars, from a whisper to a full shout, and every one of us went too early, so that the peak came at bar five. We tried it again with the score marked in pencil, and by the fifth attempt it worked.

On the last rehearsal, a week ahead of the concert, we practised in the church itself, with its long reverberation of nearly five seconds. Mr Lindgren-Okafor said that in such a space, one must sing slower and cut off every note more crisply, and that a choir must listen for its own echo. Then he arranged us in three rows on the chancel steps, the tenors on the left and the sopranos in the middle, and told us that the rows were a promise: we stood for each other. I was next to a retired postman called Barnabas, who sings bass in a voice like a cellar door.

Between the second and third rehearsals there was a small crisis about the solo in the lullaby. The soprano who was to sing it, Marguerite from the studio's finance side, developed a cough and was ordered by her doctor to rest her voice for ten days, and Mr Lindgren-Okafor had to find a replacement with a week to spare. He asked for volunteers, and there was a long silence in the hall. Then a very quiet alto named Philomena, who is seventy-four and had never sung alone in public, raised a hand. She rehearsed it three times on the Tuesday, once for the conductor at his piano at home, and on the Thursday sang it to the whole choir. There was not a sound in the hall for a moment after the last note, and then the sopranos began to cry.

There was also an argument about clothes. The choir's tradition is black trousers or skirts with a red scarf, and the studio members had all forgotten to buy a scarf in the required shade. Deepa solved this by finding a bolt of red cloth at a market stall and cutting it into eleven equal strips, which we hemmed on a Sunday evening in the studio after everyone else had gone home.

The concert was on the second Saturday of December, at seven. There were 260 people in the church, in scarves and coats, and candles along the stone sills. The choir sang all eight pieces in order, and the Zulu song was received with a burst of clapping that lasted almost a minute. The collection at the door raised 1,105 pounds for the local food bank. Afterwards there was mulled apple juice and mince pies in the vestry, and Mr Lindgren-Okafor, glowing, invited all the studio singers to join for the spring term.

Potholing trip diary, a Saturday underground in the Ingleborough caves. I had been afraid of caves since a school trip to a show cave, when the guide switched off the lights for a demonstration of darkness and I had a small, unexpected panic. Thirty years later, when my brother-in-law Tomasz proposed a beginners' caving day, I said yes to prove something to myself. We booked with a local outdoor centre, and met on a wet morning in a car park near Clapham, in the hills of North Yorkshire.

Our guide was a woman called Bronwen Achterberg, a former cave rescue volunteer, with a low, steady voice and a habit of counting heads. She handed out the kit: a boiler suit, a helmet with a lamp and a spare lamp taped to the side, rubber boots, knee pads, and gloves. She explained that the rule of caving is to keep the group together, never to leave anyone at the back, and that each person carries three sources of light. We were eight: Tomasz and me, two students from Sheffield, a married couple in their forties from Hull, and a retired dentist who had been meaning to do it for years.

The walk to the cave entrance took forty minutes across wet grass and limestone pavement, a grey landscape of flat slabs cut by deep cracks called grikes. Rain had fallen for three days, and Bronwen checked the level of the stream at the mouth of the cave with her hand, and said it was a little high but safe, and that if the weather turned we would leave at once. She said that water is the great danger in a cave, since a flood can fill a passage in minutes, and that the cave is not a place to be brave.

The first stretch was a crawl. We entered on hands and knees through a low slot into a stream passage, and the temperature dropped at once, to about eight degrees. Water ran along the floor, a hand deep, and soaked through the boiler suit within a minute. Bronwen went first, then the students, then me, and Tomasz came last. My heart was banging. The passage was about the height of a low stool and lit only by our lamps, and I found that if I concentrated on the heels of the person in front, I forgot to be afraid.

After about a hundred metres, the passage opened into a chamber the size of a small church. Our lamps did not reach the roof. Bronwen told us to switch them off, and I gritted my teeth. It was the darkest dark I have ever known, without even the ghost of a shape, and the sound of dripping water seemed to swell. Then, after a full minute, I discovered that I was not panicking, and it felt almost peaceful, and a small laugh escaped from someone, and we turned the lamps back on.

The next hour brought a series of obstacles. There was a squeeze, a narrow, twisting gap that had to be passed sideways, one arm ahead, breathing out to get through; the retired dentist stuck, gently, and was talked out by Bronwen with a calm and cheerful patter. There was a short climb up a flowstone slope, a frozen waterfall of calcite, using ledges and a fixed rope. And there was a section called the Canal, where the passage was a metre high and half full of water, and we had to lie on our backs with our noses just above the surface and wriggle along like seals. I shrieked once, and later laughed about it.

At the far end was a chamber called the Cathedral, and it was worth the journey. The ceiling soared away in darkness, and along one wall hung a curtain of stalactites, pale and translucent, glistening in our lamps. A tall stalagmite, a pillar as thick as a person, stood in the centre. Bronwen explained that each of them grows about a centimetre every hundred years, and that the tallest was probably twelve thousand years old, since the last ice age. She asked us not to touch it, because the oil in a fingertip stops the growth.

We ate lunch there, sitting on rocks in a cluster, with hot tea from a flask and a chocolate bar each. The talk was quiet. The married couple from Hull said that they had considered this a gamble, and that now they wanted to do it every month. The students had photographed everything with a waterproof camera and were looking at the screen with delight. Tomasz said, in the whisper that people use in churches, that this was the most beautiful place he had ever been.

The return trip was harder because we were cold and tired, and the water had risen by a few centimetres. Bronwen led us out slowly, counting heads at each junction. At the Canal she made us go through in pairs, one behind the other, to keep us company. At last, after four hours underground, I saw the grey blur of daylight at the far end of the passage and crawled out into a fine drizzle, which felt like a blessing.

There was a moment near the middle of the day that I want to record more carefully. In the Cathedral, prior to lunch, Bronwen asked whether anyone would like to sit alone for five minutes with the lamps off, while the rest of us went a short distance down the passage, always within calling distance. Nobody spoke. Then, to my own surprise, I said I would. The group moved away, their voices growing faint, and I was left on a rock in a dark that had no edges. I heard the water dripping, one drop every four or five seconds, each with its own small echo. I found that my breathing had slowed, and that there was no one to be afraid in front of. When Bronwen's lamp reappeared I felt almost sorry.

Bronwen told us on the way out about the rescue side of her work. In her eleven years with the cave rescue team she has been called out about forty times, most often to a caver with a broken ankle or one whose lights have failed, and once to a group of schoolboys who had been trapped by a flood. A stretcher carry out of a cave can take fourteen hours and needs fifty people. That is the reason, she said, for the rules of the day, and she wanted us to hold on to them if we ever went caving again without her.

In the car park we took off the boiler suits and steamed like horses. Bronwen gave each of us a badge that read I Survived, and told us that the cave had been explored since 1912 and had eleven kilometres of passage. The cost of the day was 68 pounds. I drove home with the heater on and a feeling of triumph, as though something that had been folded up inside me for thirty years had opened. Tomasz and I have booked a second trip in November, to a deeper cave, with a vertical pitch of ten metres and a ladder.
